Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 16, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', and Jabir. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas and from Abu al-Zubayr.

Al-Nahhas narrated through the chain of Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Nahl was revealed in Mecca except for its last three verses, which were revealed between Mecca and Medina, on the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) return from Uhud." It was said that these are His words: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the same as that with which you were afflicted﴾ (16:126), and His words: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah﴾ (16:127), concerning the mutilation of Hamzah and the dead of Uhud, and His words: ﴿Then indeed, your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ (16:110). It was said that the third is: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾ up to His words: ﴿for the best of what they used to do﴾ (16:95–96).

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command upon whom He wills of His servants, [saying]: "Warn that there is no deity except Me, so fear Me."﴾ ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He created man from a sperm-drop; then at once he is an open adversary.﴾ ﴿And the cattle He created for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back [in the evening] and when you send them out [to pasture].﴾ ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And [He created] the horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment. And He creates that which you do not know.﴾ ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and among [the ways] is one that deviates. And if He had willed, He would have guided you all.﴾

His words ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ mean: His punishment upon the polytheists. A group of exegetes said: it means the Resurrection.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is what He promised them of recompense for their disbelief. He expressed the future by the form of the past to emphasize the certainty of its occurrence. It was also said that the intended meaning of "the command of Allah" is His judgment concerning that, and it has occurred and "has come." As for what was judged, it has not yet occurred, because He, glorified is He, decreed its occurrence at a specific time; so before that time arrives, it does not come into existence. It was also said that the intended meaning of its coming is the coming of (p. 772) its precursors and preliminaries.

His words ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ are a prohibition against seeking to hasten it, meaning: do not seek its presence before that time. The polytheists used to seek to hasten the punishment of Allah, as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You﴾ (8:32), up to the end of the verse. The meaning is: the command of Allah has drawn near, so do not seek to hasten it. Their seeking its hastening was by way of mockery, not in earnest. In forbidding them from seeking its hastening there is a rebuke of them.

His words ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ mean: He is far above and exalted above their association [of partners with Him], or above having any partner. Their association here is their seeking to hasten the punishment or the Hour as a mockery and denial, for this implies their description of Him, glorified is He, as one who is not able to do that, and that He is incapable of it. Incapacity and lack of power are attributes of created beings, not of the Creator; therefore this was an association [of partners with Him].

﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command﴾. Al-Mufaddal, from 'Asim, recited (tanzilu al-malaikatu), with the underlying form being (tatanazzalu), so the verb is attributed to the angels.

Al-A'mash recited (tunazzalu), in the passive voice.

Al-Ju'fi, from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited (nunazzilu), with the nun, and the subject is Allah, glorified is He.

The rest recited (yunazzilu al-malaikata), with the ya', except that Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr pronounce the nun with a sukun. The subject is Allah, glorified is He.

The connection of this sentence with what precedes it is that when he (ﷺ) informed them from Allah that His command had drawn near, and forbade them from seeking to hasten it, they doubted the way by which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew that. So He informed that he knew it by revelation, through the tongues of the messengers of Allah, glorified is He, from among His angels. "The Spirit" means revelation. A similar usage is: ﴿He sends down the Spirit from His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ (40:15). Revelation was called a "spirit" because it gives life to the hearts of the believers, for the Qur'an is among what is revealed, and it is to the religion what the spirit is to the body. It was also said that what is meant is the spirits of creatures. It was said that the Spirit is mercy, and it was said that it is guidance, because hearts are made alive by it just as bodies are made alive by spirits.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The Spirit is that in which there is life from Allah through guidance to His command."

Abu 'Ubayd said: "The Spirit here is Gabriel." On this view the (bi) in (bi al-ruh) means "with," and the (min) in (min amrihi) is explanatory, meaning: with things; or it begins [a phrase], meaning: beginning from His command; or it is a qualifier of the Spirit; or it is connected to (yunazzilu). The meaning of ﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ is: upon whomever He has singled out for that, namely the prophets.

His words ﴿that warn﴾: Al-Zajjaj said: "(an anzirū) [that warn] is a substitute for 'the Spirit,' meaning: He sends them down with (an anzirū), [saying] warn." And (an) is either explanatory, because the descent of revelation contains the meaning of speech, or it is the light form of the heavy (an), with an implied pronoun of the matter, meaning: indeed the matter is that I say to you, warn, meaning: inform the people ﴿that there is no deity except Me﴾, meaning: command them to monotheism of Me and inform them of that together with warning them, because warning contains fear and threat. The pronoun in (annahu) refers to the matter.

﴿So fear Me﴾: the address is to those who were seeking to hasten [the punishment], by way of iltifat (a shift from third person to second), and it is a warning to them against associating [partners] with Allah.

Then, when Allah, glorified is He, guided them to His monotheism, He mentioned the proofs of monotheism, saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, meaning: He brought them into existence in the state in which they are, in truth, meaning: as evidence of His power and His oneness. It was also said that what is meant by "truth" here is their perishing and cessation.

﴿Exalted﴾: Allah is exalted and sanctified above their association [of partners with Him], or above the partnership of that which they make a partner with Him.

Then, since the human species is the noblest of the kinds of lower created beings, He placed it first and singled it out for mention, saying: ﴿He created man﴾. "Man" is a name for the genus of this species, from a sperm-drop, a lifeless substance that comes out of a living being, namely semen. Then He moved him through stages until his form was complete, breathed the spirit into him, and brought him out from his mother's womb into this world, where he lived. Then, after his creation in this state, he becomes a "khasim," meaning one who is extremely contentious and argumentative. The meaning is that he is like one who disputes with Allah, glorified is He, regarding His power. "Mubin" means manifest and clear in contention. It was also said that he expresses clearly what he argues with of falsehood. "Mubin" is one who clearly expresses what is in his heart by his speech. A similar usage is His saying: ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a sperm-drop, and then at once he is an open adversary?﴾ (36:77).

Then He followed the mention of the creation of man with the creation of the cattle, because of the benefit they provide to this species. So the favor bestowed through them is more complete than favor bestowed through other things. He said: ﴿And the cattle He created for you﴾, and they are camels, cows, and sheep. Most often "na'am" and "an'am" are used for camels, but it is also used for the collective, and it is not used for sheep individually. Among the examples is the verse of Hassan:

"And there was never ceasing, among its meadows, a companion: camels and sheep."

Here he conjoined sheep (shā') with camels (na'am), and here (na'am) refers specifically to camels.

Al-Jawhari said: "Na'am" is the singular of "an'am," and this term is used most often for camels.

Then, after He informed that He created them for the children of Adam, He explained the benefit in them for them, saying: ﴿in them is warmth﴾. "Dif'" means warmth, and it is what one is warmed by from their wool, fleece, and hair. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial phrase (hal). "Manafi'" [benefits] is conjoined to "dif'," and these are their milk, riding, offspring, plowing with them, and the like.

It has been said that "dif'" means offspring and milk.

In al-Sihah (by al-Jawhari) it says: "Dif' is the offspring of camels and their milk, and whatever benefit is derived from them." Then he said: "Dif' is also warmth." On this basis, if "dif'" is taken in the first sense, then "benefits" must be interpreted as what is other than that, of what is benefited from them. If it is taken in the second sense, then interpreting "benefits" as what we have mentioned is clear. It was said that what is meant by "benefits" is offspring only, and it was said riding.

﴿And from them you eat﴾, meaning from their meat and fat. He singled out this benefit for mention even though it is included among the benefits, because it is the greatest of them. It was said He singled it out because the benefit from their meat and fat is one in which their very substance is consumed, unlike the other benefits in them. Placing the adverbial phrase, which indicates exclusivity, first, is to indicate that eating from them is the primary purpose, while other uses are rare.

﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾, meaning: for you in them, in addition to what has been mentioned, is beauty. "Jamal" is what one adorns oneself with and beautifies oneself with, and "jamal" is also beauty. The meaning here: for you in them is adornment and embellishment in the eyes of those who look upon them.

﴿when you bring them back [in the evening] and when you send them out [to pasture]﴾, meaning at these two times: the time of their return from their pastures, and the time of their being sent out to them. "Ruwah" is their return in the evening from pasture, and "sarah" is their going out to pasture in the morning. One says: "sarrahtu al-ibil usarriha sarhan wa suruhan," when you go out with them to the pasture in the morning. He placed the time of bringing back before the time of sending out, because their appearance at the time of bringing back is more beautiful, and their state is better, since in that condition they have obtained what they need of eating and drinking, so their bellies have grown large and their udders have swollen. He singled out these two times because they are the times when onlookers see them; for when they are settled in their enclosures, no one sees them, and when they are in their pastures, they are scattered and not gathered together, each one grazing in a different direction.

﴿And they carry your loads﴾. "Athqal" is the plural of "thiql," which is a traveler's baggage of food and other things, and it was called "thiql" because carrying it burdens a person. It was said that what is meant is their bodies.

﴿to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, meaning: you would not have been able to reach it, had there not been camels with you carrying your loads, except with great hardship to yourselves, because of its distance from you, and because of the lack of anything to carry what you must have on the journey.

Its apparent meaning encompasses every distant land without specification. It was said that what is meant by "land" is Mecca. It was said Yemen, Egypt, and Syria, because they are the trading places of the Arabs. "Shiqq al-anfus" means its hardship.

The majority recited it with a kasra on the shin (shiqq), and Abu Ja'far recited it with a fatha (shaqq).

Al-Jawhari said: "Al-shiqq is hardship, and from it is His saying: ﴿you could not have reached it except with great hardship to yourselves﴾." Abu 'Ubaydah related it with a fatha on the shin. Both have the same meaning. It is possible that the one with the fatha is a verbal noun from "shaqaqtu 'alayhi ashuqqu shaqqan" (I made it hard for him), and the one with the kasra means "half," as one says "akhadhtu shiqq al-shatah wa shaqqat al-shatah" (I took half of the sheep). In that case the meaning of the verse would be: you could not have reached it except by the loss of half of your souls from fatigue.

Allah, glorified is He, has bestowed His favor upon His servants by creating the cattle in general. Then He singled out camels for mention because of the blessing of carrying loads that is in them, not cows and sheep. The exception is from the most general of the general: meaning, you could not have reached it by anything except with great hardship to yourselves.

﴿And the horses, mules, and donkeys﴾ are in the accusative case, conjoined to "the cattle," meaning: He also created these three kinds for you. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited them all in the nominative case. The horse (khayl) was called "khayl" because of its strutting in its gait (ikhtiyal). The singular of "khayl" is "khail," like "da'in" is the singular of "da'n" (sheep). It was said it has no singular.

Then, Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for the creation of these three kinds, saying: ﴿that you may ride them﴾. This reason is based on the majority of their benefits, because benefiting from them in other than riding is known, such as loading them. The conjunction of "zinah" [adornment] to the position of ﴿that you may ride them﴾ is because it occupies the accusative position as a reason for their creation. He did not say "that you may adorn yourselves with them," so as to match "that you may ride them," because riding is an action of those addressed, while adornment is the action of the one who adorns, who is the Creator. The truth in this is that riding is what is considered in the intended purpose, unlike adornment, for people of lofty aspirations do not turn to it, because it produces vanity. So it is as if He, glorified is He, said: "I created them that you may ride them, and thereby ward off from yourselves the harm of exhaustion and hardship." As for adornment with them, it exists in reality, but it is not intended in itself.

And those who hold that the flesh of horses is forbidden have cited this verse, arguing that the causal clause "that you may ride them" indicates that they were created for this benefit and no other.

They said: This is supported by the singling out of these three kinds and their separation from the livestock (al-an'am), which indicates that they share a single ruling regarding the prohibition of eating.

They said: Had eating horses been permissible, mentioning it and bestowing favour through it would have been more fitting than mentioning riding, because it is of greater benefit. This was the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa and their companions, al-Awza'i, Mujahid, Abu 'Ubayd, and others.

The majority of jurists, traditionists and others held that the flesh of horses is lawful. The proponents of the first view have no proof from the causal clause "that you may ride them", because mentioning what is most common among its benefits does not exclude other benefits. Nor do we concede that eating is more beneficial than riding, such that it should be mentioned first and its mention should precede the mention of riding. Furthermore, if this verse indicated the prohibition of horses, it would also indicate the prohibition of domestic donkeys (al-humur al-ahliyyah), and then there would be no need to specify their prohibition at the time of Khaybar. We have already mentioned that this surah is Meccan.

The conclusion is that the sound evidences indicate the lawfulness of eating horse flesh. Even if we grant that this verse provides a basis for those who argue for prohibition, the established pure Sunnah would remove this possibility and repel this inference. We have clarified this question in our writings in a manner that the reader will not need anything beyond them. [Qur'an: "And He creates what you do not know."] That is, He creates what your knowledge does not encompass of the creatures, other than what is enumerated here. It was said: what is meant is the kinds of insects and creeping creatures at the bottom of the earth and in the sea that human beings have not seen and have not heard of. It was said: it is what Allah has prepared for His servants in Paradise and in Hell, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which has not occurred to the heart of any human being. It was said: it is the creation of the weevil in plants and the worm in fruits. It was said: a spring beneath the Throne. It was said: a river of light. It was said: a white earth. There is no justification for restricting the interpretation of this verse to one of these kinds, rather what is meant is that He, glory be to Him, creates what the servants have no knowledge of, so it includes everything whose knowledge does not encompass them. The expression here is in the present tense (yakhluqu) to evoke the image, because He, glory be to Him, has already created what the servants do not know of.

[Qur'an: "And upon Allah is the direction of the way."] The word qasd is a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle, so the meaning is: upon Allah is the one who directs toward the way, that is, the guidance of the one who aims at the straight path, in accordance with His binding promise and His abundant bounty. It was said that there is an elision of a noun, and the estimate is: upon Allah is the explanation of the direction of the way. The way (al-sabil) is Islam, and its explanation is through sending the messengers and establishing proofs and evidences. Qasd in the way is its being a conveyance to the desired goal, so the meaning is: upon Allah is the explanation of the path that conveys to the desired goal. [Qur'an: "And of it is one who deviates."] The pronoun in minha refers to al-sabil in the sense of al-tariq (the path), because it is both masculine and feminine. It was said it refers to it with an elided noun, meaning: and of the kind of the way is one who deviates, inclining away from the truth, turning aside from it, so he is not guided by it. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

And of the way is the deviating and the guided,
Straight of the path, and of it is one with a flaw.

It was said that "the way" is a metonymy for its traveller, and the meaning is: and of them is one who deviates from the path of truth, that is, turns aside from it, so he is not guided to it. It was said they are the people of diverse desires; it was said they are the people of disbelieving creeds. In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "and of you is one who deviates", and 'Ali also recited it thus.

[Qur'an: "Had He willed, He would have guided you all."] That is, had He willed to guide you all to the correct path and the true method, He would have done so. But He did not will it; rather His will, glory be to Him, required the showing of the way and the indicating of it. [Qur'an: "And We guided him to the two paths" (al-Balad 10).] As for conveying people to it in actuality, that would entail that there be no disbeliever among the servants, nor anyone among the Muslims who deserves the Fire. The divine will has required that some be believers and some be disbelievers, as the Qur'an has stated in more than one place. [p. 774]

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: When [the verse] "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were alarmed, until [the verse] "So do not seek to hasten it" was revealed, and they calmed down.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id al-Zuhd, and Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Bakr ibn Hafs that he said: When [the verse] "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, they stood up, then [the verse] "So do not seek to hasten it" was revealed.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated through al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "The command of Allah has come" that it is the emergence of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij that he said: When this verse "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, some hypocrites said to one another: This man claims that the command of Allah has come. So refrain from some of what you were doing until you see what is going to happen. When they saw that nothing descended, they said: We do not see that anything has descended. Then [the verse] "The reckoning of people has drawn near" (al-Anbiya 1) was revealed, and they said: This man claims likewise also. When they saw that nothing descended, they said: We do not see that anything has descended. Then [the verse] "And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted nation" (Hud 8) was revealed, up to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His words "The command of Allah has come" that it means the rulings, the prescribed punishments and the obligations.

These same narrators reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "He sends down the angels with the Spirit" that it means with the revelation.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him: The Spirit is a command from the command of Allah and a creation from the creation of Allah, and He fashioned them in the form of the sons of Adam; and no angel descends from the heaven except that with him is one of the Spirit. Then he recited [the verse] "The day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks" (al-Naba' 38).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan regarding "He sends down the angels with the Spirit" that it means the Qur'an.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "For you therein is warmth" that it means garments, and "benefits": what you benefit from of foods and drinks. He said: the offspring of every animal.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also: the offspring of every animal.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding His words "And they carry your loads to a land" meaning Mecca, "which you could not reach except with great hardship": Were you to exert yourselves, you would not be able to reach it except with severe effort.

It has been related concerning the lawfulness of eating horse flesh that there are traditions, among them in the Two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Asma', who said: We slaughtered a horse in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and we ate it.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fed us the flesh of horses and forbade us the flesh of domestic donkeys."

Abu Dawud narrated something similar from his hadith also, and both are on the condition of Muslim.

It is also established in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys and permitted horses."

As for what Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Khalid ibn al-Walid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating every animal with fangs among the predators, and the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys," its chain includes Salih ibn Yahya ibn Abi al-Miqdam, and there is criticism concerning him.

Even if we supposed the hadith to be sound, it would not be strong enough to oppose the hadiths of permissibility, especially since this explicit hadith on prohibition is earlier than the day of Khaybar, and so it is mansukh (abrogated).

al-Khatib and Ibn 'Asakir narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His words 'and He creates what you do not know': it is the baradhin (a breed of horses)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among what Allah has created is a white earth made of a pearl," and then he went on to describe its attributes, which indicate that the hadith is fabricated (mawdu'). Then he said at its end: "That is His saying, 'and He creates what you do not know.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "And upon Allah is the direction of the way": He says: it is upon Allah to make clear guidance and misguidance. Regarding "And of it is one who deviates": he said, the scattered paths.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His words "And upon Allah is the direction of the way": upon Allah is the explanation of what is lawful and what is unlawful, of obedience and disobedience. "And of it is one who deviates": of the paths is one who swerves away from the truth. He said: and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "and of you is one who deviates."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from 'Ali that he used to recite this verse as "and of you is one who deviates."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 16, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', and Jabir. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas and from Abu al-Zubayr.

Al-Nahhas narrated through the chain of Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Nahl was revealed in Mecca except for its last three verses, which were revealed between Mecca and Medina, on the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) return from Uhud." It was said that these are His words: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the same as that with which you were afflicted﴾ (16:126), and His words: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah﴾ (16:127), concerning the mutilation of Hamzah and the dead of Uhud, and His words: ﴿Then indeed, your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ (16:110). It was said that the third is: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾ up to His words: ﴿for the best of what they used to do﴾ (16:95–96).

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command upon whom He wills of His servants, [saying]: "Warn that there is no deity except Me, so fear Me."﴾ ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He created man from a sperm-drop; then at once he is an open adversary.﴾ ﴿And the cattle He created for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back [in the evening] and when you send them out [to pasture].﴾ ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And [He created] the horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment. And He creates that which you do not know.﴾ ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and among [the ways] is one that deviates. And if He had willed, He would have guided you all.﴾

His words ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ mean: His punishment upon the polytheists. A group of exegetes said: it means the Resurrection.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is what He promised them of recompense for their disbelief. He expressed the future by the form of the past to emphasize the certainty of its occurrence. It was also said that the intended meaning of "the command of Allah" is His judgment concerning that, and it has occurred and "has come." As for what was judged, it has not yet occurred, because He, glorified is He, decreed its occurrence at a specific time; so before that time arrives, it does not come into existence. It was also said that the intended meaning of its coming is the coming of (p. 772) its precursors and preliminaries.

His words ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ are a prohibition against seeking to hasten it, meaning: do not seek its presence before that time. The polytheists used to seek to hasten the punishment of Allah, as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You﴾ (8:32), up to the end of the verse. The meaning is: the command of Allah has drawn near, so do not seek to hasten it. Their seeking its hastening was by way of mockery, not in earnest. In forbidding them from seeking its hastening there is a rebuke of them.

His words ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ mean: He is far above and exalted above their association [of partners with Him], or above having any partner. Their association here is their seeking to hasten the punishment or the Hour as a mockery and denial, for this implies their description of Him, glorified is He, as one who is not able to do that, and that He is incapable of it. Incapacity and lack of power are attributes of created beings, not of the Creator; therefore this was an association [of partners with Him].

﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command﴾. Al-Mufaddal, from 'Asim, recited (tanzilu al-malaikatu), with the underlying form being (tatanazzalu), so the verb is attributed to the angels.

Al-A'mash recited (tunazzalu), in the passive voice.

Al-Ju'fi, from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited (nunazzilu), with the nun, and the subject is Allah, glorified is He.

The rest recited (yunazzilu al-malaikata), with the ya', except that Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr pronounce the nun with a sukun. The subject is Allah, glorified is He.

The connection of this sentence with what precedes it is that when he (ﷺ) informed them from Allah that His command had drawn near, and forbade them from seeking to hasten it, they doubted the way by which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew that. So He informed that he knew it by revelation, through the tongues of the messengers of Allah, glorified is He, from among His angels. "The Spirit" means revelation. A similar usage is: ﴿He sends down the Spirit from His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ (40:15). Revelation was called a "spirit" because it gives life to the hearts of the believers, for the Qur'an is among what is revealed, and it is to the religion what the spirit is to the body. It was also said that what is meant is the spirits of creatures. It was said that the Spirit is mercy, and it was said that it is guidance, because hearts are made alive by it just as bodies are made alive by spirits.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The Spirit is that in which there is life from Allah through guidance to His command."

Abu 'Ubayd said: "The Spirit here is Gabriel." On this view the (bi) in (bi al-ruh) means "with," and the (min) in (min amrihi) is explanatory, meaning: with things; or it begins [a phrase], meaning: beginning from His command; or it is a qualifier of the Spirit; or it is connected to (yunazzilu). The meaning of ﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ is: upon whomever He has singled out for that, namely the prophets.

His words ﴿that warn﴾: Al-Zajjaj said: "(an anzirū) [that warn] is a substitute for 'the Spirit,' meaning: He sends them down with (an anzirū), [saying] warn." And (an) is either explanatory, because the descent of revelation contains the meaning of speech, or it is the light form of the heavy (an), with an implied pronoun of the matter, meaning: indeed the matter is that I say to you, warn, meaning: inform the people ﴿that there is no deity except Me﴾, meaning: command them to monotheism of Me and inform them of that together with warning them, because warning contains fear and threat. The pronoun in (annahu) refers to the matter.

﴿So fear Me﴾: the address is to those who were seeking to hasten [the punishment], by way of iltifat (a shift from third person to second), and it is a warning to them against associating [partners] with Allah.

Then, when Allah, glorified is He, guided them to His monotheism, He mentioned the proofs of monotheism, saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, meaning: He brought them into existence in the state in which they are, in truth, meaning: as evidence of His power and His oneness. It was also said that what is meant by "truth" here is their perishing and cessation.

﴿Exalted﴾: Allah is exalted and sanctified above their association [of partners with Him], or above the partnership of that which they make a partner with Him.

Then, since the human species is the noblest of the kinds of lower created beings, He placed it first and singled it out for mention, saying: ﴿He created man﴾. "Man" is a name for the genus of this species, from a sperm-drop, a lifeless substance that comes out of a living being, namely semen. Then He moved him through stages until his form was complete, breathed the spirit into him, and brought him out from his mother's womb into this world, where he lived. Then, after his creation in this state, he becomes a "khasim," meaning one who is extremely contentious and argumentative. The meaning is that he is like one who disputes with Allah, glorified is He, regarding His power. "Mubin" means manifest and clear in contention. It was also said that he expresses clearly what he argues with of falsehood. "Mubin" is one who clearly expresses what is in his heart by his speech. A similar usage is His saying: ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a sperm-drop, and then at once he is an open adversary?﴾ (36:77).

Then He followed the mention of the creation of man with the creation of the cattle, because of the benefit they provide to this species. So the favor bestowed through them is more complete than favor bestowed through other things. He said: ﴿And the cattle He created for you﴾, and they are camels, cows, and sheep. Most often "na'am" and "an'am" are used for camels, but it is also used for the collective, and it is not used for sheep individually. Among the examples is the verse of Hassan:

"And there was never ceasing, among its meadows, a companion: camels and sheep."

Here he conjoined sheep (shā') with camels (na'am), and here (na'am) refers specifically to camels.

Al-Jawhari said: "Na'am" is the singular of "an'am," and this term is used most often for camels.

Then, after He informed that He created them for the children of Adam, He explained the benefit in them for them, saying: ﴿in them is warmth﴾. "Dif'" means warmth, and it is what one is warmed by from their wool, fleece, and hair. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial phrase (hal). "Manafi'" [benefits] is conjoined to "dif'," and these are their milk, riding, offspring, plowing with them, and the like.

It has been said that "dif'" means offspring and milk.

In al-Sihah (by al-Jawhari) it says: "Dif' is the offspring of camels and their milk, and whatever benefit is derived from them." Then he said: "Dif' is also warmth." On this basis, if "dif'" is taken in the first sense, then "benefits" must be interpreted as what is other than that, of what is benefited from them. If it is taken in the second sense, then interpreting "benefits" as what we have mentioned is clear. It was said that what is meant by "benefits" is offspring only, and it was said riding.

﴿And from them you eat﴾, meaning from their meat and fat. He singled out this benefit for mention even though it is included among the benefits, because it is the greatest of them. It was said He singled it out because the benefit from their meat and fat is one in which their very substance is consumed, unlike the other benefits in them. Placing the adverbial phrase, which indicates exclusivity, first, is to indicate that eating from them is the primary purpose, while other uses are rare.

﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾, meaning: for you in them, in addition to what has been mentioned, is beauty. "Jamal" is what one adorns oneself with and beautifies oneself with, and "jamal" is also beauty. The meaning here: for you in them is adornment and embellishment in the eyes of those who look upon them.

﴿when you bring them back [in the evening] and when you send them out [to pasture]﴾, meaning at these two times: the time of their return from their pastures, and the time of their being sent out to them. "Ruwah" is their return in the evening from pasture, and "sarah" is their going out to pasture in the morning. One says: "sarrahtu al-ibil usarriha sarhan wa suruhan," when you go out with them to the pasture in the morning. He placed the time of bringing back before the time of sending out, because their appearance at the time of bringing back is more beautiful, and their state is better, since in that condition they have obtained what they need of eating and drinking, so their bellies have grown large and their udders have swollen. He singled out these two times because they are the times when onlookers see them; for when they are settled in their enclosures, no one sees them, and when they are in their pastures, they are scattered and not gathered together, each one grazing in a different direction.

﴿And they carry your loads﴾. "Athqal" is the plural of "thiql," which is a traveler's baggage of food and other things, and it was called "thiql" because carrying it burdens a person. It was said that what is meant is their bodies.

﴿to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, meaning: you would not have been able to reach it, had there not been camels with you carrying your loads, except with great hardship to yourselves, because of its distance from you, and because of the lack of anything to carry what you must have on the journey.

Its apparent meaning encompasses every distant land without specification. It was said that what is meant by "land" is Mecca. It was said Yemen, Egypt, and Syria, because they are the trading places of the Arabs. "Shiqq al-anfus" means its hardship.

The majority recited it with a kasra on the shin (shiqq), and Abu Ja'far recited it with a fatha (shaqq).

Al-Jawhari said: "Al-shiqq is hardship, and from it is His saying: ﴿you could not have reached it except with great hardship to yourselves﴾." Abu 'Ubaydah related it with a fatha on the shin. Both have the same meaning. It is possible that the one with the fatha is a verbal noun from "shaqaqtu 'alayhi ashuqqu shaqqan" (I made it hard for him), and the one with the kasra means "half," as one says "akhadhtu shiqq al-shatah wa shaqqat al-shatah" (I took half of the sheep). In that case the meaning of the verse would be: you could not have reached it except by the loss of half of your souls from fatigue.

Allah, glorified is He, has bestowed His favor upon His servants by creating the cattle in general. Then He singled out camels for mention because of the blessing of carrying loads that is in them, not cows and sheep. The exception is from the most general of the general: meaning, you could not have reached it by anything except with great hardship to yourselves.

﴿And the horses, mules, and donkeys﴾ are in the accusative case, conjoined to "the cattle," meaning: He also created these three kinds for you. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited them all in the nominative case. The horse (khayl) was called "khayl" because of its strutting in its gait (ikhtiyal). The singular of "khayl" is "khail," like "da'in" is the singular of "da'n" (sheep). It was said it has no singular.

Then, Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for the creation of these three kinds, saying: ﴿that you may ride them﴾. This reason is based on the majority of their benefits, because benefiting from them in other than riding is known, such as loading them. The conjunction of "zinah" [adornment] to the position of ﴿that you may ride them﴾ is because it occupies the accusative position as a reason for their creation. He did not say "that you may adorn yourselves with them," so as to match "that you may ride them," because riding is an action of those addressed, while adornment is the action of the one who adorns, who is the Creator. The truth in this is that riding is what is considered in the intended purpose, unlike adornment, for people of lofty aspirations do not turn to it, because it produces vanity. So it is as if He, glorified is He, said: "I created them that you may ride them, and thereby ward off from yourselves the harm of exhaustion and hardship." As for adornment with them, it exists in reality, but it is not intended in itself.

And those who hold that the flesh of horses is forbidden have cited this verse, arguing that the causal clause "that you may ride them" indicates that they were created for this benefit and no other.

They said: This is supported by the singling out of these three kinds and their separation from the livestock (al-an'am), which indicates that they share a single ruling regarding the prohibition of eating.

They said: Had eating horses been permissible, mentioning it and bestowing favour through it would have been more fitting than mentioning riding, because it is of greater benefit. This was the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa and their companions, al-Awza'i, Mujahid, Abu 'Ubayd, and others.

The majority of jurists, traditionists and others held that the flesh of horses is lawful. The proponents of the first view have no proof from the causal clause "that you may ride them", because mentioning what is most common among its benefits does not exclude other benefits. Nor do we concede that eating is more beneficial than riding, such that it should be mentioned first and its mention should precede the mention of riding. Furthermore, if this verse indicated the prohibition of horses, it would also indicate the prohibition of domestic donkeys (al-humur al-ahliyyah), and then there would be no need to specify their prohibition at the time of Khaybar. We have already mentioned that this surah is Meccan.

The conclusion is that the sound evidences indicate the lawfulness of eating horse flesh. Even if we grant that this verse provides a basis for those who argue for prohibition, the established pure Sunnah would remove this possibility and repel this inference. We have clarified this question in our writings in a manner that the reader will not need anything beyond them. [Qur'an: "And He creates what you do not know."] That is, He creates what your knowledge does not encompass of the creatures, other than what is enumerated here. It was said: what is meant is the kinds of insects and creeping creatures at the bottom of the earth and in the sea that human beings have not seen and have not heard of. It was said: it is what Allah has prepared for His servants in Paradise and in Hell, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which has not occurred to the heart of any human being. It was said: it is the creation of the weevil in plants and the worm in fruits. It was said: a spring beneath the Throne. It was said: a river of light. It was said: a white earth. There is no justification for restricting the interpretation of this verse to one of these kinds, rather what is meant is that He, glory be to Him, creates what the servants have no knowledge of, so it includes everything whose knowledge does not encompass them. The expression here is in the present tense (yakhluqu) to evoke the image, because He, glory be to Him, has already created what the servants do not know of.

[Qur'an: "And upon Allah is the direction of the way."] The word qasd is a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle, so the meaning is: upon Allah is the one who directs toward the way, that is, the guidance of the one who aims at the straight path, in accordance with His binding promise and His abundant bounty. It was said that there is an elision of a noun, and the estimate is: upon Allah is the explanation of the direction of the way. The way (al-sabil) is Islam, and its explanation is through sending the messengers and establishing proofs and evidences. Qasd in the way is its being a conveyance to the desired goal, so the meaning is: upon Allah is the explanation of the path that conveys to the desired goal. [Qur'an: "And of it is one who deviates."] The pronoun in minha refers to al-sabil in the sense of al-tariq (the path), because it is both masculine and feminine. It was said it refers to it with an elided noun, meaning: and of the kind of the way is one who deviates, inclining away from the truth, turning aside from it, so he is not guided by it. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

And of the way is the deviating and the guided,
Straight of the path, and of it is one with a flaw.

It was said that "the way" is a metonymy for its traveller, and the meaning is: and of them is one who deviates from the path of truth, that is, turns aside from it, so he is not guided to it. It was said they are the people of diverse desires; it was said they are the people of disbelieving creeds. In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "and of you is one who deviates", and 'Ali also recited it thus.

[Qur'an: "Had He willed, He would have guided you all."] That is, had He willed to guide you all to the correct path and the true method, He would have done so. But He did not will it; rather His will, glory be to Him, required the showing of the way and the indicating of it. [Qur'an: "And We guided him to the two paths" (al-Balad 10).] As for conveying people to it in actuality, that would entail that there be no disbeliever among the servants, nor anyone among the Muslims who deserves the Fire. The divine will has required that some be believers and some be disbelievers, as the Qur'an has stated in more than one place. [p. 774]

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: When [the verse] "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were alarmed, until [the verse] "So do not seek to hasten it" was revealed, and they calmed down.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id al-Zuhd, and Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Bakr ibn Hafs that he said: When [the verse] "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, they stood up, then [the verse] "So do not seek to hasten it" was revealed.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated through al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "The command of Allah has come" that it is the emergence of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij that he said: When this verse "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, some hypocrites said to one another: This man claims that the command of Allah has come. So refrain from some of what you were doing until you see what is going to happen. When they saw that nothing descended, they said: We do not see that anything has descended. Then [the verse] "The reckoning of people has drawn near" (al-Anbiya 1) was revealed, and they said: This man claims likewise also. When they saw that nothing descended, they said: We do not see that anything has descended. Then [the verse] "And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted nation" (Hud 8) was revealed, up to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His words "The command of Allah has come" that it means the rulings, the prescribed punishments and the obligations.

These same narrators reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "He sends down the angels with the Spirit" that it means with the revelation.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him: The Spirit is a command from the command of Allah and a creation from the creation of Allah, and He fashioned them in the form of the sons of Adam; and no angel descends from the heaven except that with him is one of the Spirit. Then he recited [the verse] "The day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks" (al-Naba' 38).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan regarding "He sends down the angels with the Spirit" that it means the Qur'an.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "For you therein is warmth" that it means garments, and "benefits": what you benefit from of foods and drinks. He said: the offspring of every animal.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also: the offspring of every animal.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding His words "And they carry your loads to a land" meaning Mecca, "which you could not reach except with great hardship": Were you to exert yourselves, you would not be able to reach it except with severe effort.

It has been related concerning the lawfulness of eating horse flesh that there are traditions, among them in the Two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Asma', who said: We slaughtered a horse in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and we ate it.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fed us the flesh of horses and forbade us the flesh of domestic donkeys."

Abu Dawud narrated something similar from his hadith also, and both are on the condition of Muslim.

It is also established in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys and permitted horses."

As for what Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Khalid ibn al-Walid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating every animal with fangs among the predators, and the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys," its chain includes Salih ibn Yahya ibn Abi al-Miqdam, and there is criticism concerning him.

Even if we supposed the hadith to be sound, it would not be strong enough to oppose the hadiths of permissibility, especially since this explicit hadith on prohibition is earlier than the day of Khaybar, and so it is mansukh (abrogated).

al-Khatib and Ibn 'Asakir narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His words 'and He creates what you do not know': it is the baradhin (a breed of horses)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among what Allah has created is a white earth made of a pearl," and then he went on to describe its attributes, which indicate that the hadith is fabricated (mawdu'). Then he said at its end: "That is His saying, 'and He creates what you do not know.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "And upon Allah is the direction of the way": He says: it is upon Allah to make clear guidance and misguidance. Regarding "And of it is one who deviates": he said, the scattered paths.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His words "And upon Allah is the direction of the way": upon Allah is the explanation of what is lawful and what is unlawful, of obedience and disobedience. "And of it is one who deviates": of the paths is one who swerves away from the truth. He said: and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "and of you is one who deviates."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from 'Ali that he used to recite this verse as "and of you is one who deviates."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 16, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', and Jabir. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas and from Abu al-Zubayr.

Al-Nahhas narrated through the chain of Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Nahl was revealed in Mecca except for its last three verses, which were revealed between Mecca and Medina, on the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) return from Uhud." It was said that these are His words: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the same as that with which you were afflicted﴾ (16:126), and His words: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah﴾ (16:127), concerning the mutilation of Hamzah and the dead of Uhud, and His words: ﴿Then indeed, your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ (16:110). It was said that the third is: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾ up to His words: ﴿for the best of what they used to do﴾ (16:95–96).

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command upon whom He wills of His servants, [saying]: "Warn that there is no deity except Me, so fear Me."﴾ ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He created man from a sperm-drop; then at once he is an open adversary.﴾ ﴿And the cattle He created for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them back [in the evening] and when you send them out [to pasture].﴾ ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And [He created] the horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment. And He creates that which you do not know.﴾ ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and among [the ways] is one that deviates. And if He had willed, He would have guided you all.﴾

His words ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ mean: His punishment upon the polytheists. A group of exegetes said: it means the Resurrection.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is what He promised them of recompense for their disbelief. He expressed the future by the form of the past to emphasize the certainty of its occurrence. It was also said that the intended meaning of "the command of Allah" is His judgment concerning that, and it has occurred and "has come." As for what was judged, it has not yet occurred, because He, glorified is He, decreed its occurrence at a specific time; so before that time arrives, it does not come into existence. It was also said that the intended meaning of its coming is the coming of (p. 772) its precursors and preliminaries.

His words ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ are a prohibition against seeking to hasten it, meaning: do not seek its presence before that time. The polytheists used to seek to hasten the punishment of Allah, as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You﴾ (8:32), up to the end of the verse. The meaning is: the command of Allah has drawn near, so do not seek to hasten it. Their seeking its hastening was by way of mockery, not in earnest. In forbidding them from seeking its hastening there is a rebuke of them.

His words ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ mean: He is far above and exalted above their association [of partners with Him], or above having any partner. Their association here is their seeking to hasten the punishment or the Hour as a mockery and denial, for this implies their description of Him, glorified is He, as one who is not able to do that, and that He is incapable of it. Incapacity and lack of power are attributes of created beings, not of the Creator; therefore this was an association [of partners with Him].

﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit from His command﴾. Al-Mufaddal, from 'Asim, recited (tanzilu al-malaikatu), with the underlying form being (tatanazzalu), so the verb is attributed to the angels.

Al-A'mash recited (tunazzalu), in the passive voice.

Al-Ju'fi, from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited (nunazzilu), with the nun, and the subject is Allah, glorified is He.

The rest recited (yunazzilu al-malaikata), with the ya', except that Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr pronounce the nun with a sukun. The subject is Allah, glorified is He.

The connection of this sentence with what precedes it is that when he (ﷺ) informed them from Allah that His command had drawn near, and forbade them from seeking to hasten it, they doubted the way by which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew that. So He informed that he knew it by revelation, through the tongues of the messengers of Allah, glorified is He, from among His angels. "The Spirit" means revelation. A similar usage is: ﴿He sends down the Spirit from His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ (40:15). Revelation was called a "spirit" because it gives life to the hearts of the believers, for the Qur'an is among what is revealed, and it is to the religion what the spirit is to the body. It was also said that what is meant is the spirits of creatures. It was said that the Spirit is mercy, and it was said that it is guidance, because hearts are made alive by it just as bodies are made alive by spirits.

Al-Zajjaj said: "The Spirit is that in which there is life from Allah through guidance to His command."

Abu 'Ubayd said: "The Spirit here is Gabriel." On this view the (bi) in (bi al-ruh) means "with," and the (min) in (min amrihi) is explanatory, meaning: with things; or it begins [a phrase], meaning: beginning from His command; or it is a qualifier of the Spirit; or it is connected to (yunazzilu). The meaning of ﴿upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ is: upon whomever He has singled out for that, namely the prophets.

His words ﴿that warn﴾: Al-Zajjaj said: "(an anzirū) [that warn] is a substitute for 'the Spirit,' meaning: He sends them down with (an anzirū), [saying] warn." And (an) is either explanatory, because the descent of revelation contains the meaning of speech, or it is the light form of the heavy (an), with an implied pronoun of the matter, meaning: indeed the matter is that I say to you, warn, meaning: inform the people ﴿that there is no deity except Me﴾, meaning: command them to monotheism of Me and inform them of that together with warning them, because warning contains fear and threat. The pronoun in (annahu) refers to the matter.

﴿So fear Me﴾: the address is to those who were seeking to hasten [the punishment], by way of iltifat (a shift from third person to second), and it is a warning to them against associating [partners] with Allah.

Then, when Allah, glorified is He, guided them to His monotheism, He mentioned the proofs of monotheism, saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, meaning: He brought them into existence in the state in which they are, in truth, meaning: as evidence of His power and His oneness. It was also said that what is meant by "truth" here is their perishing and cessation.

﴿Exalted﴾: Allah is exalted and sanctified above their association [of partners with Him], or above the partnership of that which they make a partner with Him.

Then, since the human species is the noblest of the kinds of lower created beings, He placed it first and singled it out for mention, saying: ﴿He created man﴾. "Man" is a name for the genus of this species, from a sperm-drop, a lifeless substance that comes out of a living being, namely semen. Then He moved him through stages until his form was complete, breathed the spirit into him, and brought him out from his mother's womb into this world, where he lived. Then, after his creation in this state, he becomes a "khasim," meaning one who is extremely contentious and argumentative. The meaning is that he is like one who disputes with Allah, glorified is He, regarding His power. "Mubin" means manifest and clear in contention. It was also said that he expresses clearly what he argues with of falsehood. "Mubin" is one who clearly expresses what is in his heart by his speech. A similar usage is His saying: ﴿Does man not see that We created him from a sperm-drop, and then at once he is an open adversary?﴾ (36:77).

Then He followed the mention of the creation of man with the creation of the cattle, because of the benefit they provide to this species. So the favor bestowed through them is more complete than favor bestowed through other things. He said: ﴿And the cattle He created for you﴾, and they are camels, cows, and sheep. Most often "na'am" and "an'am" are used for camels, but it is also used for the collective, and it is not used for sheep individually. Among the examples is the verse of Hassan:

"And there was never ceasing, among its meadows, a companion: camels and sheep."

Here he conjoined sheep (shā') with camels (na'am), and here (na'am) refers specifically to camels.

Al-Jawhari said: "Na'am" is the singular of "an'am," and this term is used most often for camels.

Then, after He informed that He created them for the children of Adam, He explained the benefit in them for them, saying: ﴿in them is warmth﴾. "Dif'" means warmth, and it is what one is warmed by from their wool, fleece, and hair. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial phrase (hal). "Manafi'" [benefits] is conjoined to "dif'," and these are their milk, riding, offspring, plowing with them, and the like.

It has been said that "dif'" means offspring and milk.

In al-Sihah (by al-Jawhari) it says: "Dif' is the offspring of camels and their milk, and whatever benefit is derived from them." Then he said: "Dif' is also warmth." On this basis, if "dif'" is taken in the first sense, then "benefits" must be interpreted as what is other than that, of what is benefited from them. If it is taken in the second sense, then interpreting "benefits" as what we have mentioned is clear. It was said that what is meant by "benefits" is offspring only, and it was said riding.

﴿And from them you eat﴾, meaning from their meat and fat. He singled out this benefit for mention even though it is included among the benefits, because it is the greatest of them. It was said He singled it out because the benefit from their meat and fat is one in which their very substance is consumed, unlike the other benefits in them. Placing the adverbial phrase, which indicates exclusivity, first, is to indicate that eating from them is the primary purpose, while other uses are rare.

﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾, meaning: for you in them, in addition to what has been mentioned, is beauty. "Jamal" is what one adorns oneself with and beautifies oneself with, and "jamal" is also beauty. The meaning here: for you in them is adornment and embellishment in the eyes of those who look upon them.

﴿when you bring them back [in the evening] and when you send them out [to pasture]﴾, meaning at these two times: the time of their return from their pastures, and the time of their being sent out to them. "Ruwah" is their return in the evening from pasture, and "sarah" is their going out to pasture in the morning. One says: "sarrahtu al-ibil usarriha sarhan wa suruhan," when you go out with them to the pasture in the morning. He placed the time of bringing back before the time of sending out, because their appearance at the time of bringing back is more beautiful, and their state is better, since in that condition they have obtained what they need of eating and drinking, so their bellies have grown large and their udders have swollen. He singled out these two times because they are the times when onlookers see them; for when they are settled in their enclosures, no one sees them, and when they are in their pastures, they are scattered and not gathered together, each one grazing in a different direction.

﴿And they carry your loads﴾. "Athqal" is the plural of "thiql," which is a traveler's baggage of food and other things, and it was called "thiql" because carrying it burdens a person. It was said that what is meant is their bodies.

﴿to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves﴾, meaning: you would not have been able to reach it, had there not been camels with you carrying your loads, except with great hardship to yourselves, because of its distance from you, and because of the lack of anything to carry what you must have on the journey.

Its apparent meaning encompasses every distant land without specification. It was said that what is meant by "land" is Mecca. It was said Yemen, Egypt, and Syria, because they are the trading places of the Arabs. "Shiqq al-anfus" means its hardship.

The majority recited it with a kasra on the shin (shiqq), and Abu Ja'far recited it with a fatha (shaqq).

Al-Jawhari said: "Al-shiqq is hardship, and from it is His saying: ﴿you could not have reached it except with great hardship to yourselves﴾." Abu 'Ubaydah related it with a fatha on the shin. Both have the same meaning. It is possible that the one with the fatha is a verbal noun from "shaqaqtu 'alayhi ashuqqu shaqqan" (I made it hard for him), and the one with the kasra means "half," as one says "akhadhtu shiqq al-shatah wa shaqqat al-shatah" (I took half of the sheep). In that case the meaning of the verse would be: you could not have reached it except by the loss of half of your souls from fatigue.

Allah, glorified is He, has bestowed His favor upon His servants by creating the cattle in general. Then He singled out camels for mention because of the blessing of carrying loads that is in them, not cows and sheep. The exception is from the most general of the general: meaning, you could not have reached it by anything except with great hardship to yourselves.

﴿And the horses, mules, and donkeys﴾ are in the accusative case, conjoined to "the cattle," meaning: He also created these three kinds for you. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited them all in the nominative case. The horse (khayl) was called "khayl" because of its strutting in its gait (ikhtiyal). The singular of "khayl" is "khail," like "da'in" is the singular of "da'n" (sheep). It was said it has no singular.

Then, Allah, glorified is He, gave the reason for the creation of these three kinds, saying: ﴿that you may ride them﴾. This reason is based on the majority of their benefits, because benefiting from them in other than riding is known, such as loading them. The conjunction of "zinah" [adornment] to the position of ﴿that you may ride them﴾ is because it occupies the accusative position as a reason for their creation. He did not say "that you may adorn yourselves with them," so as to match "that you may ride them," because riding is an action of those addressed, while adornment is the action of the one who adorns, who is the Creator. The truth in this is that riding is what is considered in the intended purpose, unlike adornment, for people of lofty aspirations do not turn to it, because it produces vanity. So it is as if He, glorified is He, said: "I created them that you may ride them, and thereby ward off from yourselves the harm of exhaustion and hardship." As for adornment with them, it exists in reality, but it is not intended in itself.

And those who hold that the flesh of horses is forbidden have cited this verse, arguing that the causal clause "that you may ride them" indicates that they were created for this benefit and no other.

They said: This is supported by the singling out of these three kinds and their separation from the livestock (al-an'am), which indicates that they share a single ruling regarding the prohibition of eating.

They said: Had eating horses been permissible, mentioning it and bestowing favour through it would have been more fitting than mentioning riding, because it is of greater benefit. This was the view of Malik, Abu Hanifa and their companions, al-Awza'i, Mujahid, Abu 'Ubayd, and others.

The majority of jurists, traditionists and others held that the flesh of horses is lawful. The proponents of the first view have no proof from the causal clause "that you may ride them", because mentioning what is most common among its benefits does not exclude other benefits. Nor do we concede that eating is more beneficial than riding, such that it should be mentioned first and its mention should precede the mention of riding. Furthermore, if this verse indicated the prohibition of horses, it would also indicate the prohibition of domestic donkeys (al-humur al-ahliyyah), and then there would be no need to specify their prohibition at the time of Khaybar. We have already mentioned that this surah is Meccan.

The conclusion is that the sound evidences indicate the lawfulness of eating horse flesh. Even if we grant that this verse provides a basis for those who argue for prohibition, the established pure Sunnah would remove this possibility and repel this inference. We have clarified this question in our writings in a manner that the reader will not need anything beyond them. [Qur'an: "And He creates what you do not know."] That is, He creates what your knowledge does not encompass of the creatures, other than what is enumerated here. It was said: what is meant is the kinds of insects and creeping creatures at the bottom of the earth and in the sea that human beings have not seen and have not heard of. It was said: it is what Allah has prepared for His servants in Paradise and in Hell, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which has not occurred to the heart of any human being. It was said: it is the creation of the weevil in plants and the worm in fruits. It was said: a spring beneath the Throne. It was said: a river of light. It was said: a white earth. There is no justification for restricting the interpretation of this verse to one of these kinds, rather what is meant is that He, glory be to Him, creates what the servants have no knowledge of, so it includes everything whose knowledge does not encompass them. The expression here is in the present tense (yakhluqu) to evoke the image, because He, glory be to Him, has already created what the servants do not know of.

[Qur'an: "And upon Allah is the direction of the way."] The word qasd is a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle, so the meaning is: upon Allah is the one who directs toward the way, that is, the guidance of the one who aims at the straight path, in accordance with His binding promise and His abundant bounty. It was said that there is an elision of a noun, and the estimate is: upon Allah is the explanation of the direction of the way. The way (al-sabil) is Islam, and its explanation is through sending the messengers and establishing proofs and evidences. Qasd in the way is its being a conveyance to the desired goal, so the meaning is: upon Allah is the explanation of the path that conveys to the desired goal. [Qur'an: "And of it is one who deviates."] The pronoun in minha refers to al-sabil in the sense of al-tariq (the path), because it is both masculine and feminine. It was said it refers to it with an elided noun, meaning: and of the kind of the way is one who deviates, inclining away from the truth, turning aside from it, so he is not guided by it. From this is the line of Imru' al-Qays:

And of the way is the deviating and the guided,
Straight of the path, and of it is one with a flaw.

It was said that "the way" is a metonymy for its traveller, and the meaning is: and of them is one who deviates from the path of truth, that is, turns aside from it, so he is not guided to it. It was said they are the people of diverse desires; it was said they are the people of disbelieving creeds. In the codex of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "and of you is one who deviates", and 'Ali also recited it thus.

[Qur'an: "Had He willed, He would have guided you all."] That is, had He willed to guide you all to the correct path and the true method, He would have done so. But He did not will it; rather His will, glory be to Him, required the showing of the way and the indicating of it. [Qur'an: "And We guided him to the two paths" (al-Balad 10).] As for conveying people to it in actuality, that would entail that there be no disbeliever among the servants, nor anyone among the Muslims who deserves the Fire. The divine will has required that some be believers and some be disbelievers, as the Qur'an has stated in more than one place. [p. 774]

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: When [the verse] "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were alarmed, until [the verse] "So do not seek to hasten it" was revealed, and they calmed down.

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id al-Zuhd, and Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Bakr ibn Hafs that he said: When [the verse] "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, they stood up, then [the verse] "So do not seek to hasten it" was revealed.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated through al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "The command of Allah has come" that it is the emergence of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Juraij that he said: When this verse "The command of Allah has come" was revealed, some hypocrites said to one another: This man claims that the command of Allah has come. So refrain from some of what you were doing until you see what is going to happen. When they saw that nothing descended, they said: We do not see that anything has descended. Then [the verse] "The reckoning of people has drawn near" (al-Anbiya 1) was revealed, and they said: This man claims likewise also. When they saw that nothing descended, they said: We do not see that anything has descended. Then [the verse] "And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted nation" (Hud 8) was revealed, up to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak regarding His words "The command of Allah has come" that it means the rulings, the prescribed punishments and the obligations.

These same narrators reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "He sends down the angels with the Spirit" that it means with the revelation.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from him: The Spirit is a command from the command of Allah and a creation from the creation of Allah, and He fashioned them in the form of the sons of Adam; and no angel descends from the heaven except that with him is one of the Spirit. Then he recited [the verse] "The day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks" (al-Naba' 38).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan regarding "He sends down the angels with the Spirit" that it means the Qur'an.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "For you therein is warmth" that it means garments, and "benefits": what you benefit from of foods and drinks. He said: the offspring of every animal.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also: the offspring of every animal.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also regarding His words "And they carry your loads to a land" meaning Mecca, "which you could not reach except with great hardship": Were you to exert yourselves, you would not be able to reach it except with severe effort.

It has been related concerning the lawfulness of eating horse flesh that there are traditions, among them in the Two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Asma', who said: We slaughtered a horse in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and we ate it.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fed us the flesh of horses and forbade us the flesh of domestic donkeys."

Abu Dawud narrated something similar from his hadith also, and both are on the condition of Muslim.

It is also established in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys and permitted horses."

As for what Abu 'Ubayd, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Khalid ibn al-Walid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating every animal with fangs among the predators, and the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys," its chain includes Salih ibn Yahya ibn Abi al-Miqdam, and there is criticism concerning him.

Even if we supposed the hadith to be sound, it would not be strong enough to oppose the hadiths of permissibility, especially since this explicit hadith on prohibition is earlier than the day of Khaybar, and so it is mansukh (abrogated).

al-Khatib and Ibn 'Asakir narrated: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said regarding His words 'and He creates what you do not know': it is the baradhin (a breed of horses)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among what Allah has created is a white earth made of a pearl," and then he went on to describe its attributes, which indicate that the hadith is fabricated (mawdu'). Then he said at its end: "That is His saying, 'and He creates what you do not know.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "And upon Allah is the direction of the way": He says: it is upon Allah to make clear guidance and misguidance. Regarding "And of it is one who deviates": he said, the scattered paths.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada regarding His words "And upon Allah is the direction of the way": upon Allah is the explanation of what is lawful and what is unlawful, of obedience and disobedience. "And of it is one who deviates": of the paths is one who swerves away from the truth. He said: and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "and of you is one who deviates."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif narrated from 'Ali that he used to recite this verse as "and of you is one who deviates."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 16, verses 1–9 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', and Jabir. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas and from Abu al-Zubayr.

Al-Nahhas narrated through the chain of Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Nahl was revealed in Mecca except for its last three verses, which were revealed between Mecca and Medina, on the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) return from Uhud." It was said that these are His words: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the same as that with which you were afflicted﴾ (16:126), and His words: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but through Allah﴾ (16:127), concerning the mutilation of Hamzah and the dead of Uhud, and His words: ﴿Then indeed, your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ (16:110). It was said that the third is: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾ up to His words: ﴿for the best of what they used to do﴾ (16:95–96).

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit of His command upon whom He wills of His servants, [saying]: "Warn that there is no deity except Me, so fear Me."﴾ ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth.
