Ibn Qutaybah said: What is meant by shajar in the verse is herbage (kala'). It was also said: shajar is whatever has a stem, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6]. Conjunction requires difference, and since the star is that which has no stem, the tree must be that which has a stem. It was answered that the conjunction of a genus with a species is permissible.

﴿Wherein you pasture﴾, i.e., in the trees you let your livestock graze. It is said: the animal "sama tasumu sawman" when it grazed, so it is "sa'imah"; and "asamtuha," i.e., I drove it out to pasture, so I am "musim," and it is "musamah" and "sa'imah." The root of sawm is distancing in the pasture.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is taken from "sawmah," which is a mark, because it leaves marks on the earth by its grazing.

﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops, the olives, the palm trees and the grapes﴾. Abu Bakr, from Asim, read "nunbitu" with the nun, and the rest read with the yā' (third person), i.e., God causes to grow for you by that water which He sent down from the sky. He placed crops first because it is the basis of the foods by which people live; He followed it with olives because it is in one respect a fruit and in another a condiment, due to the abundance of oil in it. It is the plural of zaytunah, and the tree itself is also called zaytunah. Then He mentioned palm trees because they are both food and fruit, and together with grapes they are the noblest of fruits. He made "grapes" plural because they include different varieties. Then He pointed to the rest of the fruits, saying: ﴿and of all fruits﴾, just as He summarized the animals which He had not mentioned earlier with His saying: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 8]. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "yunbitu lakum bihi al-zar'u" with "al-zar'u" in the nominative, and what follows it. Indeed in that, i.e., the sending down and the causing to grow, is a great sign indicating the perfection of power and the uniqueness of lordship, ﴿for a people who reflect﴾ upon the creatures of God and do not neglect to consider His works.

﴿And He subjected for you the night and the day﴾. The meaning of their subjection to people is making them beneficial to them according to what their interests require and their needs demand. They alternate constantly like a obedient servant to his master, who does not oppose what he commands and does not depart from his will, nor neglects striving for his benefit. The same applies to the subjection of the sun, the moon and the stars, for they proceed in a uniform pattern by which servants are guided to the measures of times, and by which they find their way and know the divisions of time. The meaning of "musakhkharat" is made subservient.

Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria read "wa al-shamsu wa al-qamaru wa al-nujumu musakhkharatun" with the nominative, as a subject and predicate. The rest read with the accusative, in conjunction with "the night and the day." Hafs, from Asim, read "al-nujumu" with the nominative, its predicate being ﴿musakhkharatun bi-amrihi﴾ ("subjected by His command"). In the accusative reading of "musakhkharatin," it is an emphatic circumstantial clause, since subjection has already been understood from His saying "and He subjected." Hafs, in one transmission, read "musakhkharatun" with the nominative while the preceding words are in the accusative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are subjected." Indeed in that subjection is ﴿signs for a people who use their intellects﴾, i.e., who employ their minds in these effects which indicate the existence of the Creator, His uniqueness, and the absence of any partner for Him. He mentioned "signs" (āyāt) because the heavenly phenomena are more evident as proof of overwhelming power and clearer testimony to majesty and greatness, and He made it plural to agree with His saying "musakhkharat." It was also said that the reason for the plural is that each of the subjection of the night and day, the sun, the moon and the stars is a sign in itself, unlike what preceded regarding growth, which is a single sign. All of this is not free from strain, and the better view is to say: each of these three places is suitable for plural or singular according to different considerations, so He did not arrange them in one manner, as a variation and an indication of the permissibility of both and the beauty of each.

﴿And what He multiplied for you in the earth﴾, i.e., created. It is said: God "dhara'a" the creation, "yadhra'uhum dharʾan," meaning He created them, so He is "dhari'," and from it comes "dhurriyyah" (offspring), which is the progeny of the two species (humans and jinn). Its verification has already been discussed. It is conjoined with "al-nujum" in the nominative and accusative, i.e., "and He subjected for you what He multiplied in the earth."

The meaning: He (glorified is He) subjected to them those heavenly creatures and those earthly creatures. ﴿Diverse its colours﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, and its "colours" (alwan) are its forms and appearances, for the creation of these things with differing colours and shapes, while all share the same bodily nature, is a great sign indicating the existence of the Creator (glorified is He) and His uniqueness. ﴿Indeed in that﴾, the subjection of these matters, is a clear sign ﴿for a people who take heed﴾, for whoever remembers considers, and whoever considers reasons toward the object sought. It was said: the first station was specified for reflection because the mentioned objection could be raised; the second station was specified for intellect because it is mentioned after removing the doubt and dispelling the cause, so whoever does not then acknowledge oneness has no intellect; and the third station was specified for remembrance for greater indication, so whoever doubts after that has no perception. There is much strain in this, as is evident.

The better view is to say here as we said before regarding the singular and plural of "sign" in some places and the plural in others: each of these three places is suitable for mention of reflection, of intellect, and of remembrance for apparent considerations that are not hidden. So in the expression with one of them in each place there is a fine variation not found in using one of them in all three places.

﴿And it is He who subjected the sea﴾. God (glorified is He) bestowed favour by subjecting the sea, by making it possible to ride upon it and extract from it game and jewels, since it is among the blessings which God has bestowed upon His servants, along with what it contains of indication of the oneness of the Lord (glorified is He) and the perfection of His power. In this station God (glorified is He) gathered for His servants a reminder of His signs, earthly, heavenly and maritime, guiding them to contemplate and reason from signs varied and different in places, completing the proof, perfecting the warning, clarifying the paths of reasoning, the foundations of demonstration, and the loci of reflection and consideration. Then He mentioned the cause of subjecting the sea, saying: ﴿that you may eat from it fresh flesh﴾. What is meant by it is fish, and it was described as fresh to indicate its delicacy, and as guidance to hasten to eating it, since it is among things that spoil quickly. ﴿And that you may extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾ (p-776), i.e., pearls and coral, as in His saying (glorified is He): ﴿From them come forth the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22]. The apparent sense of His saying "which you wear" is that it is permissible for men to wear pearls and coral, i.e., to make them ornaments for themselves, just as it is permissible for women. There is no need for what some commentators have strained to do in interpreting "which you wear" as "which their women wear," because women are among them, or because they wear them for their sake. There is nothing in the pure Sharia requiring the prohibition of men from adorning themselves with pearls and coral, so long as they do not use them in a manner exclusive to women, for that is forbidden on account of imitation of women, and the Sharia has come with prohibition of it, not on account of its being an ornament of pearl or coral. ﴿And you see the ships cleaving through it﴾, i.e., you see ships ploughing the water, pushing it with their prows.

The "makhr" of a ship is its cleaving of the water with its prow. Al-Jawhari said: "makhara al-sabih" when he cut through the water with his chest, and "makhara al-ard" when he tilled it for cultivation. It was said "mawakhir" means passing through, and it was said means crossing, and it was said means going and coming, and it was said means raging. Ibn Jarir said: makhr in the language is the sound of the blowing of wind, and it is not restricted to being in water. ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ is conjoined with "tastakhrijū," and what lies between them is parenthetical, or it is conjoined to an omitted cause, the estimate being "that you may benefit by that and seek," or to the supposed action "that you may seek," i.e., that you may trade in it so that profit comes to you from the bounty of God (glorified is He). ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾, i.e., when you find His bounty upon you and His kindness to you, you will acknowledge His blessing upon you and thus give thanks for it with tongue and limbs.

It is said: perhaps the reason for specifying this blessing as followed by thanks is that in it there is the crossing of a long distance with heavy loads without undertaking the means of travel, indeed without any movement at all, and it is among perils. To the mentioned crossing of distance in this described manner may be added what the sea contains of the finest food and most precious clothing, and abundance of blessings with their preciousness and excellent placement, which are among the greatest causes calling for and necessitating thanks.

Then He followed these blessings, which necessitate monotheism and serve as evidence for the object sought, with another blessing and a greater sign, saying: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, i.e., stable mountains. It is said "rasā yarsū" when it became firm and stood. The poet said:

﴾So I endured, a noble free woman, steadfast in that, when the soul of the coward rises in alarm.﴿

﴿Lest it shake with you﴾, i.e., lest it shake with you according to the Basrans, or "so that it does not shake with you" according to the Kufans.

"Al-mayd" is agitation to right and left: "mada al-shay'u yamidu maydan" means it moved; "madat al-aghsan" means the branches swayed; "mada al-rajul" means he swaggered. ﴿And rivers﴾, i.e., and He placed in it rivers, because "casting" here means "making" and "creating," like His saying: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Taha: 39]. ﴿And roads﴾, i.e., and He placed in it roads and made them clear and manifest so that you may be guided by them in your journeys to your destinations.

"Subul" means paths.

﴿And landmarks﴾, i.e., and He placed in it landmarks, which are the signposts of the roads.

The meaning: He (glorified is He) made landmarks for the roads by which they are guided. ﴿And by the star they are guided﴾. What is meant by "the star" is the species, i.e., they are guided by it in their journey at night.

Ibn Wathhab read "wa bi-al-nujumi" with the vowel of damma on the nun and jim, and his intention is "al-nujum" (stars), shortened; or it is a plural like "saqf" and "suquf." It was also said that what is meant by "al-najm" here is the Pole Star (al-Jadi) and the two Farqadan stars. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said: the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). It was said: the landmarks are mountains. It was said: they are stars, because among the stars are those by which one is guided and among them are those which are signs but by which one is not guided.

The majority held that what is meant in the verse is guidance in journeys. It was said it is guidance to the qibla, and there is no obstacle to interpreting what is in the verse as more general than that.

Al-Akhfash said: the speech is complete at His saying "and landmarks," and His saying "and by the star they are guided" is a separate statement from the first.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 10–19 (part 2 of 2):

Then, after enumerating the signs that point to the Creator, His oneness, and the perfection of His power, He wished to rebuke the people of polytheism and obstinacy, so He said: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ That is, He who creates these magnificent created things and performs these wondrous acts, ﴿like one who creates not﴾ any of them and has no power to bring any one of them into being. This refers to these idols that you worship and make partners with Allah, may He be glorified. He used the word *man* (مَن, "who") for them, treating them as those possessing knowledge (أُولِي العِلْمِ), in accordance with their claim that they are gods, or by way of *mushakalah* (correspondence of form, a rhetorical matching of words) with His saying ﴿Is then He who creates﴾, because they are placed in its company. In this interrogation there is a reproach and rebuke of the disbelievers that is not hidden, and how deserving they are of it, for they made one of the created things a partner to its Creator. ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate﴾ [al-A'raf: 190]. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is, the created things of Allah, which point to His existence, His singularity in lordship, and the wondrous artistry of His making, so that you may reason by them. For their clarity, mere remembrance of them suffices as proof.

Then, when He had finished enumerating the signs which, with regard to the responsible persons (المُكَلَّفِينَ), are blessings, He said: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate them.﴾ The explanation of this has already passed in surah Ibrahim. The wise have said: every single part of a human being, if even the slightest defect or the least deficiency appeared in it, would embitter the blessings upon the person, and he would wish to spend the whole world, if it were in his possession, until that defect was removed from him. He, glorified is He, manages the human body in the manner most suited to it, although the human being has no knowledge of the existence of this. How then can he encompass some of the blessings of Allah upon him, or be able to count them, or be capable of thanking even the least of them?

O our Lord, these forelocks of ours are in Your hand, humbled before the magnitude of Your blessings, acknowledging their inability to give thanks adequately for any of them. We cannot count the praise due to You, as You have praised Yourself, nor can we express gratitude to You. So pardon us, forgive us, and let down the trailing skirts of Your concealment over our faults. For if You do not do so, we will be destroyed merely by falling short in thanking Your blessings. How much more so by what has been committed by us of negligence in obeying Your commands and refraining from Your prohibitions. How good is what one who said it said:

*Pardon is hoped for from the children of Adam,*
*so how should pardon not be hoped for from the Lord?*

And I, appending a verse to this line, which is a lofty palace, said:

*For He is more merciful to me than they are;*
*He is sufficient for me, He is sufficient for me, He is sufficient for me.*

How excellent is what he concluded with this favor, which is not obscure to anyone, pointing to His great forgiveness and the vastness of His mercy, when He said: (p-777) ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ That is, He is abundant in forgiveness and mercy. He does not hold you to account for heedlessness in thanking His blessings, for falling short in counting them, or for inability to perform even the least of them. Among His mercy is the continuation of them upon you and their flowing forth at every moment, with every breath you breathe and every movement by which you move.

O Allah, I thank You as many times as the thankful have thanked You, in every tongue, in every age, and as many times as the thankful will thank You, in every tongue, in every age. You have singled me out with blessings that I have not seen bestowed upon many of Your creation. And if I have seen some of them upon some of Your creation, I have not seen the rest of them upon him. So how can I bear Your thanks, and how can I manage to express the least thanks for the least of them? How then can I manage the highest of them? How can I manage the thanks for one kind of them?

Then He explained to His servants that He knows everything that proceeds from them, and nothing is hidden from Him of it. So He said: ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare.﴾ That is, what you hold secret of matters, and what you make public, that is, what you display of them. In this there is a warning, an allusion, and a rebuke, and an admonition that the true God must be knowing of both the secret and the open, unlike the idols that they worship. For they are inanimate objects with no awareness of any of the outward things, let alone the inward secrets. How then do they worship them?

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And what He has produced for you on the earth﴾, that he said: "What He created for you on the earth of differing kinds of animals, trees, and fruits, are blessings from Allah, abundant, so be thankful for them to Allah."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding His saying ﴿that you may eat from it tender meat﴾, that it means "the fish of the sea," and ﴿and extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾, he said: "This is pearl."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And it is He who subjected the sea that you may eat from it tender meat﴾, that he said: "It is fish and what is in it of creatures."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Ja'far, who said: "There is no zakat on ornaments," then he recited ﴿and extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾.

I say: In this argument there is room for scrutiny. What should be relied upon is that the original state is exemption from zakat until a proof establishes its obligation for some kind of wealth, and then it becomes binding. It has been established for gold and silver and what is well known, but nothing has come regarding jewels, with their various kinds, that indicates the obligation of zakat upon them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding *mawakhir* (مَواخِرَ, "plowing through" the water): "Ships."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah regarding *mawakhir*, that he said: "It cuts through the water with its breast."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding *mawakhir*, that he said: "Two ships sailing with a single wind, one coming and one going."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾, that he said: "It is trade."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying *rawasiya* (رَواسِيَ, "firm mountains"), that he said: "The mountains." ﴿Lest it should shake with you﴾: he said, "So that it would not shake with you. They were on the earth, which was swaying with them and not stable. So they awoke in the morning, and Allah had made the mountains, which are the firm ones, as stakes in the earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying *subulan* (سُبُلًا, "roads"), that he said: "The *subul* are the paths between the mountains."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Khatib related from Qatadah regarding *subulan*, that he said: "Ways and landmarks." And he said: "They are the stars."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding the verse, that he said: "The landmarks of the day are the mountains."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Kalbi regarding *wa-'alamat* (وَعَلاماتٍ, "and landmarks"), that he said: "The mountains."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding *wa-'alamat*, that it means "the landmarks of the roads by day," ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾, meaning "by night."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿Is then He who creates like one who creates not?﴾, that he said: "Allah is the Creator, the Provider, while these idols that are worshipped besides Allah are created and create nothing, and they do not own for their worshippers any harm or benefit."

In this station God (glorified is He) gathered for His servants a reminder of His signs, earthly, heavenly and maritime, guiding them to contemplate and reason from signs varied and different in places, completing the proof, perfecting the warning, clarifying the paths of reasoning, the foundations of demonstration, and the loci of reflection and consideration. Then He mentioned the cause of subjecting the sea, saying: ﴿that you may eat from it fresh flesh﴾. What is meant by it is fish, and it was described as fresh to indicate its delicacy, and as guidance to hasten to eating it, since it is among things that spoil quickly. ﴿And that you may extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾ (p-776), i.e., pearls and coral, as in His saying (glorified is He): ﴿From them come forth the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22]. The apparent sense of His saying "which you wear" is that it is permissible for men to wear pearls and coral, i.e., to make them ornaments for themselves, just as it is permissible for women. There is no need for what some commentators have strained to do in interpreting "which you wear" as "which their women wear," because women are among them, or because they wear them for their sake. There is nothing in the pure Sharia requiring the prohibition of men from adorning themselves with pearls and coral, so long as they do not use them in a manner exclusive to women, for that is forbidden on account of imitation of women, and the Sharia has come with prohibition of it, not on account of its being an ornament of pearl or coral. ﴿And you see the ships cleaving through it﴾, i.e., you see ships ploughing the water, pushing it with their prows.

The "makhr" of a ship is its cleaving of the water with its prow. Al-Jawhari said: "makhara al-sabih" when he cut through the water with his chest, and "makhara al-ard" when he tilled it for cultivation. It was said "mawakhir" means passing through, and it was said means crossing, and it was said means going and coming, and it was said means raging. Ibn Jarir said: makhr in the language is the sound of the blowing of wind, and it is not restricted to being in water. ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ is conjoined with "tastakhrijū," and what lies between them is parenthetical, or it is conjoined to an omitted cause, the estimate being "that you may benefit by that and seek," or to the supposed action "that you may seek," i.e., that you may trade in it so that profit comes to you from the bounty of God (glorified is He). ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾, i.e., when you find His bounty upon you and His kindness to you, you will acknowledge His blessing upon you and thus give thanks for it with tongue and limbs.

It is said: perhaps the reason for specifying this blessing as followed by thanks is that in it there is the crossing of a long distance with heavy loads without undertaking the means of travel, indeed without any movement at all, and it is among perils. To the mentioned crossing of distance in this described manner may be added what the sea contains of the finest food and most precious clothing, and abundance of blessings with their preciousness and excellent placement, which are among the greatest causes calling for and necessitating thanks.

Then He followed these blessings, which necessitate monotheism and serve as evidence for the object sought, with another blessing and a greater sign, saying: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾, i.e., stable mountains. It is said "rasā yarsū" when it became firm and stood. The poet said:

﴾So I endured, a noble free woman, steadfast in that, when the soul of the coward rises in alarm.﴿

﴿Lest it shake with you﴾, i.e., lest it shake with you according to the Basrans, or "so that it does not shake with you" according to the Kufans.

"Al-mayd" is agitation to right and left: "mada al-shay'u yamidu maydan" means it moved; "madat al-aghsan" means the branches swayed; "mada al-rajul" means he swaggered. ﴿And rivers﴾, i.e., and He placed in it rivers, because "casting" here means "making" and "creating," like His saying: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Taha: 39]. ﴿And roads﴾, i.e., and He placed in it roads and made them clear and manifest so that you may be guided by them in your journeys to your destinations.

"Subul" means paths.

﴿And landmarks﴾, i.e., and He placed in it landmarks, which are the signposts of the roads.

The meaning: He (glorified is He) made landmarks for the roads by which they are guided. ﴿And by the star they are guided﴾. What is meant by "the star" is the species, i.e., they are guided by it in their journey at night.

Ibn Wathhab read "wa bi-al-nujumi" with the vowel of damma on the nun and jim, and his intention is "al-nujum" (stars), shortened; or it is a plural like "saqf" and "suquf." It was also said that what is meant by "al-najm" here is the Pole Star (al-Jadi) and the two Farqadan stars. This was said by al-Farra'. It was also said: the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). It was said: the landmarks are mountains. It was said: they are stars, because among the stars are those by which one is guided and among them are those which are signs but by which one is not guided.

The majority held that what is meant in the verse is guidance in journeys. It was said it is guidance to the qibla, and there is no obstacle to interpreting what is in the verse as more general than that.

Al-Akhfash said: the speech is complete at His saying "and landmarks," and His saying "and by the star they are guided" is a separate statement from the first.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 10–19 (part 2 of 2):

Then, after enumerating the signs that point to the Creator, His oneness, and the perfection of His power, He wished to rebuke the people of polytheism and obstinacy, so He said: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ That is, He who creates these magnificent created things and performs these wondrous acts, ﴿like one who creates not﴾ any of them and has no power to bring any one of them into being. This refers to these idols that you worship and make partners with Allah, may He be glorified. He used the word *man* (مَن, "who") for them, treating them as those possessing knowledge (أُولِي العِلْمِ), in accordance with their claim that they are gods, or by way of *mushakalah* (correspondence of form, a rhetorical matching of words) with His saying ﴿Is then He who creates﴾, because they are placed in its company. In this interrogation there is a reproach and rebuke of the disbelievers that is not hidden, and how deserving they are of it, for they made one of the created things a partner to its Creator. ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate﴾ [al-A'raf: 190]. ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ That is, the created things of Allah, which point to His existence, His singularity in lordship, and the wondrous artistry of His making, so that you may reason by them. For their clarity, mere remembrance of them suffices as proof.

Then, when He had finished enumerating the signs which, with regard to the responsible persons (المُكَلَّفِينَ), are blessings, He said: ﴿And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate them.﴾ The explanation of this has already passed in surah Ibrahim. The wise have said: every single part of a human being, if even the slightest defect or the least deficiency appeared in it, would embitter the blessings upon the person, and he would wish to spend the whole world, if it were in his possession, until that defect was removed from him. He, glorified is He, manages the human body in the manner most suited to it, although the human being has no knowledge of the existence of this. How then can he encompass some of the blessings of Allah upon him, or be able to count them, or be capable of thanking even the least of them?

O our Lord, these forelocks of ours are in Your hand, humbled before the magnitude of Your blessings, acknowledging their inability to give thanks adequately for any of them. We cannot count the praise due to You, as You have praised Yourself, nor can we express gratitude to You. So pardon us, forgive us, and let down the trailing skirts of Your concealment over our faults. For if You do not do so, we will be destroyed merely by falling short in thanking Your blessings. How much more so by what has been committed by us of negligence in obeying Your commands and refraining from Your prohibitions. How good is what one who said it said:

*Pardon is hoped for from the children of Adam,*
*so how should pardon not be hoped for from the Lord?*

And I, appending a verse to this line, which is a lofty palace, said:

*For He is more merciful to me than they are;*
*He is sufficient for me, He is sufficient for me, He is sufficient for me.*

How excellent is what he concluded with this favor, which is not obscure to anyone, pointing to His great forgiveness and the vastness of His mercy, when He said: (p-777) ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ That is, He is abundant in forgiveness and mercy. He does not hold you to account for heedlessness in thanking His blessings, for falling short in counting them, or for inability to perform even the least of them. Among His mercy is the continuation of them upon you and their flowing forth at every moment, with every breath you breathe and every movement by which you move.

O Allah, I thank You as many times as the thankful have thanked You, in every tongue, in every age, and as many times as the thankful will thank You, in every tongue, in every age. You have singled me out with blessings that I have not seen bestowed upon many of Your creation. And if I have seen some of them upon some of Your creation, I have not seen the rest of them upon him. So how can I bear Your thanks, and how can I manage to express the least thanks for the least of them? How then can I manage the highest of them? How can I manage the thanks for one kind of them?

Then He explained to His servants that He knows everything that proceeds from them, and nothing is hidden from Him of it. So He said: ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare.﴾ That is, what you hold secret of matters, and what you make public, that is, what you display of them. In this there is a warning, an allusion, and a rebuke, and an admonition that the true God must be knowing of both the secret and the open, unlike the idols that they worship. For they are inanimate objects with no awareness of any of the outward things, let alone the inward secrets. How then do they worship them?

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And what He has produced for you on the earth﴾, that he said: "What He created for you on the earth of differing kinds of animals, trees, and fruits, are blessings from Allah, abundant, so be thankful for them to Allah."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding His saying ﴿that you may eat from it tender meat﴾, that it means "the fish of the sea," and ﴿and extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾, he said: "This is pearl."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And it is He who subjected the sea that you may eat from it tender meat﴾, that he said: "It is fish and what is in it of creatures."

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Ja'far, who said: "There is no zakat on ornaments," then he recited ﴿and extract from it ornaments that you wear﴾.

I say: In this argument there is room for scrutiny. What should be relied upon is that the original state is exemption from zakat until a proof establishes its obligation for some kind of wealth, and then it becomes binding. It has been established for gold and silver and what is well known, but nothing has come regarding jewels, with their various kinds, that indicates the obligation of zakat upon them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding *mawakhir* (مَواخِرَ, "plowing through" the water): "Ships."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah regarding *mawakhir*, that he said: "It cuts through the water with its breast."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak regarding *mawakhir*, that he said: "Two ships sailing with a single wind, one coming and one going."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾, that he said: "It is trade."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying *rawasiya* (رَواسِيَ, "firm mountains"), that he said: "The mountains." ﴿Lest it should shake with you﴾: he said, "So that it would not shake with you. They were on the earth, which was swaying with them and not stable. So they awoke in the morning, and Allah had made the mountains, which are the firm ones, as stakes in the earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying *subulan* (سُبُلًا, "roads"), that he said: "The *subul* are the paths between the mountains."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Khatib related from Qatadah regarding *subulan*, that he said: "Ways and landmarks." And he said: "They are the stars."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding the verse, that he said: "The landmarks of the day are the mountains."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Kalbi regarding *wa-'alamat* (وَعَلاماتٍ, "and landmarks"), that he said: "The mountains."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding *wa-'alamat*, that it means "the landmarks of the roads by day," ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾, meaning "by night."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿Is then He who creates like one who creates not?﴾, that he said: "Allah is the Creator, the Provider, while these idols that are worshipped besides Allah are created and create nothing, and they do not own for their worshippers any harm or benefit."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 2):

.

He, glorified is He, proceeds to establish that the idols to which He alluded with His words ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ are incapable of bringing forth the creation of anything, and therefore do not deserve worship. So He says: ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Allah﴾, that is, the deities whom the disbelievers call upon besides Allah, glorified is He, have these described attributes, namely that they ﴿do not create anything﴾ of created things at all, neither great nor small, neither noble nor base, ﴿and they are themselves created﴾. That is, their attribute is that they are created. So how could a created thing be able to create another? In this verse there is an added clarification, for He has affirmed for them the attribute of deficiency after having negated from them the attribute of perfection. This differs from His words ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾, for that verse is limited to the mere negation of the attribute of perfection.

The reading of the majority is ﴿those whom you call upon﴾ with the second-person form (taqdi), in agreement with what precedes it.

Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim, and Hubayrah narrated from Hafs, the reading ﴿they call upon﴾ with the third-person form (ya'), and this is the reading of Ya'qub.

Then He mentioned another of their attributes, saying ﴿They are dead, not alive﴾. That is, these idols are bodies that are dead, having no life whatsoever. The addition of ﴿not alive﴾ serves to explain that they are not like some bodies that die after life has been established for them; rather, there is no life for these at all. So how can they worship them when they are superior to them? Because they are living. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿they perceive﴾ refers to the deities, and the pronoun in ﴿they will be resurrected﴾ refers to the disbelievers who worship the idols. The meaning is: these inanimate idols do not perceive when their worshippers among the disbelievers will be resurrected. This is said in the manner of mockery toward them, because the perception of an inanimate object is impossible regarding even the apparent matters, let alone matters that only Allah, glorified is He, knows. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿will be resurrected﴾ may refer to the deities, meaning: and these idols do not perceive when they will be resurrected. This is supported by what has been related, that Allah will resurrect the idols and create spirits for them, along with their devils, and then all will be commanded into the Fire. This is indicated by His words ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. It was also said that the speech is complete at His words ﴿and they are created﴾, and then He begins describing the polytheists as ﴿dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾. On this view both pronouns refer to the disbelievers. On the view that the two pronouns, or one of them, refer to the idols, the reference to them with the form used for rational beings, although they do not reason, is in accordance with the belief of those who worship them that they reason.

Al-Sulami read ﴿iyyana﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah, and both are dialectal variants. It is in the position of an accusative governed by the verb preceding it.

﴿Your God is one God.﴾ When He, glorified is He, had exposed the path of the idol-worshippers as false, He declared what is the truth in itself, namely His oneness, glorified is He. Then He mentioned what caused the disbelievers to persist in their polytheism, saying: ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying﴾ of the oneness of Allah; admonition does not affect them and reminder does not benefit them. ﴿And they are arrogant﴾ in refusing to accept the truth, exalting themselves against submitting to what is right, persisting in denial.

﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ Al-Khalil said: "La jarama" (لا جرم) is a particle of affirmation and does not occur except as a response; that is, truly, Allah knows what they conceal of their sayings and deeds and what they reveal of these. The discussion of "la jarama" has already been clarified. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾ That is, He does not love those who are arrogant toward the Oneness of Allah and toward responding to His prophets. The clause is an explanation of what the preceding speech implies.

﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ That is, when someone says to these disbelieving, denying, arrogant people, "What has your Lord sent down?" that is, "What thing has your Lord sent down?" or "What is it that He has sent down?" It was said: the speaker was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and the verse was revealed concerning him, so this statement from him was in the manner of mockery. It was also said: the speaker was whoever came to them as a visitor. It was also said: the speaker was the Muslims. The polytheists, the deniers and the arrogant, then responded, and so ﴿they said, "Legends of the former peoples"﴾ with the nominative (ar-raf'), meaning: what you, O Muslims, claim has been sent down are the legends of the former peoples. Or the polytheists intended to ridicule the Muslims and said, "What has been sent down to you is the legends of the former peoples."

On this reading, there is no objection to the view that this cannot be a reply from the polytheists, since the meaning would then be: "What our Lord has sent down is the legends of the former peoples," and the disbelievers do not acknowledge its descent. The reason it is not an objection is what we have mentioned. It was also said that it is a resumed statement, meaning: what you, O Muslims, claim to be sent down is not sent down; rather, it is the legends of the former peoples. It has been permitted, according to the requirements of grammatical science (i'rab), to read "asatir" in the accusative, even though that reading is not attested in recitation. In the accusative there must be an interpretation of the kind we have mentioned, that is: "He sent down, according to your claim, the legends of the former peoples," or they say this from themselves in the manner of mockery.

"Asatir" means falsehoods and idle tales that people narrate about the earlier generations, and they are not from the speech of Allah at all, nor from what Allah has sent down, in their assumption.

﴿So that they may bear their burdens in full﴾. That is, they uttered this saying in order that they might bear their burdens in full, without any part of them being expiated, because they did not embrace Islam, which is the cause of the expiation of sins. It was also said that the lam here is "lam al-'aqibah" (the lam of consequence, indicating an outcome rather than an intended purpose), because they did not describe the Qur'an as legends in order that they would bear burdens; but since their outcome was that, the causal expression with it is correct, like His words ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. It was also said that it is the lam of command. ﴿And some of the burdens of those whom they mislead﴾: that is, they also bear some of the burdens of those whom they led astray, because whoever establishes an evil practice bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it. It was also said that "min" (of) here is for the genus and not for partition, meaning they bear all the burdens of those whom they mislead. The position of ﴿without knowledge﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿they mislead﴾, meaning they mislead people who are ignorant, not knowing what they are calling them to, nor aware of the sins that will befall them. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the object, meaning they mislead those who have no knowledge. A similar verse is ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

The discussion of His words ﴿and no bearer bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164] has already been presented in al-An'am. ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾: that is, how wretched is the thing they bear.

Then He, glorified is He, related the condition of their counterparts among earlier generations, saying: ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾. Most exegetes held that the intended person is Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built a great structure in Babylon and intended to ascend to the heaven to fight its inhabitants. Allah then sent a wind, and that structure collapsed upon him and his people, and they perished. The more appropriate view is that the verse is general, encompassing all the wrongdoers among earlier generations who attempt to inflict harm upon the righteous. The meaning of "makr" (plotting) here is scheming and planning that does not conform to the truth. In this there is a warning to the disbelievers contemporary with him, peace and blessings be upon him, that their plotting will return upon them just as the plotting of those before them returned upon themselves. ﴿So Allah came at their structure﴾: that is, the command of Allah came, which was the wind that demolished their building.

The exegetes said: Allah sent a wind that cast the top of the tower into the sea, and the remainder fell upon them ﴿from the foundations﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "from the pillars." The meaning is that the command of Allah came to it from the direction of its foundations and shook it. ﴿And the roof fell upon them from above them.﴾ Ibn Abi Hurayrah and Ibn Muhaysin read "as-saqf" with a fatha on the sin and sukun on the qaf. The meaning is that the roof fell upon them, because after the foundations of the building collapse, everything that rests upon them collapses.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: He only said ﴿from above them﴾ to inform you that they were beneath it. The Arabs say, "A roof fell upon us" or "A wall fell upon us" when it belongs to them, even if it did not actually fall upon them. So He said ﴿from above them﴾ to remove this doubt that occurs in the speech of the Arabs; He said: "from above them," that is, it fell upon them while they were beneath it, and they perished and did not escape. It was also said that by "the roof" is meant the sky, that is, the punishment came to them from the sky that is above them. It was also said that this verse is an illustration of their destruction, and the meaning is: He destroyed them, so they became like one whose building collapsed upon him.

There has been disagreement about those upon whom the roof fell. It was said they were Nimrud, as has preceded. It was said they were Bukhtnasar and his companions. It was said they were the ones who divided (the Qur'an), whose mention preceded in surah al-Hijr. ﴿And the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾, that is, the destruction came to them from where they did not perceive it, rather from where they thought themselves secure.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear that their punishment is not restricted to the punishment of this world.

He says: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾ by admitting them into the Fire, exposing them with that and humiliating them. This clause is conjoined to an implied element, meaning: this is their punishment in this world; then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say to them, along with that, as reproach and rebuke, ﴿"Where are My partners"﴾ as you claimed and pretended? Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of al-Bazzi, read "shurakaya" without hamzah, while the rest read it with hamzah. Then He described these partners with His words ﴿those for whom you used to oppose [the believers]﴾. Nafi' read "nun" with a kasrah as an idafah (construct), while the rest read it with a fatha. That is, you used to oppose the prophets and the believers concerning them. On Nafi''s reading it means: "you used to dispute with Me concerning them and oppose Me." ﴿Call upon them, so let them relieve you of this punishment that has descended upon you.﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Undoubtedly [la jarama]﴾, that he said: "Yes" (bala).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik concerning ﴿la jarama﴾ that he said: it means the truth.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak who said: "No lie" (la kadhib).

Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and others related from Ibn Mas'ud who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of pride will enter Paradise, and no one who has in his heart an atom's weight of faith will enter the Fire." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, a man loves that his garment be fine and his sandal be fine." He said: "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people." Many hadiths exist condemning pride and praising humility, and likewise many hadiths exist that exclude the love of fine clothing and fine sandals and the like from pride.

The summary is that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained the reality of pride: that it is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people. This is the blameworthy pride.

The author of ad-Durr al-Manthur, in his exegesis of this verse, namely His words ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant﴾, cited many hadiths, which is not the place to mention them; rather the context is the mention of what is related to the explanation of the Mighty Book.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿They said, "Legends of the former peoples"﴾ that some of the polytheists of the Arabs used to sit along the path of whoever came to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). When they passed by, they asked them, and they told them what they had heard from the Prophet (ﷺ), and they said: "It is only the legends of the former peoples."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so that they may bear their burdens﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: they bear, together with their own sins, the sins of those whom they mislead without knowledge. This is like His words, glorified is He: ﴿and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid something similar, and added: "and that does not lighten the punishment of those who followed them in the least."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾ that he said: Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built the tower.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Zayd ibn Aslam that it was also Nimrud.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid something similar.

[p. 778]

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 20–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿So Allah brought their structure down from the foundations﴾, that he said: "The command of Allah came upon it from its base. ﴿So the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾, and the roof (al-saqf) is the upper parts of the houses, so their houses collapsed upon them, and Allah destroyed them and annihilated them. ﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿You used to oppose them﴾ (tushaqqunna fihim), that he said: "You oppose Me."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 2):

.

He, glorified is He, proceeds to establish that the idols to which He alluded with His words ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ are incapable of bringing forth the creation of anything, and therefore do not deserve worship. So He says: ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Allah﴾, that is, the deities whom the disbelievers call upon besides Allah, glorified is He, have these described attributes, namely that they ﴿do not create anything﴾ of created things at all, neither great nor small, neither noble nor base, ﴿and they are themselves created﴾. The reading of the majority is ﴿those whom you call upon﴾ with the second-person form (taqdi), in agreement with what precedes it.

Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim, and Hubayrah narrated from Hafs, the reading ﴿they call upon﴾ with the third-person form (ya'), and this is the reading of Ya'qub.

Then He mentioned another of their attributes, saying ﴿They are dead, not alive﴾. That is, these idols are bodies that are dead, having no life whatsoever. The meaning is: these inanimate idols do not perceive when their worshippers among the disbelievers will be resurrected. This is said in the manner of mockery toward them, because the perception of an inanimate object is impossible regarding even the apparent matters, let alone matters that only Allah, glorified is He, knows. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿will be resurrected﴾ may refer to the deities, meaning: and these idols do not perceive when they will be resurrected. This is supported by what has been related, that Allah will resurrect the idols and create spirits for them, along with their devils, and then all will be commanded into the Fire. This is indicated by His words ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. It was also said that the speech is complete at His words ﴿and they are created﴾, and then He begins describing the polytheists as ﴿dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾. On this view both pronouns refer to the disbelievers. On the view that the two pronouns, or one of them, refer to the idols, the reference to them with the form used for rational beings, although they do not reason, is in accordance with the belief of those who worship them that they reason.

﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ Al-Khalil said: "La jarama" (لا جرم) is a particle of affirmation and does not occur except as a response; that is, truly, Allah knows what they conceal of their sayings and deeds and what they reveal of these. The discussion of "la jarama" has already been clarified. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾ That is, He does not love those who are arrogant toward the Oneness of Allah and toward responding to His prophets. The clause is an explanation of what the preceding speech implies.

﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ That is, when someone says to these disbelieving, denying, arrogant people, "What has your Lord sent down?" that is, "What thing has your Lord sent down?" or "What is it that He has sent down?" It was said: the speaker was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and the verse was revealed concerning him, so this statement from him was in the manner of mockery. It was also said: the speaker was whoever came to them as a visitor. It was also said: the speaker was the Muslims. The polytheists, the deniers and the arrogant, then responded, and so ﴿they said, "Legends of the former peoples"﴾ with the nominative (ar-raf'), meaning: what you, O Muslims, claim has been sent down are the legends of the former peoples. Or the polytheists intended to ridicule the Muslims and said, "What has been sent down to you is the legends of the former peoples."

On this reading, there is no objection to the view that this cannot be a reply from the polytheists, since the meaning would then be: "What our Lord has sent down is the legends of the former peoples," and the disbelievers do not acknowledge its descent. The reason it is not an objection is what we have mentioned. It was also said that it is a resumed statement, meaning: what you, O Muslims, claim to be sent down is not sent down; rather, it is the legends of the former peoples. It has been permitted, according to the requirements of grammatical science (i'rab), to read "asatir" in the accusative, even though that reading is not attested in recitation. In the accusative there must be an interpretation of the kind we have mentioned, that is: "He sent down, according to your claim, the legends of the former peoples," or they say this from themselves in the manner of mockery.

"Asatir" means falsehoods and idle tales that people narrate about the earlier generations, and they are not from the speech of Allah at all, nor from what Allah has sent down, in their assumption.

﴿So that they may bear their burdens in full﴾. That is, they uttered this saying in order that they might bear their burdens in full, without any part of them being expiated, because they did not embrace Islam, which is the cause of the expiation of sins. It was also said that the lam here is "lam al-'aqibah" (the lam of consequence, indicating an outcome rather than an intended purpose), because they did not describe the Qur'an as legends in order that they would bear burdens; but since their outcome was that, the causal expression with it is correct, like His words ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. It was also said that it is the lam of command. ﴿And some of the burdens of those whom they mislead﴾: that is, they also bear some of the burdens of those whom they led astray, because whoever establishes an evil practice bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it. It was also said that "min" (of) here is for the genus and not for partition, meaning they bear all the burdens of those whom they mislead. The position of ﴿without knowledge﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿they mislead﴾, meaning they mislead people who are ignorant, not knowing what they are calling them to, nor aware of the sins that will befall them. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the object, meaning they mislead those who have no knowledge. Then He, glorified is He, related the condition of their counterparts among earlier generations, saying: ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾. Most exegetes held that the intended person is Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built a great structure in Babylon and intended to ascend to the heaven to fight its inhabitants. Allah then sent a wind, and that structure collapsed upon him and his people, and they perished. The more appropriate view is that the verse is general, encompassing all the wrongdoers among earlier generations who attempt to inflict harm upon the righteous. The meaning of "makr" (plotting) here is scheming and planning that does not conform to the truth. In this there is a warning to the disbelievers contemporary with him, peace and blessings be upon him, that their plotting will return upon them just as the plotting of those before them returned upon themselves. ﴿So Allah came at their structure﴾: that is, the command of Allah came, which was the wind that demolished their building.

The exegetes said: Allah sent a wind that cast the top of the tower into the sea, and the remainder fell upon them ﴿from the foundations﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "from the pillars." The meaning is that the command of Allah came to it from the direction of its foundations and shook it. ﴿And the roof fell upon them from above them.﴾ Ibn Abi Hurayrah and Ibn Muhaysin read "as-saqf" with a fatha on the sin and sukun on the qaf. The meaning is that the roof fell upon them, because after the foundations of the building collapse, everything that rests upon them collapses.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: He only said ﴿from above them﴾ to inform you that they were beneath it. The Arabs say, "A roof fell upon us" or "A wall fell upon us" when it belongs to them, even if it did not actually fall upon them. So He said ﴿from above them﴾ to remove this doubt that occurs in the speech of the Arabs; He said: "from above them," that is, it fell upon them while they were beneath it, and they perished and did not escape. It was also said that by "the roof" is meant the sky, that is, the punishment came to them from the sky that is above them. It was also said that this verse is an illustration of their destruction, and the meaning is: He destroyed them, so they became like one whose building collapsed upon him.

There has been disagreement about those upon whom the roof fell. It was said they were Nimrud, as has preceded. It was said they were Bukhtnasar and his companions. It was said they were the ones who divided (the Qur'an), whose mention preceded in surah al-Hijr. ﴿And the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾, that is, the destruction came to them from where they did not perceive it, rather from where they thought themselves secure.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear that their punishment is not restricted to the punishment of this world.

He says: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾ by admitting them into the Fire, exposing them with that and humiliating them. Then He described these partners with His words ﴿those for whom you used to oppose [the believers]﴾. Nafi' read "nun" with a kasrah as an idafah (construct), while the rest read it with a fatha. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Undoubtedly [la jarama]﴾, that he said: "Yes" (bala).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik concerning ﴿la jarama﴾ that he said: it means the truth.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak who said: "No lie" (la kadhib).

Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and others related from Ibn Mas'ud who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of pride will enter Paradise, and no one who has in his heart an atom's weight of faith will enter the Fire." The author of ad-Durr al-Manthur, in his exegesis of this verse, namely His words ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant﴾, cited many hadiths, which is not the place to mention them; rather the context is the mention of what is related to the explanation of the Mighty Book.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿They said, "Legends of the former peoples"﴾ that some of the polytheists of the Arabs used to sit along the path of whoever came to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). When they passed by, they asked them, and they told them what they had heard from the Prophet (ﷺ), and they said: "It is only the legends of the former peoples."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so that they may bear their burdens﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: they bear, together with their own sins, the sins of those whom they mislead without knowledge. This is like His words, glorified is He: ﴿and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid something similar, and added: "and that does not lighten the punishment of those who followed them in the least."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾ that he said: Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built the tower.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Zayd ibn Aslam that it was also Nimrud.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 20–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿So Allah brought their structure down from the foundations﴾, that he said: "The command of Allah came upon it from its base. ﴿So the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾, and the roof (al-saqf) is the upper parts of the houses, so their houses collapsed upon them, and Allah destroyed them and annihilated them. ﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿You used to oppose them﴾ (tushaqqunna fihim), that he said: "You oppose Me."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 20–26 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿So Allah brought their structure down from the foundations﴾, that he said: "The command of Allah came upon it from its base. ﴿So the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾, and the roof (al-saqf) is the upper parts of the houses, so their houses collapsed upon them, and Allah destroyed them and annihilated them. ﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿You used to oppose them﴾ (tushaqqunna fihim), that he said: "You oppose Me."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 2):

.

He, glorified is He, proceeds to establish that the idols to which He alluded with His words ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ are incapable of bringing forth the creation of anything, and therefore do not deserve worship. So He says: ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Allah﴾, that is, the deities whom the disbelievers call upon besides Allah, glorified is He, have these described attributes, namely that they ﴿do not create anything﴾ of created things at all, neither great nor small, neither noble nor base, ﴿and they are themselves created﴾. That is, their attribute is that they are created. So how could a created thing be able to create another? In this verse there is an added clarification, for He has affirmed for them the attribute of deficiency after having negated from them the attribute of perfection. This differs from His words ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾, for that verse is limited to the mere negation of the attribute of perfection.

The reading of the majority is ﴿those whom you call upon﴾ with the second-person form (taqdi), in agreement with what precedes it.

Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim, and Hubayrah narrated from Hafs, the reading ﴿they call upon﴾ with the third-person form (ya'), and this is the reading of Ya'qub.

Then He mentioned another of their attributes, saying ﴿They are dead, not alive﴾. That is, these idols are bodies that are dead, having no life whatsoever. The addition of ﴿not alive﴾ serves to explain that they are not like some bodies that die after life has been established for them; rather, there is no life for these at all. So how can they worship them when they are superior to them? Because they are living. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿they perceive﴾ refers to the deities, and the pronoun in ﴿they will be resurrected﴾ refers to the disbelievers who worship the idols. The meaning is: these inanimate idols do not perceive when their worshippers among the disbelievers will be resurrected. This is said in the manner of mockery toward them, because the perception of an inanimate object is impossible regarding even the apparent matters, let alone matters that only Allah, glorified is He, knows. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿will be resurrected﴾ may refer to the deities, meaning: and these idols do not perceive when they will be resurrected. This is supported by what has been related, that Allah will resurrect the idols and create spirits for them, along with their devils, and then all will be commanded into the Fire. This is indicated by His words ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. It was also said that the speech is complete at His words ﴿and they are created﴾, and then He begins describing the polytheists as ﴿dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾. On this view both pronouns refer to the disbelievers. On the view that the two pronouns, or one of them, refer to the idols, the reference to them with the form used for rational beings, although they do not reason, is in accordance with the belief of those who worship them that they reason.

Al-Sulami read ﴿iyyana﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah, and both are dialectal variants. It is in the position of an accusative governed by the verb preceding it.

﴿Your God is one God.﴾ When He, glorified is He, had exposed the path of the idol-worshippers as false, He declared what is the truth in itself, namely His oneness, glorified is He. Then He mentioned what caused the disbelievers to persist in their polytheism, saying: ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying﴾ of the oneness of Allah; admonition does not affect them and reminder does not benefit them. ﴿And they are arrogant﴾ in refusing to accept the truth, exalting themselves against submitting to what is right, persisting in denial.

﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ Al-Khalil said: "La jarama" (لا جرم) is a particle of affirmation and does not occur except as a response; that is, truly, Allah knows what they conceal of their sayings and deeds and what they reveal of these. The discussion of "la jarama" has already been clarified. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾ That is, He does not love those who are arrogant toward the Oneness of Allah and toward responding to His prophets. The clause is an explanation of what the preceding speech implies.

﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ That is, when someone says to these disbelieving, denying, arrogant people, "What has your Lord sent down?" that is, "What thing has your Lord sent down?" or "What is it that He has sent down?" It was said: the speaker was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and the verse was revealed concerning him, so this statement from him was in the manner of mockery. It was also said: the speaker was whoever came to them as a visitor. It was also said: the speaker was the Muslims. The polytheists, the deniers and the arrogant, then responded, and so ﴿they said, "Legends of the former peoples"﴾ with the nominative (ar-raf'), meaning: what you, O Muslims, claim has been sent down are the legends of the former peoples. Or the polytheists intended to ridicule the Muslims and said, "What has been sent down to you is the legends of the former peoples."

On this reading, there is no objection to the view that this cannot be a reply from the polytheists, since the meaning would then be: "What our Lord has sent down is the legends of the former peoples," and the disbelievers do not acknowledge its descent. The reason it is not an objection is what we have mentioned. It was also said that it is a resumed statement, meaning: what you, O Muslims, claim to be sent down is not sent down; rather, it is the legends of the former peoples. It has been permitted, according to the requirements of grammatical science (i'rab), to read "asatir" in the accusative, even though that reading is not attested in recitation. In the accusative there must be an interpretation of the kind we have mentioned, that is: "He sent down, according to your claim, the legends of the former peoples," or they say this from themselves in the manner of mockery.

"Asatir" means falsehoods and idle tales that people narrate about the earlier generations, and they are not from the speech of Allah at all, nor from what Allah has sent down, in their assumption.

﴿So that they may bear their burdens in full﴾. That is, they uttered this saying in order that they might bear their burdens in full, without any part of them being expiated, because they did not embrace Islam, which is the cause of the expiation of sins. It was also said that the lam here is "lam al-'aqibah" (the lam of consequence, indicating an outcome rather than an intended purpose), because they did not describe the Qur'an as legends in order that they would bear burdens; but since their outcome was that, the causal expression with it is correct, like His words ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. It was also said that it is the lam of command. ﴿And some of the burdens of those whom they mislead﴾: that is, they also bear some of the burdens of those whom they led astray, because whoever establishes an evil practice bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it. It was also said that "min" (of) here is for the genus and not for partition, meaning they bear all the burdens of those whom they mislead. The position of ﴿without knowledge﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿they mislead﴾, meaning they mislead people who are ignorant, not knowing what they are calling them to, nor aware of the sins that will befall them. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the object, meaning they mislead those who have no knowledge. A similar verse is ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

The discussion of His words ﴿and no bearer bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164] has already been presented in al-An'am. ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾: that is, how wretched is the thing they bear.

Then He, glorified is He, related the condition of their counterparts among earlier generations, saying: ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾. Most exegetes held that the intended person is Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built a great structure in Babylon and intended to ascend to the heaven to fight its inhabitants. Allah then sent a wind, and that structure collapsed upon him and his people, and they perished. The more appropriate view is that the verse is general, encompassing all the wrongdoers among earlier generations who attempt to inflict harm upon the righteous. The meaning of "makr" (plotting) here is scheming and planning that does not conform to the truth. In this there is a warning to the disbelievers contemporary with him, peace and blessings be upon him, that their plotting will return upon them just as the plotting of those before them returned upon themselves. ﴿So Allah came at their structure﴾: that is, the command of Allah came, which was the wind that demolished their building.

The exegetes said: Allah sent a wind that cast the top of the tower into the sea, and the remainder fell upon them ﴿from the foundations﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "from the pillars." The meaning is that the command of Allah came to it from the direction of its foundations and shook it. ﴿And the roof fell upon them from above them.﴾ Ibn Abi Hurayrah and Ibn Muhaysin read "as-saqf" with a fatha on the sin and sukun on the qaf. The meaning is that the roof fell upon them, because after the foundations of the building collapse, everything that rests upon them collapses.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: He only said ﴿from above them﴾ to inform you that they were beneath it. The Arabs say, "A roof fell upon us" or "A wall fell upon us" when it belongs to them, even if it did not actually fall upon them. So He said ﴿from above them﴾ to remove this doubt that occurs in the speech of the Arabs; He said: "from above them," that is, it fell upon them while they were beneath it, and they perished and did not escape. It was also said that by "the roof" is meant the sky, that is, the punishment came to them from the sky that is above them. It was also said that this verse is an illustration of their destruction, and the meaning is: He destroyed them, so they became like one whose building collapsed upon him.

There has been disagreement about those upon whom the roof fell. It was said they were Nimrud, as has preceded. It was said they were Bukhtnasar and his companions. It was said they were the ones who divided (the Qur'an), whose mention preceded in surah al-Hijr. ﴿And the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾, that is, the destruction came to them from where they did not perceive it, rather from where they thought themselves secure.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear that their punishment is not restricted to the punishment of this world.

He says: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾ by admitting them into the Fire, exposing them with that and humiliating them. This clause is conjoined to an implied element, meaning: this is their punishment in this world; then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say to them, along with that, as reproach and rebuke, ﴿"Where are My partners"﴾ as you claimed and pretended? Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of al-Bazzi, read "shurakaya" without hamzah, while the rest read it with hamzah. Then He described these partners with His words ﴿those for whom you used to oppose [the believers]﴾. Nafi' read "nun" with a kasrah as an idafah (construct), while the rest read it with a fatha. That is, you used to oppose the prophets and the believers concerning them. On Nafi''s reading it means: "you used to dispute with Me concerning them and oppose Me." ﴿Call upon them, so let them relieve you of this punishment that has descended upon you.﴾

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Undoubtedly [la jarama]﴾, that he said: "Yes" (bala).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik concerning ﴿la jarama﴾ that he said: it means the truth.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak who said: "No lie" (la kadhib).

Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and others related from Ibn Mas'ud who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of pride will enter Paradise, and no one who has in his heart an atom's weight of faith will enter the Fire." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, a man loves that his garment be fine and his sandal be fine." He said: "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty. Pride is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people." Many hadiths exist condemning pride and praising humility, and likewise many hadiths exist that exclude the love of fine clothing and fine sandals and the like from pride.

The summary is that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained the reality of pride: that it is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people. This is the blameworthy pride.

The author of ad-Durr al-Manthur, in his exegesis of this verse, namely His words ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant﴾, cited many hadiths, which is not the place to mention them; rather the context is the mention of what is related to the explanation of the Mighty Book.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿They said, "Legends of the former peoples"﴾ that some of the polytheists of the Arabs used to sit along the path of whoever came to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). When they passed by, they asked them, and they told them what they had heard from the Prophet (ﷺ), and they said: "It is only the legends of the former peoples."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿so that they may bear their burdens﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: they bear, together with their own sins, the sins of those whom they mislead without knowledge. This is like His words, glorified is He: ﴿and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid something similar, and added: "and that does not lighten the punishment of those who followed them in the least."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾ that he said: Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built the tower.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir related from Zayd ibn Aslam that it was also Nimrud.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 20–26 (part 1 of 2):
