He, glorified is He, proceeds to establish that the idols to which He alluded with His words ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾ are incapable of bringing forth the creation of anything, and therefore do not deserve worship. So He says: ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Allah﴾, that is, the deities whom the disbelievers call upon besides Allah, glorified is He, have these described attributes, namely that they ﴿do not create anything﴾ of created things at all, neither great nor small, neither noble nor base, ﴿and they are themselves created﴾. That is, their attribute is that they are created. So how could a created thing be able to create another? In this verse there is an added clarification, for He has affirmed for them the attribute of deficiency after having negated from them the attribute of perfection. This differs from His words ﴿Is one who creates like one who does not create?﴾, for that verse is limited to the mere negation of the attribute of perfection.

The reading of the majority is ﴿those whom you call upon﴾ with the second-person form (taqdi), in agreement with what precedes it.

Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim, and Hubayrah narrated from Hafs, the reading ﴿they call upon﴾ with the third-person form (ya'), and this is the reading of Ya'qub.

Then He mentioned another of their attributes, saying ﴿They are dead, not alive﴾. That is, these idols are bodies that are dead, having no life whatsoever. The addition of ﴿not alive﴾ serves to explain that they are not like some bodies that die after life has been established for them; rather, there is no life for these at all. So how can they worship them when they are superior to them? Because they are living. ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿they perceive﴾ refers to the deities, and the pronoun in ﴿they will be resurrected﴾ refers to the disbelievers who worship the idols. The meaning is: these inanimate idols do not perceive when their worshippers among the disbelievers will be resurrected. This is said in the manner of mockery toward them, because the perception of an inanimate object is impossible regarding even the apparent matters, let alone matters that only Allah, glorified is He, knows. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿will be resurrected﴾ may refer to the deities, meaning: and these idols do not perceive when they will be resurrected. This is supported by what has been related, that Allah will resurrect the idols and create spirits for them, along with their devils, and then all will be commanded into the Fire. This is indicated by His words ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya: 98]. It was also said that the speech is complete at His words ﴿and they are created﴾, and then He begins describing the polytheists as ﴿dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾. On this view both pronouns refer to the disbelievers. On the view that the two pronouns, or one of them, refer to the idols, the reference to them with the form used for rational beings, although they do not reason, is in accordance with the belief of those who worship them that they reason.

Al-Sulami read ﴿iyyana﴾ with a kasrah on the hamzah, and both are dialectal variants. It is in the position of an accusative governed by the verb preceding it.

﴿Your God is one God.﴾ When He, glorified is He, had exposed the path of the idol-worshippers as false, He declared what is the truth in itself, namely His oneness, glorified is He. Then He mentioned what caused the disbelievers to persist in their polytheism, saying: ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying﴾ of the oneness of Allah; admonition does not affect them and reminder does not benefit them. ﴿And they are arrogant﴾ in refusing to accept the truth, exalting themselves against submitting to what is right, persisting in denial.

﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ Al-Khalil said: "La jarama" (لا جرم) is a particle of affirmation and does not occur except as a response; that is, truly, Allah knows what they conceal of their sayings and deeds and what they reveal of these. The discussion of "la jarama" has already been clarified. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾ That is, He does not love those who are arrogant toward the Oneness of Allah and toward responding to His prophets. The clause is an explanation of what the preceding speech implies.

﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ That is, when someone says to these disbelieving, denying, arrogant people, "What has your Lord sent down?" that is, "What thing has your Lord sent down?" or "What is it that He has sent down?" It was said: the speaker was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and the verse was revealed concerning him, so this statement from him was in the manner of mockery. It was also said: the speaker was whoever came to them as a visitor. It was also said: the speaker was the Muslims. The polytheists, the deniers and the arrogant, then responded, and so ﴿they said, "Legends of the former peoples"﴾ with the nominative (ar-raf'), meaning: what you, O Muslims, claim has been sent down are the legends of the former peoples. Or the polytheists intended to ridicule the Muslims and said, "What has been sent down to you is the legends of the former peoples."

On this reading, there is no objection to the view that this cannot be a reply from the polytheists, since the meaning would then be: "What our Lord has sent down is the legends of the former peoples," and the disbelievers do not acknowledge its descent. The reason it is not an objection is what we have mentioned. It was also said that it is a resumed statement, meaning: what you, O Muslims, claim to be sent down is not sent down; rather, it is the legends of the former peoples. It has been permitted, according to the requirements of grammatical science (i'rab), to read "asatir" in the accusative, even though that reading is not attested in recitation. In the accusative there must be an interpretation of the kind we have mentioned, that is: "He sent down, according to your claim, the legends of the former peoples," or they say this from themselves in the manner of mockery.

"Asatir" means falsehoods and idle tales that people narrate about the earlier generations, and they are not from the speech of Allah at all, nor from what Allah has sent down, in their assumption.

﴿So that they may bear their burdens in full﴾. That is, they uttered this saying in order that they might bear their burdens in full, without any part of them being expiated, because they did not embrace Islam, which is the cause of the expiation of sins. It was also said that the lam here is "lam al-'aqibah" (the lam of consequence, indicating an outcome rather than an intended purpose), because they did not describe the Qur'an as legends in order that they would bear burdens; but since their outcome was that, the causal expression with it is correct, like His words ﴿so that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. It was also said that it is the lam of command. ﴿And some of the burdens of those whom they mislead﴾: that is, they also bear some of the burdens of those whom they led astray, because whoever establishes an evil practice bears its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it. It was also said that "min" (of) here is for the genus and not for partition, meaning they bear all the burdens of those whom they mislead. The position of ﴿without knowledge﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿they mislead﴾, meaning they mislead people who are ignorant, not knowing what they are calling them to, nor aware of the sins that will befall them. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the object, meaning they mislead those who have no knowledge. A similar verse is ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and additional burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

Then He, glorified is He, related the condition of their counterparts among earlier generations, saying: ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾. Most exegetes held that the intended person is Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built a great structure in Babylon and intended to ascend to the heaven to fight its inhabitants. Allah then sent a wind, and that structure collapsed upon him and his people, and they perished. The more appropriate view is that the verse is general, encompassing all the wrongdoers among earlier generations who attempt to inflict harm upon the righteous. The meaning of "makr" (plotting) here is scheming and planning that does not conform to the truth. In this there is a warning to the disbelievers contemporary with him, peace and blessings be upon him, that their plotting will return upon them just as the plotting of those before them returned upon themselves. ﴿So Allah came at their structure﴾: that is, the command of Allah came, which was the wind that demolished their building.

The exegetes said: Allah sent a wind that cast the top of the tower into the sea, and the remainder fell upon them ﴿from the foundations﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "from the pillars." The meaning is that the command of Allah came to it from the direction of its foundations and shook it. ﴿And the roof fell upon them from above them.﴾ Ibn Abi Hurayrah and Ibn Muhaysin read "as-saqf" with a fatha on the sin and sukun on the qaf. The meaning is that the roof fell upon them, because after the foundations of the building collapse, everything that rests upon them collapses.

The Arabs say, "A roof fell upon us" or "A wall fell upon us" when it belongs to them, even if it did not actually fall upon them. It was also said that by "the roof" is meant the sky, that is, the punishment came to them from the sky that is above them. It was also said that this verse is an illustration of their destruction, and the meaning is: He destroyed them, so they became like one whose building collapsed upon him.

There has been disagreement about those upon whom the roof fell. It was said they were Nimrud, as has preceded. It was said they were Bukhtnasar and his companions. It was said they were the ones who divided (the Qur'an), whose mention preceded in surah al-Hijr. ﴿And the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾, that is, the destruction came to them from where they did not perceive it, rather from where they thought themselves secure.

Then He, glorified is He, made clear that their punishment is not restricted to the punishment of this world.

He says: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾ by admitting them into the Fire, exposing them with that and humiliating them. This clause is conjoined to an implied element, meaning: this is their punishment in this world; then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say to them, along with that, as reproach and rebuke, ﴿"Where are My partners"﴾ as you claimed and pretended? Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of al-Bazzi, read "shurakaya" without hamzah, while the rest read it with hamzah. Then He described these partners with His words ﴿those for whom you used to oppose [the believers]﴾. Nafi' read "nun" with a kasrah as an idafah (construct), while the rest read it with a fatha. That is, you used to oppose the prophets and the believers concerning them. On Nafi''s reading it means: "you used to dispute with Me concerning them and oppose Me." ﴿Call upon them, so let them relieve you of this punishment that has descended upon you.﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Malik concerning ﴿la jarama﴾ that he said: it means the truth.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak who said: "No lie" (la kadhib).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾ that he said: Nimrud ibn Kan'an, when he built the tower.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿So Allah brought their structure down from the foundations﴾, that he said: "The command of Allah came upon it from its base. ﴿So the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾, and the roof (al-saqf) is the upper parts of the houses, so their houses collapsed upon them, and Allah destroyed them and annihilated them. ﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿You used to oppose them﴾ (tushaqqunna fihim), that he said: "You oppose Me."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 27–32:**

Allah's words: ﴿Those who were given knowledge will say﴾. It is said that they are the scholars (*ʿulamāʾ*), who said this to their peoples, those who used to admonish them and did not heed their admonition.

This statement from them was in the manner of gloating (*shamātah*). It is also said that they are the prophets, and it is said that they are the angels. The apparent meaning is the first, because mentioning them by the attribute of knowledge conveys that, although the prophets and the angels are among the people of knowledge, and indeed are more deeply rooted in it, they have a description by which they are mentioned that is more noble than this description, namely that they are prophets or that they are angels. The permissibility of applying the term to them does not undermine this, because the purpose is to indicate prominence only. ﴿Indeed, disgrace today﴾, that is, humiliation, abasement and exposure on the Day of Resurrection, and ﴿evil﴾, that is, punishment, is specific to the disbelievers.

﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾. Its explanation has already been given. The relative clause is in the genitive position as an adjective (*naʿt*) of the disbelievers, or as an apposition (*badal*) to them, or in the accusative position by specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), or in the nominative position by the assumption of a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), meaning: they are those whom they take. The accusative of ﴿wronging themselves﴾ is a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). ﴿Then they will offer submission﴾ is coordinated with ﴿then He will say, "Where are My associates"﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection. That is, they acknowledged lordship and submitted at death. Its meaning is submission (*istislām*), as said by Qutrub. It is also said that its meaning is peace-making (*musālamah*), that is, they made peace and abandoned opposition, as said by al-Akhfash. It is also said that its meaning is Islam, that is, they acknowledged Islam and abandoned what they had been in of disbelief. The clause ﴿We used to do no evil﴾ may be an explanation of "submission", with "submission" meaning the speech that indicates it. It may also be that "evil" here means polytheism, and this statement from them would be in the manner of denial and lying. Whoever does not permit lying to the people of the Resurrection interprets it to mean that they intended that they had not done evil according to their belief and their assumptions. A similar statement is their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-Anʿam: 23]. When they said this, the people of knowledge answered them with their words: ﴿Yes, indeed Allah is Knowing of what you used to do﴾ (p-780), that is: yes, you used to do evil; indeed Allah knows what you used to do, so He will recompense you for it, and this lying will benefit you nothing.

﴿So enter the gates of Hell﴾, that is, it will be said to them this at death.

The gates of Hell have already been mentioned, and that Hell has levels, some above others. ﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a predicated circumstance (*ḥāl muqaddarah*), because their abiding is future. ﴿How wretched is the abode of the arrogant﴾. The object of the dispraise is omitted, and the estimate is: how wretched is the abode of the arrogant, Hell. The arrogance here is their arrogance toward faith and worship, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no deity except Allah," they were arrogant﴾ [al-Saffat: 35].

Then He followed the descriptions of the wretched with the descriptions of the blessed, and said: ﴿And it will be said to those who feared Allah﴾, and they are the believers, ﴿"What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good."﴾, that is, He sent down good.

Al-Tha'labi said: If it is asked why the answer in His words ﴿"Legends of the former peoples"﴾ is in the nominative, while in His words "good" it is in the accusative, the answer is that the polytheists did not believe in the revelation, so it is as though they said: what Muhammad says is the legends of the former peoples; and the believers believed in the descent, so He said: He sent down good. ﴿For those who did good in this world is good﴾. It is said: this is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is also said: it is a report of the speech of those who feared Allah, and on this view it is a substitution (*badal*) for "good". On the first view it is a resumed statement (*kalām mustaʾnaf*) directed toward praising the God-fearing, and the meaning is: for those who made their deeds good in this world, a good reward (*mathūbah ḥasanah*). ﴿And the home of the Hereafter is better﴾, that is, its reward is better than what they were given in this world. ﴿And excellent is the home of the God-fearing﴾, the home of the Hereafter; the object of praise has been omitted because what precedes it indicates it.

The nominative of ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ is because it is a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) whose predicate is what follows it, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject. It is said that it may be that it is the object of the praise, and ﴿they will enter them﴾ is either the predicate of the subject or a predicate after a predicate. On the assumption that ʿAdn is indefinite, it is a qualifier (*ṣifah*) of "gardens"; likewise ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾. It is also said that the two clauses may be in the accusative position as circumstantial states, on the assumption that the word ʿAdn is a proper name. The meaning of rivers flowing beneath the gardens has already been mentioned. ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish﴾, that is, for them in the gardens is whatever their wish reaches, easily and without effort, which is obtained for them simply by that. ﴿Thus Allah recompenses the God-fearing﴾, that is, He recompenses them with a recompense like that. By "the God-fearing" is meant everyone who guards against polytheism and what necessitates the Fire of sins.

The relative clause in His words ﴿Those whom the angels take in a good state﴾ is in the accusative position as a qualifier (*naʿt*) of the God-fearing mentioned before it. Al-Aʿmash and Hamzah read ﴿tatawaffāhumu﴾ in this place and in the first place with the yāʾ (third person), and the rest read it with the tāʾ (second person). Abu ʿUbayd preferred the first reading, citing what was narrated from Ibn Masʿud that he said: The Quraysh claimed that the angels are females, so you remind them.

As for ﴿good﴾ there are several views: pure from polytheism; or righteous; or their deeds and words are pure; or good of soul, confident in what they will meet of the reward of Allah; or their souls are good in returning to Allah; or good in their death, that is, it is easy for them, with no hardship in it. The clause ﴿saying, "Peace be upon you"﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the angels, that is, saying: peace be upon you. Its meaning may bear two aspects: the first is that the peace is a warning to them of death. The second is that it is good news to them of Paradise, because peace is security. It is said that the angels say: Peace be upon you, friend of Allah; Allah sends His peace upon you. ﴿Enter Paradise because of what you used to do﴾, that is, because of your deeds. It is said this may bear two aspects: the first is that it is good news of entering Paradise at death; the second is that they will say this to them in the Hereafter.

This does not contradict entering Paradise by Allah's grace, as in the sound hadith: "Be steadfast and close to the mark, and know that no one will enter Paradise by his deeds." It was asked: "Not even you, Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." We have already discussed this matter.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And it will be said to those who feared Allah﴾, that he said: These are the believers. It is said to them, ﴿"What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ and they say, ﴿"Good, for those who did good"﴾, that is, they believed in Allah and His books, and commanded obedience to Him, urged the servants of Allah toward good, and called them to it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿Those whom the angels take in a good state﴾, that he said: alive and dead; Allah decreed that for them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verse 33–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them﴾ and the verse. This is the answer to another doubt of those who deny prophethood. They asked the Prophet ﷺ to send down to them an angel from the sky to bear witness to the truth of his claim to prophethood. So He said: Do they await, in confirming your prophethood, ﴿anything but that the angels should come to them﴾ bearing witness to that? It is also possible to say that when they criticised the Qur'an as "tales of the ancients," Allah threatened them with His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them﴾ to seize their souls, ﴿or that the command of your Lord should come﴾, that is, His punishment in this world that will uproot them, or the intended meaning of the command of Allah is the Resurrection.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿that the angels should come to them﴾ with the yā' (third person masculine), and the rest read it with the tā' (third person feminine). The meaning of their "awaiting" (yanzurun, i.e., they await) the coming of the angels (p-781) or the coming of the command of Allah, according to the other interpretation, is that they have done the deed of one upon whom punishment is due and who has become awaiting it. It is not meant that they literally await that, for they do not believe in it nor affirm it. ﴿Thus did those before them do﴾, that is, like the deeds of these people of persistence in disbelief, denial and mockery, did those who passed before them of the groups of unbelievers. Then the command of Allah came to them and they were destroyed. ﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾ by destroying them with punishment, for He sent upon them what they deserved because of their disbelief. ﴿But they used to wrong themselves﴾ by the abominations they committed. In this there is that their wronging is restricted to themselves in terms of its outcome.

The clause ﴿So the evil consequences of what they did befell them﴾ is conjoined to the act of those before them, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. It has been said that there is inversion in the speech, and the sense is: Thus did those before them, so the evil consequences of what they did befell them and Allah did not wrong them. The meaning is: there befell them the recompense of the evils of their deeds, or the recompense of their evil deeds. ﴿And there encompassed them﴾, that is, descended upon them in a comprehensive manner, ﴿what they used to mock at﴾, that is, the punishment they used to mock at, or the penalty of their mockery.

﴿And those who associated said﴾: This is another kind of their disbelief which Allah related about them. By ﴿those who associated﴾ here is meant the people of Makkah. ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾, that is, had He willed that we not worship anything other than Him, we would not have worshipped that. ﴿Neither we nor our fathers﴾ who were upon what we are upon now of the religion of disbelief and of associating others with Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: They said this by way of mockery, and had they said it out of conviction they would have been believers. The discussion of the like of this has already passed in Surat al-An'am. ﴿Nor would we have forbidden anything besides Him﴾, such as the sawa'ib and the bahair and the like. Their purpose by this statement, made contingent upon the will, is to attack the message, that is: if what the Messenger said were true, regarding the prohibition of worshipping other than Allah and the prohibition of forbidding what Allah has not forbidden, relating that from Allah, then nothing contrary to what He willed from us would have occurred, for He has willed that, and what He willed came to be and what He did not will did not come to be. So when worshipping others and forbidding what He did not forbid occurred from us, that was evidence that this is what conforms to His intention and agrees with His will. Yet in reality they do not acknowledge this nor affirm it, but they intended the attack upon the messengers that we have mentioned. ﴿Thus did those before them do﴾ of the groups of disbelief, for they associated others with Allah, forbade what He had not forbidden, disputed with His messengers falsely, and mocked them. ﴿And those who associated said﴾: This is another kind of their disbelief which Allah related about them. By ﴿those who associated﴾ here is meant the people of Makkah. ﴿Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾, that is, had He willed that we not worship anything other than Him, we would not have worshipped that. ﴿Neither we nor our fathers﴾ who were upon what we are upon now of the religion of disbelief and of associating others with Allah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 41–50 (part 1 of 2):

.
The precise meaning of hijrah (migration, leaving one's family and homeland) has already been established in Surah al-Nisa'. The phrase ﴿hajaru fi Allah﴾ means: for the sake of Allah, seeking His pleasure. It was also said that "in Allah" means "in the religion of Allah." It was also said that "fi" here carries the meaning of "li" (for), i.e., for Allah. ﴿min ba'di ma zulimu﴾ means: after they had been wronged, that is, tortured and humiliated. The people of Makkah tortured a group of the Muslims until they said what [the polytheists] wanted from them. When [the polytheists] left them alone, they emigrated.
There is a difference of opinion regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse. It was said: it was revealed concerning Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab, and Ammar.
It was objected that the surah is Meccan, and that this contradicts His saying ﴿wa alladhina hajaru﴾ (and those who emigrated).
It was answered that this verse may be among the Medinan verses in this surah, as we mentioned in its introduction. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ when the polytheists in Makkah wronged them and expelled them, until a group of them joined [the migration] to Abyssinia.
﴿la-nubawwi'annahum fi al-dunya hasanah﴾: The meaning of this has been disputed in several opinions. It was said that what is meant is their settling in Madinah; this was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, and Qatadah. It was said that what is meant is good provision; this was said by Mujahid. It was said that it is victory over their enemy; this was said by al-Dahhak. It was said that it is what they conquered of the lands and the governorships they obtained there. It was said that it is the good praise that remained for them and the nobility that came to their descendants.
There is no barrier to applying the verse to all of these matters. (p-783) The meaning of ﴿la-nubawwi'annahum fi al-dunya hasanah﴾ is: We will surely settle them in a good settlement, or a good settling. So ﴿hasanah﴾ is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun. ﴿wa la-ajru al-akhirah﴾ means: the reward for their deeds in the Hereafter is greater than anyone among Allah's creation can know before witnessing it. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa idha ra'ayta thamma ra'ayta na'iman wa mulkan kabira﴾ (Al-Insan: 20). ﴿law kanu ya'lamun﴾ means: if these wrongdoers knew that. It was also said that the pronoun in ya'lamun refers to the believers, i.e., if they saw the reward of the Hereafter and witnessed it, they would know that it is greater than the good of this world.
﴿alladhina sabaru﴾: The relative clause is in the accusative position as a praise, or in the nominative by supposing an implied subject, or it is a substitute for the first relative pronoun, or for the pronoun in ﴿la-nubawwi'annahum﴾. ﴿wa 'ala rabbihim yatawakkalun﴾ means: upon their Lord alone they rely in all their affairs, turning away from everything else. The clause is conjoined to the relative clause, or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.
﴿wa ma arsalna min qablika illa rijalan nuhi ilayhim﴾: Hafs, from Asim, read nuhi with the nun; the rest read yuha with the yā' (the verb in the passive). This verse is a refutation of Quraysh, who claimed that Allah, exalted is He, is too great to send a messenger from among humans. Allah refuted them by saying that this is His custom and practice: He sends only men from among humans to whom He reveals.
Abu Ali al-Jubba'i claimed that the meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, did not send His revelation to the prophets except through one who is in the form of men from among the angels.
This is refuted by the fact that Jibril used to come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in different forms.
Since the disbelievers of Makkah acknowledged that the Jews and Christians are the people of knowledge concerning what Allah revealed in the Torah and the Gospel, He turned the address to them and commanded them to return to the People of the Book, saying: ﴿fas'alu ahl al-dhikr in kuntum la ta'lamun﴾ (ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know). That is: ask, O polytheists, the believing People of the Book, if you do not know, for they will inform you that all the prophets were humans. Or: ask the People of the Book without restricting it to their believers, as the apparent wording indicates, for they used to acknowledge that and not conceal it. It was also said that the meaning is: ask the people of the Qur'an.
﴿bil-bayyinat wa al-zuburi﴾ is connected to ﴿arsalna﴾, so it falls under the rule of the exception together with ﴿rijalan﴾. Al-Farra' rejected this.
He said: the modifier of what precedes ﴿illa﴾ does not come after it, because the thing excepted from is the whole of what precedes ﴿illa﴾ together with its complement. For example, if one said "We sent, except men, with clear proofs," since this whole has not been mentioned in its entirety, it is impermissible to place the exception upon it. It was said that there is inversion in the sentence, and the implied sense is: "And We did not send before you with clear proofs and scriptures except men." It was said: it is connected to a deleted element indicated by what was mentioned, i.e., "We sent them with clear proofs and scriptures," and it serves as an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "For what did He send them?" and He said: "We sent them with clear proofs and scriptures." It was said: it is connected to ﴿ta'lamun﴾ with it as its object, and the ba' is extra, i.e., "if you do not know by means of the clear proofs and scriptures." It was said: it is connected to ﴿rijalan﴾, i.e., men clothed with the clear proofs and scriptures. It was said: it is connected to ﴿nuhi﴾, i.e., We reveal to them with the clear proofs and scriptures. It was said: it is in the accusative by an implied "I mean," and the ba' is extra. And ﴿ahl al-dhikr﴾ are the People of the Book, as previously mentioned.
Al-Zajjaj said: ask everyone who is mentioned as having knowledge. The clear proofs (al-bayyinat) are the arguments and demonstrations, and the scriptures (al-zubur) are the books.
This matter has already been discussed in Al 'Imran.
﴿wa anzalna ilayka al-dhikr﴾ means: the Qur'an. Then He stated the purpose sought from the revelation, saying: ﴿li-tubayyina li-l-nas﴾ (so that you may clarify for the people), all of them, ﴿ma nuzzila ilayhim﴾ (what was sent down to them) in this reminder of legal rulings, promise, and warning, ﴿wa la'allahum yatafakkarun﴾ means: in hope that they will reflect and apply their minds, so that they may take heed.
﴿afa-amina alladhina makaru al-sayyi'at﴾: It is possible that al-sayyi'at is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, i.e., they plotted evil plots. It is possible that it is the object of the mentioned verb, by embedding in it the meaning of "to do," i.e., they did evil deeds. Or it is an adjective of a deleted object, i.e., "Are those who plot safe from the evil punishments?" Or by deleting the preposition, i.e., they plotted with evil deeds. ﴿an yakhsifa Allahu bihim al-ardh﴾: this is the object of amina, or a substitute for its object according to the view that its object is deleted and that al-sayyi'at is an adjective of the deleted object. The interrogation is for rebuke and reproach. The plotting of evil deeds is their striving to harm the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions secretly, and their scheming to nullify Islam and the devices of its people. ﴿an yakhsifa Allahu bihim﴾ means: as He caused Qarun to be swallowed up. One says: "khusifa al-makan yakhsifu khusufan," meaning it went into the earth; and "khasafa Allahu bihi al-ardh khusufan," meaning He caused it to sink into the earth with him. From this is His saying: ﴿fa-khasafna bihi wa bi-darihi al-ard﴾ (Al-Qasas: 81). "Khusifa huwa fi al-ard" means he was swallowed into the earth, and "khusifa bihi" means he was caused to sink. ﴿aw ya'tiyahumu al-'adhabu min haythu la yash'urun﴾ means: the punishment comes upon them from a direction they do not perceive, while they are heedless of it, as He did to the people of Lut and others. It was said: it refers to the day of Badr, for they were destroyed that day when it was not in their reckoning.
﴿aw ya'khudhahum fi taqallubihim﴾: The exegetes mentioned several meanings for this. It was said: what is meant is during their journeys and trading, for He, exalted is He, is able to destroy them while traveling just as He destroys them at home, and they cannot escape Him by means of their traveling in the land and their distance from their homelands. It was said: what is meant is during their turning about in fulfilling their needs by finding stratagems, so Allah will come between them and their aims and stratagems. It was said: during their turning at night on their beds. It was said: during their coming and going, and their departing and returning, by day and by night. The meaning of "turning" (taqallub) in the first sense is taken from His saying: ﴿la yaghurrannaka taqallubu alladhina kafaru fi al-bilad﴾ (Al 'Imran: 196), and in the second sense it is taken from His saying: ﴿wa qallabu laka al-umur﴾ (At-Tawbah: 48). ﴿fa-ma hum bi-mu'jizin﴾ means: they cannot escape nor prevent it.
﴿aw ya'khudahum 'ala takhawwuf﴾ means: in a state of apprehension and expectation of calamities, such that they are anticipating the punishment, fearful of it, not heedless of it. This is contrary to what preceded in His saying ﴿aw ya'tiyahumu al-'adhabu min haythu la yash'urun﴾. It was said that the meaning of ﴿'ala takhawwuf﴾ is "upon diminishing." Ibn al-A'rabi said: that is, upon a diminishing of wealth, lives, and fruits until He destroys them.
Al-Wahidi said: most exegetes said: ("'ala takhawwuf") means diminishing, either by killing or by death, meaning by a reduction from their extremities and their regions, He takes them first, then first, until the seizing comes upon all of them.
He said: and takhawwuf means tanaqqus (diminution). One says: "he takhawwafa the wealth," meaning he diminishes it and takes from its edges. End of quote. (p-184) It is said: "takhawwafahu al-dahr" and "takhawwanahu" (with fa' and nun), meaning time diminished him. Dhu al-Rummah said:
"No, it is longing for a dwelling that the passing clouds and the dry winds have worn away."
And Labid said:
"My dismounting and my departing have diminished its flesh and its fat."
Al-Haytham ibn Adi said: takhawwuf with the fa' means diminution in the language of the Azd Shanu'ah, and he recited:
"Their enemy diminished my wealth, while they gave away chains upon the necks that ring."
It was said: ﴿'ala takhawwuf﴾ means "hastily," as said by al-Layth ibn Sa'd. It was said: "with reproach for what they had committed of their sins," as narrated from Ibn Abbas. It was said: ﴿'ala takhawwuf﴾ means: that He punishes and overlooks, as said by Qatadah. ﴿fa-inna rabbakum la-ra'ufun rahim﴾ means: He does not hasten, but gives respite out of compassion and mercy toward you, despite their deserving punishment.
﴿awa lam yarawu ila ma khalaqa Allahu min shay'﴾: When He, exalted is He, warned the schemers with what He warned them, He followed it with the mention of what indicates the perfection of His power in arranging the affairs of the upper and lower worlds and their places. The interrogative in ﴿awa lam yarawu﴾ is for denial. Ma is indefinite and is explained by "min shay'" (of any thing). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and al-A'mash read "tarawu" with the second-person (ta'), addressing all people. The rest read it with the third-person (ya'), referring the pronoun back to "those who plotted the evil deeds."
Abu Amr and Ya'qub read "tatafayya'u zilaluhu" with the ta'. The rest read it with the ya', and Abu Ubayd preferred it. That is: it inclines from side to side, and at the beginning of the day it is in one state and it contracts, then at the end of the day it returns to another state.
Al-Azhari said: tafayyu' of shadows is their returning after midday, so tafayyu' occurs only in the afternoon and in what the sun and the moon have turned away from; what occurs in the morning is shadow (zill).
Tha'lab said: I was told on the authority of Abu Ubaydah that Ru'bah said: "Whatever the sun was upon and then left, that is fay' (returned shade), and whatever the sun was not upon, that is zill (shadow)." The meaning of "min shay'" is "from a thing that has a shadow," which is bodies. It is general in wording, but the specific is intended. ﴿zilaluhu﴾ is the plural of zill, and it is attached to a singular noun because it is singular in form but intends plurality. ﴿'an al-yamini wa al-shama'il﴾ means: from the direction of their right sides and their left sides, that is, from the two sides of each one of them.
Al-Farra' said: He made "right" (al-yamin) singular because He intended one of the things that have shadows, and He made "left" (al-shama'il) plural because He intended all of them, since ﴿ma khalaqa Allah﴾ is singular in wording and plural in meaning.
Al-Wahidi said: He made "right" singular while intending the whole, for conciseness of expression, like His saying: ﴿wa yuwallunna al-duburu﴾ (Al-Qamar: 45). The plural "left" indicates that the intended meaning is plural. It was said that when the Arabs mention two plural forms, they express one of them with the singular form, like His saying: ﴿wa ja'ala al-zulumati wa al-nur﴾ (Al-An'am: 1), and ﴿khatama Allahu 'ala qulubihim wa 'ala sam'ihim﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 7). It was also said that "right" refers to the point where the sun rises, and that it is one. The "left" is an expression for the deviation in the orbit of shadows after they fall upon the earth, and that is many. He expressed the east by "right" because the stronger side of a human being is his right, and from it the strong movement appears. ﴿sujjadan li-Allah﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, i.e., the shadows are prostrating to Allah.
Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that these things are created upon obedience.
He also said: the prostration of a body is its submission, and what is seen of the trace of the craftsmanship. ﴿wa hum dakhirun﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, i.e., humbled and abased. Al-dukhur is lowliness and humiliation. One says: "dakhara al-rajulu fahuwa dakhir," and "adkharahu Allah" (Allah made him abased).
The poet said:
"Nothing remained but one abased in a pen, and one who hides in a hole other than your land, in a den."

Mukhayyas: the name of a prison that was in Iraq.

﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures that move﴾, that is, to Him alone submits and yields, not to other than Him, whatever is in the heavens entirely, and whatever is on the earth of creatures that crawl upon the earth; what is meant by it is every creature.

Al-Akhfash said: it is like your saying, "No man came to me like him," and "No men came to me, his likeness."

And within the generality of "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" enters all the things that exist in them both. He singled out the creature (dābbah) for mention because it is already known from His saying: ﴿Have they not considered what things Allah has created?﴾ that inanimate objects also submit. The mention of the angels after those before them (is by way of) honouring them and magnifying them, as they are included in what is conjoined to: ﴿and they are not arrogant﴾, that is, while they are not arrogant against worshipping their Lord. What is meant is the angels, and it is possible that the sentence is a new (independent) sentence.

In this there is a refutation of the Quraysh, when they claimed that the angels are the daughters of Allah. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "prostrates" and what is conjoined to it, that is: prostrating to Allah are whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and the angels, and they all are not arrogant against prostrating.

﴿They fear their Lord from above them﴾. This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, that is: while they fear their Lord from above them; or it is a new sentence explaining the negation of their arrogance, and among the effects of fear is not being arrogant. "From above them" is connected to "they fear," with an omitted noun, that is: they fear the punishment of their Lord from above them. Or it may be a circumstantial clause from "the Lord," meaning: they fear their Lord while He is from above them. It has been said that the meaning of ﴿they fear their Lord from above them﴾ is that they fear the angels, so it would be with an omitted noun, that is: they fear the angels of their Lord existing from above them; but this is a forced reading with no need for it. What necessitated such distant interpretations is the defence of positions that have taken firm root in minds and become settled in hearts. It has been said: this fear is the fear of reverence, and al-Zajjaj chose it, saying: ﴿they fear their Lord﴾ with the fear of those who revere. What confirms this meaning is His saying: ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 61], and His saying, reporting about Pharaoh: ﴿And indeed We are over them dominant﴾ [al-A'raf: 127].

﴿And they do what they are commanded﴾, that is, what they are commanded with of obedience to Allah: meaning the angels, or all of those previously mentioned. Taking these clauses as referring to the angels is preferable, because among the creatures of Allah there are those who are arrogant against His worship, who do not fear Him and do not do what they are commanded, such as the disbelievers and the disobedient who do not possess these attributes, and Iblis and his hosts.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And those who emigrated for Allah after they had been wronged﴾, he said: they are a people from the people of Makkah who emigrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after their being wronged.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi (p-785) Hatim and Ibn ʿAsakir transmitted from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, who said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And those who emigrated for Allah﴾ (the verse), he said: these are the companions of Muhammad. The people of Makkah wronged them and expelled them from their homes, until groups of them reached the land of Abyssinia. Then Allah settled them in Madinah after that, made it a abode of emigration for them, and made for them helpers from among the believers. ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater﴾, he said, meaning, by Allah, what Allah bestows upon them of His Paradise and His blessing is greater ﴿if only they knew﴾.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Shaʿbi, regarding His saying: ﴿in this world a good [place]﴾, he said: Madinah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding the verse, he said: ﴿We will surely settle them in this world with a good provision.﴾

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "When Allah sent Muhammad as a messenger, the Arabs denied that, so Allah revealed: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him regarding His saying: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder﴾ (the verse), meaning the polytheists of Quraysh, that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah in the Torah and the Gospel.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and a group of the people of the Torah.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding His saying: "with the clear proofs," he said: the signs, and "the scriptures," he said: the books.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿Then are those who plot evil deeds secure﴾, he said: Nimrod ibn Kanʿan and his people.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah regarding the verse, he said: that is, the polytheism.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: their denial of the messengers and their engagement in acts of disobedience.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿Or He seizes them in their going back and forth﴾, he said: in their differing. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "in their going back and forth," he said: if You wish, He seizes him in his journey. ﴿Or He seizes them with gradual decline﴾, meaning: after the death of their companion.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "with gradual decline," he said: a diminishing of their deeds.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from ʿUmar that he asked them about this verse, "Or He seizes them with gradual decline." They said: "We see nothing except that it is with the decrease of what he holds of the signs." ʿUmar said: "I see nothing except that it is upon what they diminish of the disobediences to Allah." A man from among those who were with ʿUmar then went out and met a Bedouin, and said: "O so-and-so, what has your Lord done?" He said: "I have taḥayyafa Him," meaning: I have diminished Him. He returned to ʿUmar and informed him, and he said: "I have indeed seen it so."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿Or He seizes them with gradual decline﴾, he said: He seizes them by the diminishing of some of them by others.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "yatafayya'u" (shadows), he said: "yatamayyalu" (incline).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And they are humbled (dākhirūn)﴾, he said: "ṣāghirūn" (abased).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid the like of it.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah regarding His saying: "And to Allah prostrates" (the verse), he said: He has left nothing of His creation except that it has been made to worship Him, whether willingly or unwillingly.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan regarding the verse, he said: whoever is in the heavens prostrates willingly, and whoever is on the earth prostrates willingly and unwillingly.
