"Min" (from) here is partitive, because the good things are not all gathered together except in Paradise. Then Allah, glorified is He, concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Then is it in falsehood that they believe?﴾ The interrogation is for reproachful denial, and the "fa" is for coordination with an implied element, meaning: they disbelieve in Allah and so believe in falsehood. "Bi al-batil" (in falsehood) has been placed before the verb to indicate that they have no faith except in it. The falsehood is their belief about their idols that they harm and benefit. It is said the falsehood is what Satan adorned for them of forbidding the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah and similar things.

The majority read ﴿yu'minun﴾ with the third person, and Abu Bakr read it with the second person, in address: ﴿And in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve﴾, meaning what He has bestowed upon them, which cannot be encompassed by enumeration. The placement of "the blessing" first and the insertion of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) is evidence that their disbelief is specifically concerning that, and does not go beyond it, for the sake of emphasis and intensification.

﴿And they worship other than Allah﴾: this is coordinated with "they disbelieve" and falls under the reproachful denial, a denial from Him, glorified is He, against them, since they worship idols, which neither benefit nor harm. For this He said: ﴿what does not possess for them any provision from the heavens and the earth at all﴾. Al-Akhfash said: shay'an (at all) is a substitute (badal) for "provision."

Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative by the application of "provision" to it, making rizqan (provision) a verbal noun operating on shay'an. Al-Akhfash made it a noun for provision. It is said it may be an emphasis for His saying ﴿does not possess﴾, meaning they do not possess any part of possession. The meaning is: these disbelievers worship objects of worship that do not possess for them any provision whatsoever. And ﴿from the heavens and the earth﴾ is a description of "provision," meaning existing from them both. The pronoun in ﴿and they are not able﴾ refers to "what" (ma), and it was made plural in the manner of rational beings according to their false assumption. The benefit of negating ability from them is that one who does not possess anything may be described as having the ability to acquire possession by some means; so He, glorified is He, explained that they neither possess nor are able. It is said: the pronoun in "they are able" may refer to the disbelievers, meaning: these disbelievers, despite being living and acting, are not able, so how about lifeless things that have no life and are not able to act?

Then He, glorified is He, forbade them from likening Him to His creation, and so He said: ﴿So do not strike for Allah examples﴾, for the one who strikes an example likens a state to a state and a story to a story.

Al-Zajjaj said: Do not make for Allah a likeness, for He is One, having no likeness. They used to say: the God of the world is too exalted to be worshipped directly by any one of us, so they sought intercession through idols and stars, just as the lesser people serve the greater ones in the presence of the king, and those greater ones serve the king. So they were forbidden from that, and He gave the reason for the prohibition with His saying: Indeed Allah is All-Knowing, He knows what worship is upon you ﴿while you do not know﴾ what in worshipping them is of bad consequence and exposure to the punishment of Allah, glorified is He; or you do not know anything of that at all, and your action is from a corrupt assumption, a false thought, and a disordered imagination. It is also permissible that the meaning is: "So do not strike for Allah examples": Indeed Allah knows how examples are struck, while you do not know that.

Ibn Jarir reported from 'Ali, regarding His saying ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾, that he said: seventy-five years.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, who said: it is senility (al-kharaf).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an will not be returned to the most abject age," then he recited ﴿so that he will not know anything after knowledge﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Tawus, who said: the scholar does not become senile.

It is established from him (ﷺ) in the Sahih and elsewhere that "he used to seek refuge in Allah from being returned to the most abject age."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾, that he said: They would not make their slaves partners with them in their wealth and their women, so how would they make My slaves partners with Me in My dominion?

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding the verse, that he said: this is a parable for the false gods along with Allah.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah regarding His saying ﴿And Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾, that he said: He created Adam, then He created his wife from him.

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying ﴿sons and grandchildren﴾, that he said: al-hafadah are the in-laws.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: al-hafadah are the in-laws (al-aṣhār).

Both of them reported from him, who said: al-hafadah are the child and the child's child.

Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him, who said: al-hafadah are the sons of sons.

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu Jamrah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas was asked about His saying ﴿sons and grandchildren﴾, and he said: Whoever helps you has served you (hafadak). Have you not heard the poet saying:
"The maidservants hastened around them, and the reins of the camels submitted to their hands."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: "al-Hafadah (grandchildren, the sons of a man's wife) are not from him."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah regarding ﴿Will they then believe in falsehood?﴾ He said: "It is shirk (associating partners with God)."

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj who said: "It is the devil." ﴿And the favour of God﴾ — he said: "It is Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿And they worship besides God﴾ (the verse), he said: "These are the idols that are worshipped besides God; they do not possess for those who worship them ﴿any provision from the heavens and the earth﴾, nor any good, nor life, nor resurrection. ﴿So do not strike forth comparisons for God﴾, for He is the One, the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad), who has not begotten nor been begotten, and there is none comparable to Him."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas regarding His, glory be to Him, words: ﴿So do not strike forth comparisons for God﴾, meaning their taking of idols. He says: "Do not make another god alongside Me, for there is no god other than Me."

So they should not think that they give them anything; it is only My provision that I cause to flow through their hands, and they are all equal in that, having no superiority over their slaves. Thus the implied element coordinated with would be a verb suited to this meaning, as if it were said: "They do not understand that, so they deny the blessing of Allah."

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the other state of man's conditions, and so He said: ﴿And Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾. The exegetes said: meaning women, for He created Hawwa' from the rib of Adam. Or the meaning is: He created for you spouses from your own kind, so that you might find companionship in them, because a kind finds companionship with its own kind and is uneasy with other than its kind. Through this companionship occurs between men and women that which is the cause of offspring, which is the aim of marriage. For this reason He said: ﴿And He has made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren (hafadah)﴾. Al-hafadah is the plural of hafid; it is said hafada yahfidu hafdan and hufudan: when he hastens. So everyone who hastens in service is a hafid. Abu 'Ubayd said: al-hafd is work and service.

Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: al-hafadah among the Arabs are servants, and from this is the verse of the poet, who is al-A'sha:

That is, the servants and helpers.

"Had my soul obeyed me, there would have become for her many a hafad among those counted."
"But it is a soul proud over me, averse to the in-laws of the base, abhorrent."
It is said: al-hafadah are the in-laws (al-aṣhār).

Al-Asma'i said: al-khatn is whoever is from the woman's side, like her son, her brother and the like, and al-aṣhār are from both of them together. It is said: so-and-so became in-laws (asharah) to the sons of so-and-so and intermarried (sahara). It is said: they are the children of a man's wife from another husband. It is said: they are the children who serve him. It is said: they are daughters serving their father.

Many scholars preferred that they are the children of children, because He, glorified is He, bestowed a favour upon His servants by making for them sons and grandchildren from their spouses. The grandchildren are apparently conjoined to the sons, though it is permissible that the meaning be: He made for you sons from your spouses and made for you grandchildren. But on this apparent meaning, it is not impossible that "sons" refers to those who do not serve, and "grandchildren" refers to those among them who serve the father; or "grandchildren" refers only to daughters. Then Allah, glorified is He, concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Then is it in falsehood that they believe?﴾ The interrogation is for reproachful denial, and the "fa" is for coordination with an implied element, meaning: they disbelieve in Allah and so believe in falsehood. It is said the falsehood is what Satan adorned for them of forbidding the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah and similar things.

The majority read ﴿yu'minun﴾ with the third person, and Abu Bakr read it with the second person, in address: ﴿And in the blessing of Allah they disbelieve﴾, meaning what He has bestowed upon them, which cannot be encompassed by enumeration. The placement of "the blessing" first and the insertion of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) is evidence that their disbelief is specifically concerning that, and does not go beyond it, for the sake of emphasis and intensification.

﴿And they worship other than Allah﴾: this is coordinated with "they disbelieve" and falls under the reproachful denial, a denial from Him, glorified is He, against them, since they worship idols, which neither benefit nor harm. The meaning is: these disbelievers worship objects of worship that do not possess for them any provision whatsoever. The pronoun in ﴿and they are not able﴾ refers to "what" (ma), and it was made plural in the manner of rational beings according to their false assumption. It is said: the pronoun in "they are able" may refer to the disbelievers, meaning: these disbelievers, despite being living and acting, are not able, so how about lifeless things that have no life and are not able to act?

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "So do not strike for Allah examples": Indeed Allah knows how examples are struck, while you do not know that.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi, who said: it is senility (al-kharaf).

God struck a parable: a slave owned, who has no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with a goodly provision from Us, so that he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to God; but most of them do not know.

God struck another parable: two men, one of them dumb, who has no power over anything and is a burden on his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who enjoins justice and is on a straight path?

To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or nearer. Indeed God is competent over all things.

God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts, that you may be grateful.

Have they not seen the birds made subservient in the expanse of the sky? Nothing holds them up except God. Surely in that are signs for a people who believe.

(Commentary of al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on surah 16, verses 75–80, part 1 of 2)

God's statement, ﴿God struck a parable﴾: when He, glorified is He, said that God knows (i.e., with the things known, among which is how He strikes parables) while you do not know, He taught them, glorified is He, how parables are struck, so He said: ﴿God struck a parable﴾, i.e., He mentioned something by which one may infer the difference in state between the Creator, glorified is He, and what they had made His partner among the idols. Then He mentioned that, saying: ﴿a slave owned﴾. The mathal (parable, example) is in reality a condition of the slave that befalls him, namely being owned and being incapable of disposing of anything. So His statement ﴿a slave owned who has no power over anything﴾ is an explanation of the parable and a substitute for it. He described him as owned because the slave and the free man are both shared in each being a slave of God, glorified is He. He described him as ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ because the mukatab (a slave contracted for manumission) and the ma'dhun (a slave licensed to trade) have power over some dispositions; so this description serves to distinguish him from them. ﴿And one whom We have provided﴾: man here is the relative pronoun, and it is coordinated with "a slave", i.e., "and one whom We have provided from Us", i.e., from Our side, ﴿with a goodly provision﴾ from the free men who own wealth and dispose of it as they wish. The meaning of the provision being goodly is that it is of what is pleasing in the eyes of people, being abundant provision containing precious, pleasing things that delight those who look at it. The fa' in His statement ﴿so he spends from it﴾ indicates the sequence of spending upon the provision, i.e., he spends from it in the ways of goodness and directs from it to kinds of righteousness and kindness. The accusative of ﴿secretly and openly﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl), i.e., he spends from it in the state of secrecy and in the state of openness. The purpose is to show the generality of spending across times, and the mention of secrecy before openness indicates its superiority over it and that the reward for it is greater. It has been said that man in ﴿and one whom We have provided﴾ is a descriptive (mawṣūfa), as if it were said: "and a free man whom We have provided", to correspond with "a slave". ﴿Are they equal?﴾, i.e., the free man and the slave described with the aforementioned attributes. The pronoun is in the plural because of the position of man, since it is an indefinite noun in which one, two, plural, masculine and feminine are equal. It has also been said that by the slave and the one who is joined by the relative pronoun, which is an expression for the free man, is meant the genus, i.e., whoever is characterized by those attributes from both kinds. The interrogation is for denial, i.e., are the slaves and the free men characterized by those attributes equal, while both groups are created by God, glorified is He, from among mankind? It is known that they are not equal in their own estimation. So how do they make partners for God, glorified is He, that do not possess for them harm or benefit, and make them deserving of worship alongside God, glorified is He? The sum of the meaning: just as a owned slave who has no power over his affairs and a free man whom God has provided with a goodly provision, so that he spends from it, are not equal in your sight, so likewise the Lord, the Creator, the Provider, and the lifeless idols that you worship, which neither see nor hear nor harm nor benefit, are not equal. It has been said that what is meant by the owned slave in the verse is the disbeliever deprived of obedience to God and servitude to Him, and "the other" (p-٧٩٤) is the believer, and the purpose is that the two are not equal in rank and nobility. It has been said: the slave is the idol, and the second is the worshipper of the idol, and what is meant is that the two are not equal in power and disposal, because the first is an inanimate object and the second is a human being. ﴿Praise be to God﴾, i.e., all praise belongs to God, because He is the Benefactor; no servant other than Him deserves any part of it. How then would the idols deserve any part of it, when they have no blessing from them at all, neither originally nor by intermediation? It has been said that He meant: praise be to God for what He has bestowed upon His friends of the blessing of monotheism. It has been said that He meant: "Say: praise be to God", and the address is either to Muhammad (ﷺ) or to the one whom God has provided with a goodly provision. It has been said: when He mentioned a parable corresponding to the purpose and revealing the intended meaning, He said: "Praise be to God", i.e., for the strength of this argument. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that, so that they would worship the One who deserves worship and recognize the Benefactor who bestowed on them the magnificent blessings. The negation of knowledge from them is either because they are in a state of ignorance such that they do not comprehend by its means what is obligatory upon them, or they abandon the truth out of obstinacy while knowing it, so they are like one who has no knowledge. He restricted the negation of knowledge to "most": either because He intends all creation, and most of them are polytheists, or He mentioned "most" and intends all, or what is meant is most of the polytheists, because among them are those who know but do not act according to the requirement of knowledge.

Then, glorified is He, mentioned a second parable which He struck for Himself, and for what He pours upon His servants of religious and worldly blessings, and for the idols, which are dead and neither harm nor benefit. So He said: ﴿And God struck a parable﴾, i.e., another parable, clearer and more manifest than what came before it. ﴿And two men﴾ is a substitute for "a parable" and an explanation of it. The abkam (dumb) is the one who is incapable of speech and tongue-tied. It has been said that he is the one whose tongue is cut off and who does not speak well. Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi that he is the one who neither hears nor sees. Then He described the dumb man, saying: ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ of the things related to himself or to others, because of his lack of understanding and his inability to speak. The meaning of ﴿a burden upon his master﴾ is: a heavy weight upon his guardian and kin, a dependant upon whoever takes charge of his affairs and supports him, and a calamity upon his brothers. The orphan is sometimes called kall (burden) because of his heaviness upon the one who sponsors him; from this is the poet's saying:

"Devourer of the wealth of the burden before his youth, when the bone of the burden is not strong."

In this is an explanation of his inability to establish the interests of his own self after the mention of his inability to do anything absolutely.

Then He described him with a fourth attribute, saying: ﴿wherever he directs him, he brings no good﴾, i.e., whenever he directs him to any direction, he never brings any good at all, because he does not understand nor comprehend what is said to him, and he is not able to say anything.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿wherever he is directed﴾ in the passive voice, and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wherever he turns﴾ in the past tense form. ﴿Is he equal, he himself,﴾ in his own person with these attributes that he has? ﴿And one who enjoins justice﴾, i.e., who commands people to justice, while he himself speaks what he wishes to say and understands, and is able to dispose of things, ﴿on a straight path﴾, i.e., on an upright religion and a righteous way of conduct, free of any inclination toward either extreme of excess or deficiency. He matched the attributes of the first with these two attributes of the second, because the sum of the first's attributes is his not deserving anything, while the sum of the second's attributes is that he deserves the most perfect deservingness. The purpose is to infer, from the non-equality of these two mentioned, the impossibility of equality between Him, glorified is He, and what they make a partner to Him.

When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the two parables, He praised Himself with His statement: ﴿To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., that belongs exclusively to Him; no other shares in it and none independently possesses it. What is meant is that He knows what is hidden from the servants in both of them, or He intends by their unseen the Day of Resurrection, because His knowledge is hidden from the servants. The meaning of the idafa (genitive construction) to them both is the connection with them.

The meaning: a rebuke and reprimand for the polytheists, i.e., that worship is only deserved by one who has these attributes, not by one who is ignorant, incapable, who neither harms nor benefits, and knows nothing of any kind of knowledge. ﴿And the matter of the Hour﴾, which is the greatest thing in which disputes occur among the unseen matters exclusive to Him, glorified is He, ﴿is but as a glance of the eye﴾. The lamh (glance) is looking swiftly, and there must be in it a time in which the pupil turns toward the seen object, and every time is divisible. For this reason He said: ﴿or it is nearer﴾, i.e., their matter is nearer. This is not from the category of hyperbole; rather it is a statement of utmost truth, because the duration between the address and the establishment of the Hour is finite, and from it to eternity is infinite, and there is no ratio of the finite to the infinite. Or it may be said: since the Hour is certainly coming, it was made as near as a glance of the eye.

Al-Zajjaj said: He did not mean that the Hour comes in the blink of an eye; rather He described the swiftness of the power to bring it about, because He says to a thing "Be," and it is. It has been said: the meaning is: it is so with God, even if it is not so with created beings. A similar statement is His, glorified is He: ﴿They see it as far, but We see it as near﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 6–7]. The word "or" in ﴿or it is nearer﴾ is not for doubt, but for comparison. It has been said that it entered for the doubt of the addressee. It has been said that it is in the position of "rather" (bal). ﴿Indeed God is competent over all things﴾, and the coming of the Hour swiftly is among the things within His power.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned another state of man which indicates the utmost of His power and the extent of His compassion, so He said: ﴿And God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing﴾. This is coordinated with His statement: ﴿And God made for you from yourselves spouses﴾, and is linked with it in the string of proofs of monotheism, i.e., He brought you out from the wombs of your mothers as infants with no knowledge of anything. The clause ﴿knowing nothing﴾ is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl). It has been said that what is meant is that you know nothing of what was taken from you in the covenant; it has been said you know nothing of what He decreed upon you of happiness and misery; it has been said you know nothing of your benefits. The better view is generalization, so that the verse includes these matters and others, taking into account the generality of the wording, since shay' (thing) is an indefinite noun in the context of negation.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab and Hamzah read ﴿immahatikum﴾ (your mothers) with a kasra on the hamza and the mim here, and in al-Nur, al-Zumar and al-Najm. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the mim. The rest read with a damma on the hamza and a fatha on the mim.

﴿And made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾, i.e., He set these things in you. It is coordinated with "brought you out", and there is no indication in it that this making is delayed after the bringing out, because what the conjunction wa' signifies is simply joint occurrence. The meaning: He made these things for you so that you might obtain by them the knowledge that was taken from you when you came out from your mothers' wombs, and act in accordance with that knowledge, by thanking the Benefactor, worshipping Him, and fulfilling His rights. (p-٧٩٥) The af'idah (hearts) is the plural of fu'ad, which is the midst of the heart, placed in the same position relative to the heart as the heart relative to the chest. We have already mentioned the reason for the singular "hearing" and plural "sight" and "hearts": that the singular of hearing, being originally a verbal noun, covers the few and the many. ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, i.e., so that you may direct every instrument to what it was created for; then you will recognize the measure of what God has bestowed upon you and thank Him for it, or this directing is itself gratitude.

Then, glorified is He, mentioned another proof of the perfection of His power, saying: ﴿Have they not seen the birds made subservient﴾, i.e., have they not looked at them in the state of being subservient: made submissive to flying by what God has created for them of wings and other means suited to that, such as the thinness of the air's substance, and His inspiring them to spread and fold the wing as a swimmer does in water. ﴿In the atmosphere of the sky﴾, i.e., in the air distant from the earth in the direction of height. Its idafa to the sky is because it is on its side. Nothing holds them up in the air except God, glorified is He, by His overwhelming power, since the weight of their bodies and the thinness of the air's substance would necessitate their falling, for they are not attached to anything above them nor do they rest upon anything beneath them.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Ya'qub read ﴿Have you not seen﴾ with the second-person ta' (i.e., addressing), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The rest read it with the third-person ya'. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., indeed in that subjection in that state are manifest signs indicating the oneness of God, glorified is He, and His overwhelming power, ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glorified is He, and in what His messengers brought of the laws that God legislated.

Al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 75–80 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Allah sets forth an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "It means the disbeliever, that he is not able to spend any expenditure in the way of Allah. ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us﴾ up to the end of the verse, he said: It means the believer. And this example is about spending."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related something similar to it, but more extensive than it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding the verse, and regarding His saying: ﴿Two men, one of them dumb﴾, he said: "All of this is an example: the God of truth and what you invoke besides Him is falsehood."

Ibn al-Mundhir related through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Regarding the first example, he means by it the gods that possess no power to harm or benefit, and are not able to do anything that benefits them." ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly﴾, he said: "The public [act] of the one who spends secretly and openly is for Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir related from him, who said: This verse ﴿Allah sets forth an example: a slave owned﴾ was revealed concerning a man from Quraysh and ʿAbdah ibn Hisham ibn ʿAmr, and he is the one who spends secretly and openly; and concerning ʿAbdah, Abu al-Jawza, who used to forbid him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah sets forth an example: two men, one of them dumb﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "By the dumb one he means the disbeliever, who is a burden upon his master. ﴿And one who enjoins justice﴾ is the believer. And this example is about deeds."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir also related from him, who said: This verse ﴿And Allah sets forth an example: two men﴾ up to the end of the verse was revealed concerning ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan and a disbelieving client of his, who was Usayd ibn Abi al-ʿIs, who disliked Islam. ʿUthman used to spend on him, support him, and relieve him of hardship, while the other one would forbid him from giving charity and doing good. So these verses were revealed concerning the two of them.

Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah related from him also, regarding His saying: ﴿one who enjoins justice﴾, that he said: "ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding His saying: "kall" (a burden), that he said: "Kall means dependents. When they moved on, they would carry him on a docile camel, and place with him a group of men to hold him, lest he fall upon them. So he is a hardship, a torment, and a burden upon them." ﴿Is he equal, he and one who enjoins justice, while he is on a straight path?﴾ meaning himself.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye﴾, that it is His saying "Be," and it is as a glance of the eye ﴿or it is nearer﴾: the Hour is like a glance of the eye, or it is nearer.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers﴾, that he said: "From the womb."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿in the air of the sky﴾, meaning in the midst of the sky.

God struck a parable: a slave owned, who has no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with a goodly provision from Us, so that he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to God; but most of them do not know.

God struck another parable: two men, one of them dumb, who has no power over anything and is a burden on his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who enjoins justice and is on a straight path?

To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or nearer. Indeed God is competent over all things.

God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts, that you may be grateful.

Have they not seen the birds made subservient in the expanse of the sky? Nothing holds them up except God. Surely in that are signs for a people who believe.

Its idafa to the sky is because it is on its side. Nothing holds them up in the air except God, glorified is He, by His overwhelming power, since the weight of their bodies and the thinness of the air's substance would necessitate their falling, for they are not attached to anything above them nor do they rest upon anything beneath them.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Ya'qub read ﴿Have you not seen﴾ with the second-person ta' (i.e., addressing), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The rest read it with the third-person ya'. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., indeed in that subjection in that state are manifest signs indicating the oneness of God, glorified is He, and His overwhelming power, ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glorified is He, and in what His messengers brought of the laws that God legislated.

Al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 75–80 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Allah sets forth an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "It means the disbeliever, that he is not able to spend any expenditure in the way of Allah. ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us﴾ up to the end of the verse, he said: It means the believer. And this example is about spending."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related something similar to it, but more extensive than it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding the verse, and regarding His saying: ﴿Two men, one of them dumb﴾, he said: "All of this is an example: the God of truth and what you invoke besides Him is falsehood."

Ibn al-Mundhir related through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Regarding the first example, he means by it the gods that possess no power to harm or benefit, and are not able to do anything that benefits them." ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly﴾, he said: "The public [act] of the one who spends secretly and openly is for Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir related from him, who said: This verse ﴿Allah sets forth an example: a slave owned﴾ was revealed concerning a man from Quraysh and ʿAbdah ibn Hisham ibn ʿAmr, and he is the one who spends secretly and openly; and concerning ʿAbdah, Abu al-Jawza, who used to forbid him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah sets forth an example: two men, one of them dumb﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "By the dumb one he means the disbeliever, who is a burden upon his master. ﴿And one who enjoins justice﴾ is the believer. And this example is about deeds."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir also related from him, who said: This verse ﴿And Allah sets forth an example: two men﴾ up to the end of the verse was revealed concerning ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan and a disbelieving client of his, who was Usayd ibn Abi al-ʿIs, who disliked Islam. ʿUthman used to spend on him, support him, and relieve him of hardship, while the other one would forbid him from giving charity and doing good. So these verses were revealed concerning the two of them.

Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah related from him also, regarding His saying: ﴿one who enjoins justice﴾, that he said: "ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding His saying: "kall" (a burden), that he said: "Kall means dependents. When they moved on, they would carry him on a docile camel, and place with him a group of men to hold him, lest he fall upon them. So he is a hardship, a torment, and a burden upon them." ﴿Is he equal, he and one who enjoins justice, while he is on a straight path?﴾ meaning himself.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye﴾, that it is His saying "Be," and it is as a glance of the eye ﴿or it is nearer﴾: the Hour is like a glance of the eye, or it is nearer.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers﴾, that he said: "From the womb."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿in the air of the sky﴾, meaning in the midst of the sky.

God struck a parable: a slave owned, who has no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with a goodly provision from Us, so that he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to God; but most of them do not know.

God struck another parable: two men, one of them dumb, who has no power over anything and is a burden on his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who enjoins justice and is on a straight path?

To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or nearer. Indeed God is competent over all things.

God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts, that you may be grateful.

Have they not seen the birds made subservient in the expanse of the sky? Nothing holds them up except God. Surely in that are signs for a people who believe.

(Commentary of al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on surah 16, verses 75–80, part 1 of 2)

God's statement, ﴿God struck a parable﴾: when He, glorified is He, said that God knows (i.e., with the things known, among which is how He strikes parables) while you do not know, He taught them, glorified is He, how parables are struck, so He said: ﴿God struck a parable﴾, i.e., He mentioned something by which one may infer the difference in state between the Creator, glorified is He, and what they had made His partner among the idols. Then He mentioned that, saying: ﴿a slave owned﴾. The mathal (parable, example) is in reality a condition of the slave that befalls him, namely being owned and being incapable of disposing of anything. So His statement ﴿a slave owned who has no power over anything﴾ is an explanation of the parable and a substitute for it. He described him as owned because the slave and the free man are both shared in each being a slave of God, glorified is He. He described him as ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ because the mukatab (a slave contracted for manumission) and the ma'dhun (a slave licensed to trade) have power over some dispositions; so this description serves to distinguish him from them. ﴿And one whom We have provided﴾: man here is the relative pronoun, and it is coordinated with "a slave", i.e., "and one whom We have provided from Us", i.e., from Our side, ﴿with a goodly provision﴾ from the free men who own wealth and dispose of it as they wish. The meaning of the provision being goodly is that it is of what is pleasing in the eyes of people, being abundant provision containing precious, pleasing things that delight those who look at it. The fa' in His statement ﴿so he spends from it﴾ indicates the sequence of spending upon the provision, i.e., he spends from it in the ways of goodness and directs from it to kinds of righteousness and kindness. The accusative of ﴿secretly and openly﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl), i.e., he spends from it in the state of secrecy and in the state of openness. The purpose is to show the generality of spending across times, and the mention of secrecy before openness indicates its superiority over it and that the reward for it is greater. It has been said that man in ﴿and one whom We have provided﴾ is a descriptive (mawṣūfa), as if it were said: "and a free man whom We have provided", to correspond with "a slave". ﴿Are they equal?﴾, i.e., the free man and the slave described with the aforementioned attributes. The pronoun is in the plural because of the position of man, since it is an indefinite noun in which one, two, plural, masculine and feminine are equal. It has also been said that by the slave and the one who is joined by the relative pronoun, which is an expression for the free man, is meant the genus, i.e., whoever is characterized by those attributes from both kinds. The interrogation is for denial, i.e., are the slaves and the free men characterized by those attributes equal, while both groups are created by God, glorified is He, from among mankind? It is known that they are not equal in their own estimation. So how do they make partners for God, glorified is He, that do not possess for them harm or benefit, and make them deserving of worship alongside God, glorified is He? The sum of the meaning: just as a owned slave who has no power over his affairs and a free man whom God has provided with a goodly provision, so that he spends from it, are not equal in your sight, so likewise the Lord, the Creator, the Provider, and the lifeless idols that you worship, which neither see nor hear nor harm nor benefit, are not equal. It has been said that what is meant by the owned slave in the verse is the disbeliever deprived of obedience to God and servitude to Him, and "the other" (p-٧٩٤) is the believer, and the purpose is that the two are not equal in rank and nobility. It has been said: the slave is the idol, and the second is the worshipper of the idol, and what is meant is that the two are not equal in power and disposal, because the first is an inanimate object and the second is a human being. ﴿Praise be to God﴾, i.e., all praise belongs to God, because He is the Benefactor; no servant other than Him deserves any part of it. How then would the idols deserve any part of it, when they have no blessing from them at all, neither originally nor by intermediation? It has been said that He meant: praise be to God for what He has bestowed upon His friends of the blessing of monotheism. It has been said that He meant: "Say: praise be to God", and the address is either to Muhammad (ﷺ) or to the one whom God has provided with a goodly provision. It has been said: when He mentioned a parable corresponding to the purpose and revealing the intended meaning, He said: "Praise be to God", i.e., for the strength of this argument. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that, so that they would worship the One who deserves worship and recognize the Benefactor who bestowed on them the magnificent blessings. The negation of knowledge from them is either because they are in a state of ignorance such that they do not comprehend by its means what is obligatory upon them, or they abandon the truth out of obstinacy while knowing it, so they are like one who has no knowledge. He restricted the negation of knowledge to "most": either because He intends all creation, and most of them are polytheists, or He mentioned "most" and intends all, or what is meant is most of the polytheists, because among them are those who know but do not act according to the requirement of knowledge.

Then, glorified is He, mentioned a second parable which He struck for Himself, and for what He pours upon His servants of religious and worldly blessings, and for the idols, which are dead and neither harm nor benefit. So He said: ﴿And God struck a parable﴾, i.e., another parable, clearer and more manifest than what came before it. ﴿And two men﴾ is a substitute for "a parable" and an explanation of it. The abkam (dumb) is the one who is incapable of speech and tongue-tied. It has been said that he is the one whose tongue is cut off and who does not speak well. Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi that he is the one who neither hears nor sees. Then He described the dumb man, saying: ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ of the things related to himself or to others, because of his lack of understanding and his inability to speak. The meaning of ﴿a burden upon his master﴾ is: a heavy weight upon his guardian and kin, a dependant upon whoever takes charge of his affairs and supports him, and a calamity upon his brothers. The orphan is sometimes called kall (burden) because of his heaviness upon the one who sponsors him; from this is the poet's saying:

"Devourer of the wealth of the burden before his youth, when the bone of the burden is not strong."

In this is an explanation of his inability to establish the interests of his own self after the mention of his inability to do anything absolutely.

Then He described him with a fourth attribute, saying: ﴿wherever he directs him, he brings no good﴾, i.e., whenever he directs him to any direction, he never brings any good at all, because he does not understand nor comprehend what is said to him, and he is not able to say anything.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿wherever he is directed﴾ in the passive voice, and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wherever he turns﴾ in the past tense form. ﴿Is he equal, he himself,﴾ in his own person with these attributes that he has? ﴿And one who enjoins justice﴾, i.e., who commands people to justice, while he himself speaks what he wishes to say and understands, and is able to dispose of things, ﴿on a straight path﴾, i.e., on an upright religion and a righteous way of conduct, free of any inclination toward either extreme of excess or deficiency. He matched the attributes of the first with these two attributes of the second, because the sum of the first's attributes is his not deserving anything, while the sum of the second's attributes is that he deserves the most perfect deservingness. The purpose is to infer, from the non-equality of these two mentioned, the impossibility of equality between Him, glorified is He, and what they make a partner to Him.

When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the two parables, He praised Himself with His statement: ﴿To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., that belongs exclusively to Him; no other shares in it and none independently possesses it. What is meant is that He knows what is hidden from the servants in both of them, or He intends by their unseen the Day of Resurrection, because His knowledge is hidden from the servants. The meaning of the idafa (genitive construction) to them both is the connection with them.

The meaning: a rebuke and reprimand for the polytheists, i.e., that worship is only deserved by one who has these attributes, not by one who is ignorant, incapable, who neither harms nor benefits, and knows nothing of any kind of knowledge. ﴿And the matter of the Hour﴾, which is the greatest thing in which disputes occur among the unseen matters exclusive to Him, glorified is He, ﴿is but as a glance of the eye﴾. The lamh (glance) is looking swiftly, and there must be in it a time in which the pupil turns toward the seen object, and every time is divisible. For this reason He said: ﴿or it is nearer﴾, i.e., their matter is nearer. This is not from the category of hyperbole; rather it is a statement of utmost truth, because the duration between the address and the establishment of the Hour is finite, and from it to eternity is infinite, and there is no ratio of the finite to the infinite. Or it may be said: since the Hour is certainly coming, it was made as near as a glance of the eye.

Al-Zajjaj said: He did not mean that the Hour comes in the blink of an eye; rather He described the swiftness of the power to bring it about, because He says to a thing "Be," and it is. It has been said: the meaning is: it is so with God, even if it is not so with created beings. A similar statement is His, glorified is He: ﴿They see it as far, but We see it as near﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 6–7]. The word "or" in ﴿or it is nearer﴾ is not for doubt, but for comparison. It has been said that it entered for the doubt of the addressee. It has been said that it is in the position of "rather" (bal). ﴿Indeed God is competent over all things﴾, and the coming of the Hour swiftly is among the things within His power.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned another state of man which indicates the utmost of His power and the extent of His compassion, so He said: ﴿And God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing﴾. This is coordinated with His statement: ﴿And God made for you from yourselves spouses﴾, and is linked with it in the string of proofs of monotheism, i.e., He brought you out from the wombs of your mothers as infants with no knowledge of anything. The clause ﴿knowing nothing﴾ is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl). It has been said that what is meant is that you know nothing of what was taken from you in the covenant; it has been said you know nothing of what He decreed upon you of happiness and misery; it has been said you know nothing of your benefits. The better view is generalization, so that the verse includes these matters and others, taking into account the generality of the wording, since shay' (thing) is an indefinite noun in the context of negation.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab and Hamzah read ﴿immahatikum﴾ (your mothers) with a kasra on the hamza and the mim here, and in al-Nur, al-Zumar and al-Najm. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the mim. The rest read with a damma on the hamza and a fatha on the mim.

﴿And made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾, i.e., He set these things in you. It is coordinated with "brought you out", and there is no indication in it that this making is delayed after the bringing out, because what the conjunction wa' signifies is simply joint occurrence. The meaning: He made these things for you so that you might obtain by them the knowledge that was taken from you when you came out from your mothers' wombs, and act in accordance with that knowledge, by thanking the Benefactor, worshipping Him, and fulfilling His rights. (p-٧٩٥) The af'idah (hearts) is the plural of fu'ad, which is the midst of the heart, placed in the same position relative to the heart as the heart relative to the chest. We have already mentioned the reason for the singular "hearing" and plural "sight" and "hearts": that the singular of hearing, being originally a verbal noun, covers the few and the many. ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, i.e., so that you may direct every instrument to what it was created for; then you will recognize the measure of what God has bestowed upon you and thank Him for it, or this directing is itself gratitude.

Then, glorified is He, mentioned another proof of the perfection of His power, saying: ﴿Have they not seen the birds made subservient﴾, i.e., have they not looked at them in the state of being subservient: made submissive to flying by what God has created for them of wings and other means suited to that, such as the thinness of the air's substance, and His inspiring them to spread and fold the wing as a swimmer does in water. ﴿In the atmosphere of the sky﴾, i.e., in the air distant from the earth in the direction of height. Its idafa to the sky is because it is on its side. Nothing holds them up in the air except God, glorified is He, by His overwhelming power, since the weight of their bodies and the thinness of the air's substance would necessitate their falling, for they are not attached to anything above them nor do they rest upon anything beneath them.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Ya'qub read ﴿Have you not seen﴾ with the second-person ta' (i.e., addressing), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The rest read it with the third-person ya'. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., indeed in that subjection in that state are manifest signs indicating the oneness of God, glorified is He, and His overwhelming power, ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glorified is He, and in what His messengers brought of the laws that God legislated.

How then would the idols deserve any part of it, when they have no blessing from them at all, neither originally nor by intermediation? It has been said that He meant: "Say: praise be to God", and the address is either to Muhammad (ﷺ) or to the one whom God has provided with a goodly provision. It has been said: when He mentioned a parable corresponding to the purpose and revealing the intended meaning, He said: "Praise be to God", i.e., for the strength of this argument. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that, so that they would worship the One who deserves worship and recognize the Benefactor who bestowed on them the magnificent blessings. The negation of knowledge from them is either because they are in a state of ignorance such that they do not comprehend by its means what is obligatory upon them, or they abandon the truth out of obstinacy while knowing it, so they are like one who has no knowledge. He restricted the negation of knowledge to "most": either because He intends all creation, and most of them are polytheists, or He mentioned "most" and intends all, or what is meant is most of the polytheists, because among them are those who know but do not act according to the requirement of knowledge.

Then, glorified is He, mentioned a second parable which He struck for Himself, and for what He pours upon His servants of religious and worldly blessings, and for the idols, which are dead and neither harm nor benefit. So He said: ﴿And God struck a parable﴾, i.e., another parable, clearer and more manifest than what came before it. ﴿And two men﴾ is a substitute for "a parable" and an explanation of it. The abkam (dumb) is the one who is incapable of speech and tongue-tied. It has been said that he is the one whose tongue is cut off and who does not speak well. Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi that he is the one who neither hears nor sees. Then He described the dumb man, saying: ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ of the things related to himself or to others, because of his lack of understanding and his inability to speak. The meaning of ﴿a burden upon his master﴾ is: a heavy weight upon his guardian and kin, a dependant upon whoever takes charge of his affairs and supports him, and a calamity upon his brothers. The orphan is sometimes called kall (burden) because of his heaviness upon the one who sponsors him; from this is the poet's saying:

"Devourer of the wealth of the burden before his youth, when the bone of the burden is not strong."

In this is an explanation of his inability to establish the interests of his own self after the mention of his inability to do anything absolutely.

Then He described him with a fourth attribute, saying: ﴿wherever he directs him, he brings no good﴾, i.e., whenever he directs him to any direction, he never brings any good at all, because he does not understand nor comprehend what is said to him, and he is not able to say anything.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿wherever he is directed﴾ in the passive voice, and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wherever he turns﴾ in the past tense form. ﴿Is he equal, he himself,﴾ in his own person with these attributes that he has? ﴿And one who enjoins justice﴾, i.e., who commands people to justice, while he himself speaks what he wishes to say and understands, and is able to dispose of things, ﴿on a straight path﴾, i.e., on an upright religion and a righteous way of conduct, free of any inclination toward either extreme of excess or deficiency. He matched the attributes of the first with these two attributes of the second, because the sum of the first's attributes is his not deserving anything, while the sum of the second's attributes is that he deserves the most perfect deservingness. The purpose is to infer, from the non-equality of these two mentioned, the impossibility of equality between Him, glorified is He, and what they make a partner to Him.

When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the two parables, He praised Himself with His statement: ﴿To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., that belongs exclusively to Him; no other shares in it and none independently possesses it. What is meant is that He knows what is hidden from the servants in both of them, or He intends by their unseen the Day of Resurrection, because His knowledge is hidden from the servants. The meaning of the idafa (genitive construction) to them both is the connection with them.

The meaning: a rebuke and reprimand for the polytheists, i.e., that worship is only deserved by one who has these attributes, not by one who is ignorant, incapable, who neither harms nor benefits, and knows nothing of any kind of knowledge. ﴿And the matter of the Hour﴾, which is the greatest thing in which disputes occur among the unseen matters exclusive to Him, glorified is He, ﴿is but as a glance of the eye﴾. The lamh (glance) is looking swiftly, and there must be in it a time in which the pupil turns toward the seen object, and every time is divisible. For this reason He said: ﴿or it is nearer﴾, i.e., their matter is nearer. This is not from the category of hyperbole; rather it is a statement of utmost truth, because the duration between the address and the establishment of the Hour is finite, and from it to eternity is infinite, and there is no ratio of the finite to the infinite. Or it may be said: since the Hour is certainly coming, it was made as near as a glance of the eye.

Al-Zajjaj said: He did not mean that the Hour comes in the blink of an eye; rather He described the swiftness of the power to bring it about, because He says to a thing "Be," and it is. It has been said: the meaning is: it is so with God, even if it is not so with created beings. A similar statement is His, glorified is He: ﴿They see it as far, but We see it as near﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 6–7]. The word "or" in ﴿or it is nearer﴾ is not for doubt, but for comparison. It has been said that it entered for the doubt of the addressee. It has been said that it is in the position of "rather" (bal). ﴿Indeed God is competent over all things﴾, and the coming of the Hour swiftly is among the things within His power.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned another state of man which indicates the utmost of His power and the extent of His compassion, so He said: ﴿And God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing﴾. This is coordinated with His statement: ﴿And God made for you from yourselves spouses﴾, and is linked with it in the string of proofs of monotheism, i.e., He brought you out from the wombs of your mothers as infants with no knowledge of anything. The clause ﴿knowing nothing﴾ is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl). It has been said that what is meant is that you know nothing of what was taken from you in the covenant; it has been said you know nothing of what He decreed upon you of happiness and misery; it has been said you know nothing of your benefits. The better view is generalization, so that the verse includes these matters and others, taking into account the generality of the wording, since shay' (thing) is an indefinite noun in the context of negation.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab and Hamzah read ﴿immahatikum﴾ (your mothers) with a kasra on the hamza and the mim here, and in al-Nur, al-Zumar and al-Najm. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the mim. The rest read with a damma on the hamza and a fatha on the mim.

﴿And made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾, i.e., He set these things in you. It is coordinated with "brought you out", and there is no indication in it that this making is delayed after the bringing out, because what the conjunction wa' signifies is simply joint occurrence. The meaning: He made these things for you so that you might obtain by them the knowledge that was taken from you when you came out from your mothers' wombs, and act in accordance with that knowledge, by thanking the Benefactor, worshipping Him, and fulfilling His rights. (p-٧٩٥) The af'idah (hearts) is the plural of fu'ad, which is the midst of the heart, placed in the same position relative to the heart as the heart relative to the chest. We have already mentioned the reason for the singular "hearing" and plural "sight" and "hearts": that the singular of hearing, being originally a verbal noun, covers the few and the many. ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, i.e., so that you may direct every instrument to what it was created for; then you will recognize the measure of what God has bestowed upon you and thank Him for it, or this directing is itself gratitude.

Then, glorified is He, mentioned another proof of the perfection of His power, saying: ﴿Have they not seen the birds made subservient﴾, i.e., have they not looked at them in the state of being subservient: made submissive to flying by what God has created for them of wings and other means suited to that, such as the thinness of the air's substance, and His inspiring them to spread and fold the wing as a swimmer does in water. ﴿In the atmosphere of the sky﴾, i.e., in the air distant from the earth in the direction of height. Its idafa to the sky is because it is on its side. Nothing holds them up in the air except God, glorified is He, by His overwhelming power, since the weight of their bodies and the thinness of the air's substance would necessitate their falling, for they are not attached to anything above them nor do they rest upon anything beneath them.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Ya'qub read ﴿Have you not seen﴾ with the second-person ta' (i.e., addressing), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The rest read it with the third-person ya'. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., indeed in that subjection in that state are manifest signs indicating the oneness of God, glorified is He, and His overwhelming power, ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glorified is He, and in what His messengers brought of the laws that God legislated.

Al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 75–80 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Allah sets forth an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "It means the disbeliever, that he is not able to spend any expenditure in the way of Allah. ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us﴾ up to the end of the verse, he said: It means the believer. And this example is about spending."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related something similar to it, but more extensive than it.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding the verse, and regarding His saying: ﴿Two men, one of them dumb﴾, he said: "All of this is an example: the God of truth and what you invoke besides Him is falsehood."

Ibn al-Mundhir related through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Regarding the first example, he means by it the gods that possess no power to harm or benefit, and are not able to do anything that benefits them." ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly﴾, he said: "The public [act] of the one who spends secretly and openly is for Allah."

The mathal (parable, example) is in reality a condition of the slave that befalls him, namely being owned and being incapable of disposing of anything. He described him as owned because the slave and the free man are both shared in each being a slave of God, glorified is He. The meaning of the provision being goodly is that it is of what is pleasing in the eyes of people, being abundant provision containing precious, pleasing things that delight those who look at it. The fa' in His statement ﴿so he spends from it﴾ indicates the sequence of spending upon the provision, i.e., he spends from it in the ways of goodness and directs from it to kinds of righteousness and kindness. The accusative of ﴿secretly and openly﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl), i.e., he spends from it in the state of secrecy and in the state of openness. The purpose is to show the generality of spending across times, and the mention of secrecy before openness indicates its superiority over it and that the reward for it is greater. The pronoun is in the plural because of the position of man, since it is an indefinite noun in which one, two, plural, masculine and feminine are equal. It has also been said that by the slave and the one who is joined by the relative pronoun, which is an expression for the free man, is meant the genus, i.e., whoever is characterized by those attributes from both kinds. The interrogation is for denial, i.e., are the slaves and the free men characterized by those attributes equal, while both groups are created by God, glorified is He, from among mankind? It is known that they are not equal in their own estimation.
