Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding the verse, and regarding His saying: ﴿Two men, one of them dumb﴾, he said: "All of this is an example: the God of truth and what you invoke besides Him is falsehood."

Ibn al-Mundhir related through the route of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Regarding the first example, he means by it the gods that possess no power to harm or benefit, and are not able to do anything that benefits them." ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly﴾, he said: "The public [act] of the one who spends secretly and openly is for Allah."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir related from him, who said: This verse ﴿Allah sets forth an example: a slave owned﴾ was revealed concerning a man from Quraysh and ʿAbdah ibn Hisham ibn ʿAmr, and he is the one who spends secretly and openly; and concerning ʿAbdah, Abu al-Jawza, who used to forbid him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah sets forth an example: two men, one of them dumb﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "By the dumb one he means the disbeliever, who is a burden upon his master. ﴿And one who enjoins justice﴾ is the believer. And this example is about deeds."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsakir also related from him, who said: This verse ﴿And Allah sets forth an example: two men﴾ up to the end of the verse was revealed concerning ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan and a disbelieving client of his, who was Usayd ibn Abi al-ʿIs, who disliked Islam. ʿUthman used to spend on him, support him, and relieve him of hardship, while the other one would forbid him from giving charity and doing good. So these verses were revealed concerning the two of them.

Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya in al-Mukhtarah related from him also, regarding His saying: ﴿one who enjoins justice﴾, that he said: "ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, regarding His saying: "kall" (a burden), that he said: "Kall means dependents. When they moved on, they would carry him on a docile camel, and place with him a group of men to hold him, lest he fall upon them. So he is a hardship, a torment, and a burden upon them." ﴿Is he equal, he and one who enjoins justice, while he is on a straight path?﴾ meaning himself.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye﴾, that it is His saying "Be," and it is as a glance of the eye ﴿or it is nearer﴾: the Hour is like a glance of the eye, or it is nearer.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah brought you out of the wombs of your mothers﴾, that he said: "From the womb."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿in the air of the sky﴾, meaning in the midst of the sky.

God struck a parable: a slave owned, who has no power over anything, and one whom We have provided with a goodly provision from Us, so that he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to God; but most of them do not know.

God struck another parable: two men, one of them dumb, who has no power over anything and is a burden on his master; wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who enjoins justice and is on a straight path?

To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. And the matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or nearer. Indeed God is competent over all things.

God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts, that you may be grateful.

Have they not seen the birds made subservient in the expanse of the sky? Nothing holds them up except God. Surely in that are signs for a people who believe.

(Commentary of al-Shawkani, Fath al-Qadir, on surah 16, verses 75–80, part 1 of 2)

God's statement, ﴿God struck a parable﴾: when He, glorified is He, said that God knows (i.e., with the things known, among which is how He strikes parables) while you do not know, He taught them, glorified is He, how parables are struck, so He said: ﴿God struck a parable﴾, i.e., He mentioned something by which one may infer the difference in state between the Creator, glorified is He, and what they had made His partner among the idols. Then He mentioned that, saying: ﴿a slave owned﴾. The mathal (parable, example) is in reality a condition of the slave that befalls him, namely being owned and being incapable of disposing of anything. So His statement ﴿a slave owned who has no power over anything﴾ is an explanation of the parable and a substitute for it. He described him as owned because the slave and the free man are both shared in each being a slave of God, glorified is He. He described him as ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ because the mukatab (a slave contracted for manumission) and the ma'dhun (a slave licensed to trade) have power over some dispositions; so this description serves to distinguish him from them. ﴿And one whom We have provided﴾: man here is the relative pronoun, and it is coordinated with "a slave", i.e., "and one whom We have provided from Us", i.e., from Our side, ﴿with a goodly provision﴾ from the free men who own wealth and dispose of it as they wish. The meaning of the provision being goodly is that it is of what is pleasing in the eyes of people, being abundant provision containing precious, pleasing things that delight those who look at it. The fa' in His statement ﴿so he spends from it﴾ indicates the sequence of spending upon the provision, i.e., he spends from it in the ways of goodness and directs from it to kinds of righteousness and kindness. The accusative of ﴿secretly and openly﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl), i.e., he spends from it in the state of secrecy and in the state of openness. The purpose is to show the generality of spending across times, and the mention of secrecy before openness indicates its superiority over it and that the reward for it is greater. It has been said that man in ﴿and one whom We have provided﴾ is a descriptive (mawṣūfa), as if it were said: "and a free man whom We have provided", to correspond with "a slave". ﴿Are they equal?﴾, i.e., the free man and the slave described with the aforementioned attributes. The pronoun is in the plural because of the position of man, since it is an indefinite noun in which one, two, plural, masculine and feminine are equal. It has also been said that by the slave and the one who is joined by the relative pronoun, which is an expression for the free man, is meant the genus, i.e., whoever is characterized by those attributes from both kinds. The interrogation is for denial, i.e., are the slaves and the free men characterized by those attributes equal, while both groups are created by God, glorified is He, from among mankind? It is known that they are not equal in their own estimation. So how do they make partners for God, glorified is He, that do not possess for them harm or benefit, and make them deserving of worship alongside God, glorified is He? The sum of the meaning: just as a owned slave who has no power over his affairs and a free man whom God has provided with a goodly provision, so that he spends from it, are not equal in your sight, so likewise the Lord, the Creator, the Provider, and the lifeless idols that you worship, which neither see nor hear nor harm nor benefit, are not equal. It has been said that what is meant by the owned slave in the verse is the disbeliever deprived of obedience to God and servitude to Him, and "the other" (p-٧٩٤) is the believer, and the purpose is that the two are not equal in rank and nobility. It has been said: the slave is the idol, and the second is the worshipper of the idol, and what is meant is that the two are not equal in power and disposal, because the first is an inanimate object and the second is a human being. ﴿Praise be to God﴾, i.e., all praise belongs to God, because He is the Benefactor; no servant other than Him deserves any part of it. How then would the idols deserve any part of it, when they have no blessing from them at all, neither originally nor by intermediation? It has been said that He meant: praise be to God for what He has bestowed upon His friends of the blessing of monotheism. It has been said that He meant: "Say: praise be to God", and the address is either to Muhammad (ﷺ) or to the one whom God has provided with a goodly provision. It has been said: when He mentioned a parable corresponding to the purpose and revealing the intended meaning, He said: "Praise be to God", i.e., for the strength of this argument. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that, so that they would worship the One who deserves worship and recognize the Benefactor who bestowed on them the magnificent blessings. The negation of knowledge from them is either because they are in a state of ignorance such that they do not comprehend by its means what is obligatory upon them, or they abandon the truth out of obstinacy while knowing it, so they are like one who has no knowledge. He restricted the negation of knowledge to "most": either because He intends all creation, and most of them are polytheists, or He mentioned "most" and intends all, or what is meant is most of the polytheists, because among them are those who know but do not act according to the requirement of knowledge.

Then, glorified is He, mentioned a second parable which He struck for Himself, and for what He pours upon His servants of religious and worldly blessings, and for the idols, which are dead and neither harm nor benefit. So He said: ﴿And God struck a parable﴾, i.e., another parable, clearer and more manifest than what came before it. ﴿And two men﴾ is a substitute for "a parable" and an explanation of it. The abkam (dumb) is the one who is incapable of speech and tongue-tied. It has been said that he is the one whose tongue is cut off and who does not speak well. Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi that he is the one who neither hears nor sees. Then He described the dumb man, saying: ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ of the things related to himself or to others, because of his lack of understanding and his inability to speak. The meaning of ﴿a burden upon his master﴾ is: a heavy weight upon his guardian and kin, a dependant upon whoever takes charge of his affairs and supports him, and a calamity upon his brothers. The orphan is sometimes called kall (burden) because of his heaviness upon the one who sponsors him; from this is the poet's saying:

"Devourer of the wealth of the burden before his youth, when the bone of the burden is not strong."

In this is an explanation of his inability to establish the interests of his own self after the mention of his inability to do anything absolutely.

Then He described him with a fourth attribute, saying: ﴿wherever he directs him, he brings no good﴾, i.e., whenever he directs him to any direction, he never brings any good at all, because he does not understand nor comprehend what is said to him, and he is not able to say anything.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿wherever he is directed﴾ in the passive voice, and Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿wherever he turns﴾ in the past tense form. ﴿Is he equal, he himself,﴾ in his own person with these attributes that he has? ﴿And one who enjoins justice﴾, i.e., who commands people to justice, while he himself speaks what he wishes to say and understands, and is able to dispose of things, ﴿on a straight path﴾, i.e., on an upright religion and a righteous way of conduct, free of any inclination toward either extreme of excess or deficiency. He matched the attributes of the first with these two attributes of the second, because the sum of the first's attributes is his not deserving anything, while the sum of the second's attributes is that he deserves the most perfect deservingness. The purpose is to infer, from the non-equality of these two mentioned, the impossibility of equality between Him, glorified is He, and what they make a partner to Him.

When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the two parables, He praised Himself with His statement: ﴿To God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., that belongs exclusively to Him; no other shares in it and none independently possesses it. What is meant is that He knows what is hidden from the servants in both of them, or He intends by their unseen the Day of Resurrection, because His knowledge is hidden from the servants. The meaning of the idafa (genitive construction) to them both is the connection with them.

The meaning: a rebuke and reprimand for the polytheists, i.e., that worship is only deserved by one who has these attributes, not by one who is ignorant, incapable, who neither harms nor benefits, and knows nothing of any kind of knowledge. ﴿And the matter of the Hour﴾, which is the greatest thing in which disputes occur among the unseen matters exclusive to Him, glorified is He, ﴿is but as a glance of the eye﴾. The lamh (glance) is looking swiftly, and there must be in it a time in which the pupil turns toward the seen object, and every time is divisible. For this reason He said: ﴿or it is nearer﴾, i.e., their matter is nearer. This is not from the category of hyperbole; rather it is a statement of utmost truth, because the duration between the address and the establishment of the Hour is finite, and from it to eternity is infinite, and there is no ratio of the finite to the infinite. Or it may be said: since the Hour is certainly coming, it was made as near as a glance of the eye.

Al-Zajjaj said: He did not mean that the Hour comes in the blink of an eye; rather He described the swiftness of the power to bring it about, because He says to a thing "Be," and it is. It has been said: the meaning is: it is so with God, even if it is not so with created beings. A similar statement is His, glorified is He: ﴿They see it as far, but We see it as near﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 6–7]. The word "or" in ﴿or it is nearer﴾ is not for doubt, but for comparison. It has been said that it entered for the doubt of the addressee. It has been said that it is in the position of "rather" (bal). ﴿Indeed God is competent over all things﴾, and the coming of the Hour swiftly is among the things within His power.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned another state of man which indicates the utmost of His power and the extent of His compassion, so He said: ﴿And God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing﴾. This is coordinated with His statement: ﴿And God made for you from yourselves spouses﴾, and is linked with it in the string of proofs of monotheism, i.e., He brought you out from the wombs of your mothers as infants with no knowledge of anything. The clause ﴿knowing nothing﴾ is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl). It has been said that what is meant is that you know nothing of what was taken from you in the covenant; it has been said you know nothing of what He decreed upon you of happiness and misery; it has been said you know nothing of your benefits. The better view is generalization, so that the verse includes these matters and others, taking into account the generality of the wording, since shay' (thing) is an indefinite noun in the context of negation.

Al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab and Hamzah read ﴿immahatikum﴾ (your mothers) with a kasra on the hamza and the mim here, and in al-Nur, al-Zumar and al-Najm. Al-Kisa'i read with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the mim. The rest read with a damma on the hamza and a fatha on the mim.

﴿And made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾, i.e., He set these things in you. It is coordinated with "brought you out", and there is no indication in it that this making is delayed after the bringing out, because what the conjunction wa' signifies is simply joint occurrence. The meaning: He made these things for you so that you might obtain by them the knowledge that was taken from you when you came out from your mothers' wombs, and act in accordance with that knowledge, by thanking the Benefactor, worshipping Him, and fulfilling His rights. (p-٧٩٥) The af'idah (hearts) is the plural of fu'ad, which is the midst of the heart, placed in the same position relative to the heart as the heart relative to the chest. We have already mentioned the reason for the singular "hearing" and plural "sight" and "hearts": that the singular of hearing, being originally a verbal noun, covers the few and the many. ﴿That you may be grateful﴾, i.e., so that you may direct every instrument to what it was created for; then you will recognize the measure of what God has bestowed upon you and thank Him for it, or this directing is itself gratitude.

Then, glorified is He, mentioned another proof of the perfection of His power, saying: ﴿Have they not seen the birds made subservient﴾, i.e., have they not looked at them in the state of being subservient: made submissive to flying by what God has created for them of wings and other means suited to that, such as the thinness of the air's substance, and His inspiring them to spread and fold the wing as a swimmer does in water. ﴿In the atmosphere of the sky﴾, i.e., in the air distant from the earth in the direction of height. Its idafa to the sky is because it is on its side. Nothing holds them up in the air except God, glorified is He, by His overwhelming power, since the weight of their bodies and the thinness of the air's substance would necessitate their falling, for they are not attached to anything above them nor do they rest upon anything beneath them.

Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Ya'qub read ﴿Have you not seen﴾ with the second-person ta' (i.e., addressing), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading. The rest read it with the third-person ya'. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, i.e., indeed in that subjection in that state are manifest signs indicating the oneness of God, glorified is He, and His overwhelming power, ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glorified is He, and in what His messengers brought of the laws that God legislated.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 16, verses 81–83:**

His words, ﴿And Allah has made for you﴾, are conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes it. What is mentioned here is part of the states of man and part of the enumeration of Allah's blessings upon him. *Sakan* (a repose or dwelling place) is a verbal noun (masdar) that may be applied to the singular and the plural, and it carries the meaning of *maskun* (a place of dwelling). That is, you dwell in them and your limbs rest from movement. This is a blessing, for if Allah, glory be to Him, had willed, He would have created the servant in constant agitation like the celestial spheres, and if He had willed, He would have created him perpetually still like the earth. ﴿And He made for you from the hides of livestock houses﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the houses of cities, which are for long-term residence, He followed it with mention of the houses of the desert and of travel. That is: He made for you, from the hides of livestock, which are the leather mats and tanned skins, houses like tents and domes. ﴿Which you find light﴾, meaning that carrying them is light for you during journeys and other occasions. For this reason He said, ﴿on the day of your traveling (za'n)﴾. *Za'n* may be pronounced with an open or a sukun ʿayn, and both readings are recited. It refers to the journeying of desert people in search of pasture and their moving from one place to another. From it is the verse of Antarah:

*They departed, those whose separation I await, and the black-and-white crow flew between them.*

*Za'n* also means the litter (howdah) carried on a camel. ﴿And from their wool, their fur and their hair, furnishings (athath) and provision﴾ is conjoined to *ja'ala* (made), meaning: and He made for you from the wool, fur and hair of livestock. *Al-an'am* (livestock) encompasses camels, cattle and sheep, as has been mentioned previously. Wool is for sheep, fur is for camels, and hair is for goats, and goats are part of the sheep category. Therefore the mention of these three is by way of classification, each one corresponding to one of the three: camels and the two kinds of sheep. *Athath* is household goods, and its root meaning is abundance and gathering together. From it comes *sh'ir athith*, meaning thick, abundant hair. The poet said:

*And a branch adorning the back, jet-black, thick like a date-palm cluster dense with fruit.*

Al-Khalil said: *athath* means that some of it is joined to other parts, from *atta*, when it became abundant. Al-Farra' said: it has no singular form. *Mata'* (provision) is that which is enjoyed in various kinds of enjoyment. According to the view of Abu Zayd al-Ansari, that *athath* is all property together: camels, sheep, slaves and goods, then conjoining *mata'* to *athath* is conjoining the specific to the general. It has also been said that *athath* is what a person wears and uses of covering and bedding, and *mata'* is what is spread out in homes and used for adornment. The meaning of ﴿for a time﴾ is until you fulfill your needs from it, or until it wears out and perishes, or until death, or until the Resurrection.

Then, since a person may not have tents or structures to shelter him because of poverty or another circumstance, and so needs to take shade under a tree, a wall, a cloud or the like, He, glory be to Him, drew attention to this and said: ﴿And He made for you, from what He has created, shades﴾, meaning things under which you take shelter, like the things mentioned.

The summary is that *zilal* (shades) covers all things that provide shade. Then, since the traveler may need a corner to which he retreats when he stops, and something to protect himself from the harms of heat and cold, He, glory be to Him, drew attention to this and said: ﴿And He made for you from the mountains refuges (aknan)﴾. *Aknan* is the plural of *kinn*, which is that by which one is sheltered from rain. Here it means caves in the mountains. Allah, glory be to Him, made them a provision for creation: they shelter in them, take refuge in them, and withdraw from people within them. ﴿And He made for you garments (sarabil)﴾. *Sarabil* is the plural of *sirbal*, which means shirts and clothing of wool, cotton, linen and others.

Al-Zajjaj said: everything you wear is a *sirbal*. The meaning of ﴿which protect you from the heat﴾ is that they ward off the harm of heat from you. He specified heat and did not mention cold, being satisfied with the mention of one of the two opposites over the other, because what protects from heat also protects from cold.

The reason for specifying heat in the mention is that protection from it was of greater concern to them than protection from cold, because heat predominated in their lands. ﴿And garments that protect you from your violence (ba's)﴾. These are coats of mail and light armour, by which they guard against stabbing, striking and shooting. The meaning is that they protect you from the violence that passes between some of you and others in war. ﴿Thus He completes His blessing upon you﴾, meaning: like this complete completion, He completes His blessing upon you. He, glory be to Him, has bestowed upon His servants kinds of blessings, those mentioned here and others, and by His grace and kindness He will complete for them the blessing of religion and of the world. ﴿So that you may submit (tuslimun)﴾, meaning in the hope that you will submit, for whoever reflects deeply on these blessings will have no recourse but to submit and yield to the truth.

Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd recited *tatimmu ni'matuhu* with two upper dots (ta' forms), taking its subject as *ni'matuhu* (His blessing). The rest read it with the lower-dotted yaʾ, taking the subject to be Allah, glory be to Him.

Ibn ʿAbbas and Ikrimah recited *taslamun* with a fatha on the ta and the lam, from *salama* (safety from wounds). The rest read it with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the lam, from *islam* (submission).

Abu ʿUbayd said: the preferred reading is that of the majority, because what Allah has bestowed upon us of Islam is better than what He has bestowed upon us of safety from wounds. It has also been said that the address is to the people of Makkah, meaning: perhaps you, people of Makkah, will devote lordship to Allah alone. The more apt interpretation is to take it in its general sense. The singular *ni'mah* is used here because what is meant by it is the verbal noun.

﴿So if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance﴾, meaning: if they turn away from you and do not accept what you have brought, your excuse has been established. ﴿Upon you is only the conveyance﴾ of what you were sent to them with. ﴿Clear (mubin)﴾ means evident, and nothing else is incumbent upon you. The address is turned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as consolation for him.

The clause ﴿They recognize the blessing of Allah, then they deny it﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) explaining their turning away. That is: they recognize the blessing of Allah that He enumerated, and they acknowledge that it is from Allah, glory be to Him, and then they deny it through their ugly actions, such as worshipping other than Allah, and through their false statements, where they say: it is from Allah but through the intercession of idols; and where they say that they inherited those blessings from their forefathers. Also, [they deny it] by their not using these blessings to seek the pleasure of the Lord, glory be to Him, and in the good causes for which Allah commanded them to spend them. **Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 16, verses 81–83:**

His words, ﴿And Allah has made for you﴾, are conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes it. What is mentioned here is part of the states of man and part of the enumeration of Allah's blessings upon him. *Sakan* (a repose or dwelling place) is a verbal noun (masdar) that may be applied to the singular and the plural, and it carries the meaning of *maskun* (a place of dwelling). That is, you dwell in them and your limbs rest from movement. This is a blessing, for if Allah, glory be to Him, had willed, He would have created the servant in constant agitation like the celestial spheres, and if He had willed, He would have created him perpetually still like the earth. ﴿And He made for you from the hides of livestock houses﴾. When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the houses of cities, which are for long-term residence, He followed it with mention of the houses of the desert and of travel. That is: He made for you, from the hides of livestock, which are the leather mats and tanned skins, houses like tents and domes. ﴿Which you find light﴾, meaning that carrying them is light for you during journeys and other occasions. For this reason He said, ﴿on the day of your traveling (za'n)﴾. *Za'n* may be pronounced with an open or a sukun ʿayn, and both readings are recited. It refers to the journeying of desert people in search of pasture and their moving from one place to another. From it is the verse of Antarah:

*They departed, those whose separation I await, and the black-and-white crow flew between them.*

*Za'n* also means the litter (howdah) carried on a camel. ﴿And from their wool, their fur and their hair, furnishings (athath) and provision﴾ is conjoined to *ja'ala* (made), meaning: and He made for you from the wool, fur and hair of livestock. *Al-an'am* (livestock) encompasses camels, cattle and sheep, as has been mentioned previously. Wool is for sheep, fur is for camels, and hair is for goats, and goats are part of the sheep category. Therefore the mention of these three is by way of classification, each one corresponding to one of the three: camels and the two kinds of sheep. *Athath* is household goods, and its root meaning is abundance and gathering together. From it comes *sh'ir athith*, meaning thick, abundant hair. The poet said:

*And a branch adorning the back, jet-black, thick like a date-palm cluster dense with fruit.*

Al-Khalil said: *athath* means that some of it is joined to other parts, from *atta*, when it became abundant. Al-Farra' said: it has no singular form. *Mata'* (provision) is that which is enjoyed in various kinds of enjoyment. According to the view of Abu Zayd al-Ansari, that *athath* is all property together: camels, sheep, slaves and goods, then conjoining *mata'* to *athath* is conjoining the specific to the general. It has also been said that *athath* is what a person wears and uses of covering and bedding, and *mata'* is what is spread out in homes and used for adornment. The meaning of ﴿for a time﴾ is until you fulfill your needs from it, or until it wears out and perishes, or until death, or until the Resurrection.

Then, since a person may not have tents or structures to shelter him because of poverty or another circumstance, and so needs to take shade under a tree, a wall, a cloud or the like, He, glory be to Him, drew attention to this and said: ﴿And He made for you, from what He has created, shades﴾, meaning things under which you take shelter, like the things mentioned.

The summary is that *zilal* (shades) covers all things that provide shade. Then, since the traveler may need a corner to which he retreats when he stops, and something to protect himself from the harms of heat and cold, He, glory be to Him, drew attention to this and said: ﴿And He made for you from the mountains refuges (aknan)﴾. *Aknan* is the plural of *kinn*, which is that by which one is sheltered from rain. Here it means caves in the mountains. Allah, glory be to Him, made them a provision for creation: they shelter in them, take refuge in them, and withdraw from people within them. ﴿And He made for you garments (sarabil)﴾. *Sarabil* is the plural of *sirbal*, which means shirts and clothing of wool, cotton, linen and others.

Al-Zajjaj said: everything you wear is a *sirbal*. The meaning of ﴿which protect you from the heat﴾ is that they ward off the harm of heat from you. He specified heat and did not mention cold, being satisfied with the mention of one of the two opposites over the other, because what protects from heat also protects from cold.

The reason for specifying heat in the mention is that protection from it was of greater concern to them than protection from cold, because heat predominated in their lands. ﴿And garments that protect you from your violence (ba's)﴾. These are coats of mail and light armour, by which they guard against stabbing, striking and shooting. The meaning is that they protect you from the violence that passes between some of you and others in war. ﴿Thus He completes His blessing upon you﴾, meaning: like this complete completion, He completes His blessing upon you. He, glory be to Him, has bestowed upon His servants kinds of blessings, those mentioned here and others, and by His grace and kindness He will complete for them the blessing of religion and of the world. ﴿So that you may submit (tuslimun)﴾, meaning in the hope that you will submit, for whoever reflects deeply on these blessings will have no recourse but to submit and yield to the truth.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 84–90 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, had explained the state of these people, that they recognised God's blessing and then denied it, and that most of them are disbelievers, He followed it with the various kinds of threat of the Day of Resurrection. He said: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness﴾. That is, mention the Day when We raise up, or [it means]: the Day when We raise up, they will fall into what they fell into. The witness of every nation is its prophet, who testifies for them to faith and affirmation, and against them to disbelief, denial and rejection. ﴿Then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved﴾, that is, to make excuses, since they have no proof and no excuse, as in His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿Nor will they be permitted, so they could make excuse﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. Or [it means]: to speak at length. Or: to return to the worldly abode. The use of "then" (thumma) here indicates that their being afflicted with being prevented from making excuses, which indicates total despair, is more severe than their being afflicted with the testimony of the prophets. ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾, because reproach (`itab) is only sought for the purpose of returning to good pleasure; so when there is a resolve of wrath, there is no benefit in reproach.

The meaning: they will not be asked to be pleased, that is, they will not be required to please their Lord, because the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation, and they will not be left to return to the world so that they might repent. The root of the word is from `atab, which means "to be aggrieved." It is said: `atiba `alayhi, ya`tibu, when he was aggrieved with him. When he pours upon him what he was aggrieved about, it is said `atabahu (he reproached him). When he returns to his gladness, it is said a`tabahu (he appeased him). The noun is al-`utba, which is the return of the one who was reproached to what pleases the reproacher. Al-Harawi said this, and from it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"If I am wronged, [it is] a slave whom you have wronged; and if I have grievance, one like you appeases."

﴿And when those who wronged see the punishment﴾, that is, when those who associated partners [with God] see the punishment that they deserve for their polytheism, which is the punishment of Hell, that punishment will not be lightened for them ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, that is, they will not be given respite to repent, since there is no repentance there.

﴿And when those who associated partners see their partners﴾, that is, their idols and images which they worshipped, because it has been established that they will be raised together with the polytheists, so that it will be said to them: "Whoever used to worship something, let him follow it," as established in the Sahih from the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿They will say: "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You."﴾ That is, those whom we used to worship besides You.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The intent of the polytheists in this statement is to shift the blame onto those idols, making excuses and seeking relief by it, while knowing that the punishment is inevitably befalling them; but the drowning person clutches at whatever his hand falls upon. ﴿Then they will throw to them the word﴾, that is, those idols, images, devils and the like will cast to the polytheists the word ﴿"Indeed, you are liars."﴾ That is, they will say to them: "Indeed you, O polytheists, are liars in what you claim of shifting the blame onto us, which is your intent in this statement."

If it is said: The polytheists pointed to the idols and the like, [saying] "These are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You," and they were truthful in that; so how did the idols and the like deny them? The answer: their meaning by saying "These are our partners" was: these are partners of God in being worshipped; so the idols denied them in claiming this partnership. The idols and images, although they cannot speak, God, glory be to Him, will make them speak in that state in order to shame and rebuke the polytheists. This is like what the angels said: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ [Saba': 41], meaning that the jinn were the ones who were pleased with their worship of them.

﴿And they will offer submission to God that Day﴾, that is, the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection will offer submission and compliance to His punishment and humility before His might. It was also said: the worshipper and the worshipped both submitted and complied with His judgment concerning them. ﴿And what they used to invent will be lost to them﴾, that is, what they used to fabricate, that God, glory be to Him, has partners, and what they used to claim of their intercession for them, and that their worship of them brings them nearer to God, glory be to Him, will perish and be void.

Those who disbelieved within themselves and barred others ﴿from the way of God﴾, that is, from the path of truth, which is the path of Islam and faith, by preventing them from following it and compelling them to disbelief. It was also said that what is meant by barring from the way of God is barring from the Sacred Mosque, but the more appropriate view is generality.

Then He informed about those who did this deed by His saying: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾, that is, God will increase them in punishment for the sake of leading others astray, over and above the punishment they deserved for their own error. It was also said that the meaning is: We will increase the leaders in punishment over the punishment of their followers, that is, more severe than it. It was also said that this increase is their being brought out of the Fire to the zamharir (freezing cold). And other things have been said.

﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up in every nation a witness against them﴾, that is, a prophet who testifies against them from among themselves, from their own kind, to complete the proof and cut off excuse. This is a repetition of what preceded, for the purpose of emphasis and warning. ﴿And We have brought you, O Muhammad, as a witness over these﴾, that is, you will bear witness over these nations and testify for them. It was also said: over your own nation. Something similar has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah and al-Nisa'. ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾, that is, the Qur'an. The clause is either independent, or in the place of a circumstantial accusative with the implied qad. ﴿As an explanation of all things﴾, that is, a clarification of it. The ta' is for emphasis (intensive), and its parallel among verbal nouns is al-tilqa'; no other examples exist. A similar verse is His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An`am: 38]. The meaning of it being an explanation of all things is that it contains clarification of many rulings, and for what remains of them it refers to the Sunnah; and He commanded them to follow His Messenger (ﷺ) in what he brings of rulings, and to obey him, as in the Qur'anic verses indicating this. It is authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed I have been given the Qur'an and its like with it." And it is guidance and mercy for the servants (p-798) ﴿and good tidings for the Muslims﴾, specifically and to the exclusion of others; or the guidance, mercy and good tidings are specifically for them, since they are the ones who benefit from it.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned that in the Qur'an there is an explanation of all things, He followed it with a verse comprehensive of all the foundations of obligation, as confirmation of that, saying: ﴿Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct﴾.

The people of knowledge have differed in interpreting "justice" and "good conduct." It was said: justice is "there is no god but God," and good conduct is performing the obligations. It was said: justice is the obligatory, and good conduct is the supererogatory.

It was said: justice is the equality of the outward and the inward, and good conduct is that the inward be better than the outward.

It was said: justice is fairness, and good conduct is bestowing favour.

The more appropriate interpretation of justice is by its linguistic meaning, which is moderation between the two extremes of excess and deficiency. So the meaning of His command, glory be to Him, to justice is that His servants should be in a moderate state in religion, not inclining toward the side of excess, which is blameworthy extremism in religion, nor toward the side of deficiency, which is neglecting anything that is part of the religion. This is of the category of specific after general if giving to relatives has entered under justice and good conduct; and it was said it is of the category of mandub (recommended) being joined to wajib (obligatory). It was also said it is polytheism. As for transgression (baghy), it was said to be arrogance, it was said wrongdoing, it was said malice, it was said aggression; its reality is exceeding the limit, so it includes those mentioned, and all its kinds fall under the munkar. ("That you may be reminded") means: that you may remember what should be remembered, and so be admonished by what God has admonished you with.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from Qatadah.

In its chain is Shahr ibn Hawshab.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: its chain is not objectionable.

[He said] "*al-munkar*": he said, "Shirk (associating partners with Allah) and transgression." [He said] "*al-baghy*": he said, "Pride and oppression." ﴿He admonishes you﴾: he said, "He enjoins you." ﴿So that you may remember﴾.

The most comprehensive verse in the Book of Allah for good and evil is the verse in al-Nahl ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾. Al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from al-Hasan that he recited this verse ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾ to its end, then said: "Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has gathered for you all good and all evil in one verse. By Allah, justice and excellence have left out nothing of obedience to Allah without including it, and indecency, the reprehensible, and transgression have left out nothing of disobedience to Allah without including it."

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* narrated through al-Kalbi from his father, who said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by a people who were conversing and said, 'What are you discussing?' They said, 'We are discussing *al-muru'ah* (manliness and chivalrous conduct).' He said, 'Has Allah, Mighty and Majestic, not sufficed you with that in His Book when He says: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾? Justice is equity, and excellence is generosity beyond what is due. What remains after this?'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 84–90 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, had explained the state of these people, that they recognised God's blessing and then denied it, and that most of them are disbelievers, He followed it with the various kinds of threat of the Day of Resurrection. He said: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness﴾. That is, mention the Day when We raise up, or [it means]: the Day when We raise up, they will fall into what they fell into. The witness of every nation is its prophet, who testifies for them to faith and affirmation, and against them to disbelief, denial and rejection. ﴿Then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved﴾, that is, to make excuses, since they have no proof and no excuse, as in His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿Nor will they be permitted, so they could make excuse﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. Or [it means]: to speak at length. Or: to return to the worldly abode. The use of "then" (thumma) here indicates that their being afflicted with being prevented from making excuses, which indicates total despair, is more severe than their being afflicted with the testimony of the prophets. ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾, because reproach (`itab) is only sought for the purpose of returning to good pleasure; so when there is a resolve of wrath, there is no benefit in reproach.

The meaning: they will not be asked to be pleased, that is, they will not be required to please their Lord, because the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation, and they will not be left to return to the world so that they might repent. The root of the word is from `atab, which means "to be aggrieved." It is said: `atiba `alayhi, ya`tibu, when he was aggrieved with him. When he pours upon him what he was aggrieved about, it is said `atabahu (he reproached him). When he returns to his gladness, it is said a`tabahu (he appeased him). The noun is al-`utba, which is the return of the one who was reproached to what pleases the reproacher. Al-Harawi said this, and from it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"If I am wronged, [it is] a slave whom you have wronged; and if I have grievance, one like you appeases."

﴿And when those who wronged see the punishment﴾, that is, when those who associated partners [with God] see the punishment that they deserve for their polytheism, which is the punishment of Hell, that punishment will not be lightened for them ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, that is, they will not be given respite to repent, since there is no repentance there.

﴿And when those who associated partners see their partners﴾, that is, their idols and images which they worshipped, because it has been established that they will be raised together with the polytheists, so that it will be said to them: "Whoever used to worship something, let him follow it," as established in the Sahih from the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿They will say: "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You."﴾ That is, those whom we used to worship besides You.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The intent of the polytheists in this statement is to shift the blame onto those idols, making excuses and seeking relief by it, while knowing that the punishment is inevitably befalling them; but the drowning person clutches at whatever his hand falls upon. ﴿Then they will throw to them the word﴾, that is, those idols, images, devils and the like will cast to the polytheists the word ﴿"Indeed, you are liars."﴾ That is, they will say to them: "Indeed you, O polytheists, are liars in what you claim of shifting the blame onto us, which is your intent in this statement."

If it is said: The polytheists pointed to the idols and the like, [saying] "These are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You," and they were truthful in that; so how did the idols and the like deny them? The answer: their meaning by saying "These are our partners" was: these are partners of God in being worshipped; so the idols denied them in claiming this partnership. The idols and images, although they cannot speak, God, glory be to Him, will make them speak in that state in order to shame and rebuke the polytheists. This is like what the angels said: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ [Saba': 41], meaning that the jinn were the ones who were pleased with their worship of them.

﴿And they will offer submission to God that Day﴾, that is, the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection will offer submission and compliance to His punishment and humility before His might. It was also said: the worshipper and the worshipped both submitted and complied with His judgment concerning them. ﴿And what they used to invent will be lost to them﴾, that is, what they used to fabricate, that God, glory be to Him, has partners, and what they used to claim of their intercession for them, and that their worship of them brings them nearer to God, glory be to Him, will perish and be void.

The most intense verse in the Book of Allah in hope is ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar 39:53], [and so on] to the end of the verse."

Al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from al-Hasan that he recited this verse ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾ to its end, then said: "Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has gathered for you all good and all evil in one verse. By Allah, justice and excellence have left out nothing of obedience to Allah without including it, and indecency, the reprehensible, and transgression have left out nothing of disobedience to Allah without including it."

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* narrated through al-Kalbi from his father, who said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by a people who were conversing and said, 'What are you discussing?' They said, 'We are discussing *al-muru'ah* (manliness and chivalrous conduct).' He said, 'Has Allah, Mighty and Majestic, not sufficed you with that in His Book when He says: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾? Justice is equity, and excellence is generosity beyond what is due. What remains after this?'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 84–90 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, had explained the state of these people, that they recognised God's blessing and then denied it, and that most of them are disbelievers, He followed it with the various kinds of threat of the Day of Resurrection. He said: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness﴾. That is, mention the Day when We raise up, or [it means]: the Day when We raise up, they will fall into what they fell into. The witness of every nation is its prophet, who testifies for them to faith and affirmation, and against them to disbelief, denial and rejection. ﴿Then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved﴾, that is, to make excuses, since they have no proof and no excuse, as in His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿Nor will they be permitted, so they could make excuse﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. Or [it means]: to speak at length. Or: to return to the worldly abode. The use of "then" (thumma) here indicates that their being afflicted with being prevented from making excuses, which indicates total despair, is more severe than their being afflicted with the testimony of the prophets. ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾, because reproach (`itab) is only sought for the purpose of returning to good pleasure; so when there is a resolve of wrath, there is no benefit in reproach.

The meaning: they will not be asked to be pleased, that is, they will not be required to please their Lord, because the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation, and they will not be left to return to the world so that they might repent. The root of the word is from `atab, which means "to be aggrieved." It is said: `atiba `alayhi, ya`tibu, when he was aggrieved with him. When he pours upon him what he was aggrieved about, it is said `atabahu (he reproached him). When he returns to his gladness, it is said a`tabahu (he appeased him). The noun is al-`utba, which is the return of the one who was reproached to what pleases the reproacher. Al-Harawi said this, and from it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"If I am wronged, [it is] a slave whom you have wronged; and if I have grievance, one like you appeases."

﴿And when those who wronged see the punishment﴾, that is, when those who associated partners [with God] see the punishment that they deserve for their polytheism, which is the punishment of Hell, that punishment will not be lightened for them ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, that is, they will not be given respite to repent, since there is no repentance there.

﴿And when those who associated partners see their partners﴾, that is, their idols and images which they worshipped, because it has been established that they will be raised together with the polytheists, so that it will be said to them: "Whoever used to worship something, let him follow it," as established in the Sahih from the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿They will say: "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You."﴾ That is, those whom we used to worship besides You.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The intent of the polytheists in this statement is to shift the blame onto those idols, making excuses and seeking relief by it, while knowing that the punishment is inevitably befalling them; but the drowning person clutches at whatever his hand falls upon. ﴿Then they will throw to them the word﴾, that is, those idols, images, devils and the like will cast to the polytheists the word ﴿"Indeed, you are liars."﴾ That is, they will say to them: "Indeed you, O polytheists, are liars in what you claim of shifting the blame onto us, which is your intent in this statement."

If it is said: The polytheists pointed to the idols and the like, [saying] "These are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You," and they were truthful in that; so how did the idols and the like deny them? The answer: their meaning by saying "These are our partners" was: these are partners of God in being worshipped; so the idols denied them in claiming this partnership. The idols and images, although they cannot speak, God, glory be to Him, will make them speak in that state in order to shame and rebuke the polytheists. This is like what the angels said: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ [Saba': 41], meaning that the jinn were the ones who were pleased with their worship of them.

﴿And they will offer submission to God that Day﴾, that is, the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection will offer submission and compliance to His punishment and humility before His might. It was also said: the worshipper and the worshipped both submitted and complied with His judgment concerning them. ﴿And what they used to invent will be lost to them﴾, that is, what they used to fabricate, that God, glory be to Him, has partners, and what they used to claim of their intercession for them, and that their worship of them brings them nearer to God, glory be to Him, will perish and be void.

Those who disbelieved within themselves and barred others ﴿from the way of God﴾, that is, from the path of truth, which is the path of Islam and faith, by preventing them from following it and compelling them to disbelief. It was also said that what is meant by barring from the way of God is barring from the Sacred Mosque, but the more appropriate view is generality.

Then He informed about those who did this deed by His saying: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾, that is, God will increase them in punishment for the sake of leading others astray, over and above the punishment they deserved for their own error. It was also said that the meaning is: We will increase the leaders in punishment over the punishment of their followers, that is, more severe than it. It was also said that this increase is their being brought out of the Fire to the zamharir (freezing cold). And other things have been said.

﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up in every nation a witness against them﴾, that is, a prophet who testifies against them from among themselves, from their own kind, to complete the proof and cut off excuse. This is a repetition of what preceded, for the purpose of emphasis and warning. ﴿And We have brought you, O Muhammad, as a witness over these﴾, that is, you will bear witness over these nations and testify for them. It was also said: over your own nation. Something similar has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah and al-Nisa'. ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾, that is, the Qur'an. The clause is either independent, or in the place of a circumstantial accusative with the implied qad. ﴿As an explanation of all things﴾, that is, a clarification of it. The ta' is for emphasis (intensive), and its parallel among verbal nouns is al-tilqa'; no other examples exist. A similar verse is His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ [al-An`am: 38]. The meaning of it being an explanation of all things is that it contains clarification of many rulings, and for what remains of them it refers to the Sunnah; and He commanded them to follow His Messenger (ﷺ) in what he brings of rulings, and to obey him, as in the Qur'anic verses indicating this. It is authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed I have been given the Qur'an and its like with it." And it is guidance and mercy for the servants (p-798) ﴿and good tidings for the Muslims﴾, specifically and to the exclusion of others; or the guidance, mercy and good tidings are specifically for them, since they are the ones who benefit from it.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned that in the Qur'an there is an explanation of all things, He followed it with a verse comprehensive of all the foundations of obligation, as confirmation of that, saying: ﴿Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct﴾.

The people of knowledge have differed in interpreting "justice" and "good conduct." It was said: justice is "there is no god but God," and good conduct is performing the obligations. It was said: justice is the obligatory, and good conduct is the supererogatory.

It was said: justice is the equality of the outward and the inward, and good conduct is that the inward be better than the outward.

It was said: justice is fairness, and good conduct is bestowing favour.

The more appropriate interpretation of justice is by its linguistic meaning, which is moderation between the two extremes of excess and deficiency. So the meaning of His command, glory be to Him, to justice is that His servants should be in a moderate state in religion, not inclining toward the side of excess, which is blameworthy extremism in religion, nor toward the side of deficiency, which is neglecting anything that is part of the religion. As for good conduct, its linguistic meaning indicates that it is bestowing favour with what is not obligatory, like voluntary charity; and among good conduct is doing what the servant is rewarded for, of what God has not made obligatory upon him, in acts of worship and other things. It is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he explained good conduct as worshipping God as if you see Him. He said in the hadith of Ibn `Umar, which is established in the Two Sahihs: "Good conduct is that you worship God as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." This is the meaning of good conduct in the Shari`ah. ﴿And giving to close relatives﴾, that is, giving relatives what their need calls for. In the verse there is guidance to maintaining ties of kinship and encouragement to give charity to them. This is of the category of specific after general if giving to relatives has entered under justice and good conduct; and it was said it is of the category of mandub (recommended) being joined to wajib (obligatory). A similar verse is His statement: ﴿And give the close relative his right﴾. The reason He specified close relatives is that their right is more emphatic, for God has derived the name of the womb (rahim) from His own name, and made joining it part of His joining, and severing it part of His severing. ﴿And He forbids immorality﴾: it is the matter that increases in ugliness, in speech or deed. It was said it is fornication; it was said stinginess. And the munkar is what the Shari`ah has disapproved by prohibiting it, and it encompasses all sins across their varieties. It was also said it is polytheism. As for transgression (baghy), it was said to be arrogance, it was said wrongdoing, it was said malice, it was said aggression; its reality is exceeding the limit, so it includes those mentioned, and all its kinds fall under the munkar. It was singled out for mention out of concern for it, because of its severe harm and the evil of its consequence. It is among the sins that return upon their doer, as in His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿Your transgression is only against yourselves﴾ [Yunus: 23]. This verse is among the verses indicating the obligation of enjoining good and forbidding evil. Then God, glory be to Him, concluded this verse with His statement: ﴿He admonishes you that you may be reminded﴾, that is, He admonishes you with what He has mentioned in this verse of what He has commanded you and forbidden you from, for it is sufficient in the matter of admonition and reminding. ("That you may be reminded") means: that you may remember what should be remembered, and so be admonished by what God has admonished you with.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His statement: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness﴾, he said: its witness is its prophet, that he conveyed the messages of his Lord. God said: ﴿And We have brought you as a witness over these﴾. He said: It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) when he recited this verse, his eyes would overflow.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His statement: ﴿Then they will throw to them the word﴾, he said: they will speak to them.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿And they will offer submission to God that Day﴾, he said: they submitted.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from Qatadah.

`Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa`id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad ibn al-Sarri, Abu Ya`la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba`th wa'l-Nushur transmitted from Ibn Mas`ud concerning His statement: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾, he said: they will be increased scorpions with fangs like tall palm trees.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib transmitted from al-Bara' that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the statement of God, exalted be He: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾, so he said: "Scorpions like tall palm trees, which sting them in Hell."

Abu Ya`la, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn `Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾, he said: five rivers of fire which God pours upon them, by which they are punished, some of them by night and some of them by day.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Jabir from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The increase is five rivers flowing from beneath the Throne upon the heads of the people of the Fire: three rivers according to the measure of the night, and two rivers according to the measure of the day; therefore this is His statement: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas`ud that he said: Indeed God has sent down in this Book an explanation of all things, but our knowledge falls short of what has been made clear to us in the Qur'an. Then he recited: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾.

Sa`id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, `Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, Ibn al-Duraysi in Fada'il al-Qur'an, Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salah, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu`ab transmitted from Ibn Mas`ud that he said: Whoever desires knowledge, let him probe the Qur'an deeply, for in it is the knowledge of the first and the last.

Ahmad transmitted from `Uthman ibn Abi al-`As, who said: I was sitting with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when his gaze became fixed, and he said: "Gabriel came to me and commanded me to place this verse in this position of the surah": ﴿Indeed, God commands justice and good conduct﴾ to the end of the verse.

In its chain is Shahr ibn Hawshab.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: its chain is not objectionable.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it at greater length from the hadith of Ibn `Abbas, and Ibn Kathir rated its chain as hasan.

Al-Bawardi, Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Mandah, and Abu Nu'aym in *Ma'rifat al-Sahabah* narrated from Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr that when this verse reached Aktham ibn Sayfi, the sage of the Arabs, he said: "I see that it commands noble character and forbids what is contrary to it." Then he said to his people: "Be leaders in this matter and do not be followers in it; be first in it and do not be last in it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) regarding His words ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice﴾: he said, "It is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and *ihsan* (excellence) is the performance of the obligations." ﴿And giving to kinsmen﴾: he said, "Giving to the near of kin the right that Allah has made obligatory upon you by reason of kinship and the ties of blood." ﴿And He forbids indecency﴾: he said, "Fornication and the reprehensible." [He said] "*al-munkar*": he said, "Shirk (associating partners with Allah) and transgression." [He said] "*al-baghy*": he said, "Pride and oppression." ﴿He admonishes you﴾: he said, "He enjoins you." ﴿So that you may remember﴾.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, Muhammad ibn Nasr in *al-Salat*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated that he said: "The greatest verse in the Book of Allah is ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all existence﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:255]. The most comprehensive verse in the Book of Allah for good and evil is the verse in al-Nahl ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾. The verse in the Book of Allah most full of *tafwid* (entrusting one's affairs to Allah) is ﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾ [al-Talaq 65:2–3]. The most intense verse in the Book of Allah in hope is ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar 39:53], [and so on] to the end of the verse."

Al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from al-Hasan that he recited this verse ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾ to its end, then said: "Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has gathered for you all good and all evil in one verse. By Allah, justice and excellence have left out nothing of obedience to Allah without including it, and indecency, the reprehensible, and transgression have left out nothing of disobedience to Allah without including it."

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* narrated through al-Kalbi from his father, who said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by a people who were conversing and said, 'What are you discussing?' They said, 'We are discussing *al-muru'ah* (manliness and chivalrous conduct).' He said, 'Has Allah, Mighty and Majestic, not sufficed you with that in His Book when He says: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾? Justice is equity, and excellence is generosity beyond what is due. What remains after this?'"

Then God, glory be to Him, concluded this verse with His statement: ﴿He admonishes you that you may be reminded﴾, that is, He admonishes you with what He has mentioned in this verse of what He has commanded you and forbidden you from, for it is sufficient in the matter of admonition and reminding. ("That you may be reminded") means: that you may remember what should be remembered, and so be admonished by what God has admonished you with.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Qatadah concerning His statement: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness﴾, he said: its witness is its prophet, that he conveyed the messages of his Lord. God said: ﴿And We have brought you as a witness over these﴾. He said: It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) when he recited this verse, his eyes would overflow.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His statement: ﴿Then they will throw to them the word﴾, he said: they will speak to them.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Jurayj concerning ﴿And they will offer submission to God that Day﴾, he said: they submitted.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted similarly from Qatadah.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib transmitted from al-Bara' that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the statement of God, exalted be He: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾, so he said: "Scorpions like tall palm trees, which sting them in Hell."

Abu Ya`la, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn `Abbas concerning His statement: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾, he said: five rivers of fire which God pours upon them, by which they are punished, some of them by night and some of them by day.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from the hadith of Jabir from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The increase is five rivers flowing from beneath the Throne upon the heads of the people of the Fire: three rivers according to the measure of the night, and two rivers according to the measure of the day; therefore this is His statement: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas`ud that he said: Indeed God has sent down in this Book an explanation of all things, but our knowledge falls short of what has been made clear to us in the Qur'an. Then he recited: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾.
