Then, when Almighty God mentioned the righteous deed and its reward, He followed it with the mention of seeking refuge (al-istiʿādha), by which righteous deeds are purified from satanic whisperings. He said: ﴿So when you recite the Qurʾān, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾. The particle "fa" (so) indicates that seeking refuge follows from the righteous deed. It has been said that this verse is connected to His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ (al-Naḥl 16:89), and the implied meaning is: "So when you begin to recite it, seek refuge."

Al-Zajjāj and others among the leading linguists said: its meaning is "when you intend to recite the Qurʾān, seek refuge," and it does not mean "seek refuge after you have recited the Qurʾān." A similar example is: "When you eat, say: In the name of God."

Al-Wāḥidī said: this is the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the jurists that seeking refuge comes before recitation, except what is narrated from Abū Hurayra, Ibn Sīrīn, Dāwūd, Mālik, and Ḥamza among the reciters; they said that seeking refuge is after recitation, following the apparent meaning of the verse. The meaning of "seek refuge in God" is: ask Him, glorified is He, to protect you from the accursed Satan, that is, from his whisperings. The specification of reciting the Qurʾān among the righteous deeds for seeking refuge when one intends to recite it is to alert that it is even more important for the other righteous deeds when one intends them; for if the command to seek refuge comes at the recitation of the Qurʾān, which falsehood cannot approach from before it or from behind it, then it is more fitting at the intention of other than it. So it has been said.

The address is directed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to indicate that others are more deserving than he of performing the seeking of refuge; for if he is commanded to seek refuge to repel Satan's whisperings despite his infallibility, how about the rest of his community? The majority hold that the command in the verse is for recommendation (nadb). It is narrated from ʿAṭāʾ that it is obligatory, following the apparent meaning of the command.

The discussion of seeking refuge has been fully covered earlier in the beginning of this exegesis.

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed, he has no authority﴾ refers either to the matter (al-shaʾn) or to Satan. That is: he has no power to lead astray ﴿those who believe and upon their Lord they rely﴾. Al-Wāḥidī related from all the exegetes that they interpreted "authority" (sulṭān) as "proof" (ḥujja). They said: the meaning is that he has no proof against the believers in leading them astray and calling them to error. The meaning of ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ is that they entrust their affairs to Him in every saying and deed, for faith in God and reliance upon Him prevent Satan from his whisperings to them, and if he whispers to any of them, his whispering does not affect him. This clause (p-802) is an explanation of the command to seek refuge. These who combine faith and reliance are those about whom Iblīs said: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:40), and God said about them: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:42).

Then Almighty God limited Satan's authority, saying: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾, that is, his power of seduction is only over those who make him a guardian (walī) and obey his whisperings, ﴿and those who associate others with Him﴾. The pronoun in "with Him" refers to God Most High, that is: those who associate others with God. It has been said that it refers to Satan, and the meaning is: those who, because of him and by reason of his whisperings, associate others with God.

﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of a verse﴾. This is the beginning, from Him, glorified is He, of the narration of a disbelieving doubt and its refutation. The meaning of substitution (tabdīl) is removing a thing while placing another in its place. The substitution of a verse is the removal of it by another verse, which is its abrogation (naskh) by another verse. The discussion of abrogation has already been covered in Al-Baqara. They said, that is, the Quraysh disbelievers who were ignorant of the wisdom in abrogation: "You, O Muḥammad, are only a forger (muftarin)," that is, a liar who fabricates against God, inventing against Him what He did not say, since you claim that He commanded you with something and then claim that He commanded you with its opposite. So God, glorified is He, answered them with what shows their ignorance, saying: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ anything of knowledge at all, or they do not know the wisdom in abrogation. For it is based on the interests which God, glorified is He, knows. Thus there may be in the legislation of a thing an interest limited to a certain time, and then after that time the interest lies in the legislation of something else. Had the veil been lifted for these disbelievers, they would have known that this is the path of right, the method of justice, gentleness, and kindness.

Then Almighty God explained to these objectors to the wisdom of abrogation, who claimed that it was not from God and that His Messenger (ﷺ) had invented it, saying: ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down﴾, that is, the Qurʾān indicated by the mention of the verse, ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the Holy Spirit is Gabriel. "Qudus" means purification. The meaning is: it was brought down by the Spirit purified from the defilements of humanity. So it is an idāfa of a qualified noun to its adjective. ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the beginning of its descent is from Him, glorified is He. ﴿with truth﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, while being truly established, for a perfect wisdom, ﴿to make firm those who believe﴾ in faith, so that they say: each of the abrogating and the abrogated is from our Lord. Also, when they know the interests in abrogation, their feet are made firm in faith and their creeds are rooted.

It is also read as "liyathbut" from the causative (al-ithbāt), ﴿and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims﴾. These two are coordinated with the grammatical position of "to make firm," that is: as making them firm, as guidance, and as good tidings. Within this is an allusion to the attainment of the opposites of these qualities by others.

Then Almighty God mentioned another of their doubts, saying: ﴿And We certainly know that they say: "It is only a human being who teaches him"﴾. The "lām" is the preparatory lām (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa), that is: We certainly know that these disbelievers say: "It is only a human of the children of Adam, other than an angel, who teaches Muḥammad the Qurʾān."

The people of knowledge differed about the identity of this human being whom they accused of what they alleged. It has been said he was the slave of al-Fākih ibn al-Mughīra, whose name was Jabr, and he was a Christian who then became Muslim. When the disbelievers of Quraysh heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) reports of earlier generations, despite his being unlettered, they said: "It is only Jabr who teaches him."

It has been said his name was Yaʿīsh, a slave of the Ḥaḍramī family, who used to read foreign books.

It has been said he was a slave of the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy.

It has been said they were two slaves: the name of one was Yasār, and the name of the other was Jabr, and they were sword-polishers who made swords. They used to read a book belonging to them. It has been said they used to read the Torah and the Gospel.

It has been said they meant Salmān al-Fārisī. It has been said they meant a Christian in Mecca named Balʿām, who used to read the Torah.

It has been said they meant a Christian man named Abū Maysara, who spoke Roman (Greek), and in one narration his name was ʿAddās.

Al-Naḥḥās said: these statements are not contradictory, for it is possible that they claimed all of them teach him. But it is not possible to combine them with respect to the statement of the one who said it was Salmān, because this verse is Meccan, and he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in Medina.

Then Almighty God answered their saying, saying: ﴿The tongue of the one to whom they incline is foreign﴾. Al-Ilḥād (deviation) means inclination. It is said: laḥada and alḥada, that is, he deviated from the straight course. It has already been mentioned in Al-Aʿrāf. Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "yalḥadūna" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and the ḥāʾ. The rest read it with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a kasra on the ḥāʾ. That is: the tongue of the one toward whom they incline and whom they claim teaches you is foreign. It is said: a man is aʿjam and a woman is ʿajmāʾ, that is, they cannot express clearly. ʿUjma is concealment, and it is the opposite of clarity (bayān). The Arabs call everyone who does not know their language and does not speak it "aʿjamī."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the aʿjam is the one who has a foreign quality in his speech even if he is an Arab, while the aʿjamī is one whose origin is from the non-Arab peoples (al-ʿajam). Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the ʿajamī is one attributed to the non-Arabs (al-ʿajam) who does not speak eloquently, whether he is an Arab or a non-Arab; likewise the aʿjam. The aʿjamī is one attributed to the non-Arabs even if he is eloquent.

﴿And this is a clear Arabic tongue﴾. The reference is to the Qurʾān, and it is called a "tongue" because the Arabs call a qaṣīda or a verse a "tongue." From this is the statement of the poet:

"A tongue of evil you bring us, and you betrayed; I did not think you would betray."

Or the intended meaning of "tongue" is eloquence, so it is as if He said: this Qurʾān has Arabic eloquence and clear expression; how then do you claim that a human from the non-Arabs teaches it? You yourselves have been unable to produce a sūra like it, and you are people of the Arabic tongue, men of eloquence, and leaders of rhetoric. These two sentences are independent (mustaʾnafa), brought to nullify their accusation and to repel their lie.

When Almighty God mentioned their answer, He rebuked and threatened them, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, that is, do not affirm them, ﴿God does not guide them﴾ to the truth, which is the path of salvation, with a guidance that leads to the desired goal, because of what He knows of their wretchedness. ﴿And for them is a great punishment in the Hereafter﴾ because of their disbelief and denial of God's signs.

Then, when they attributed fabrication to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), He answered them by saying: ﴿Only those fabricate lies who do not believe in the signs of God﴾. So how could fabrication come from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who is the foremost of the believers in them and the one calling to belief in them, while these disbelievers are the ones who do not believe in them? They are the ones who fabricate lies.

Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is that only those who, when they see signs that none but God can produce, deny them, fabricate lies. These are the greatest of liars. Then He called them liars, saying: ﴿Those are the liars﴾, that is, those characterized by that are the liars; that is (p-803) lying is an inseparable attribute of theirs and one of their habits, so they are the perfect liars, since there is no greater lie than their denial of God's signs.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he was asked about the good life mentioned in the verse, and he said: "The good life is lawful provision in this worldly life, and when one reaches his Lord, He will reward him with the best of what he used to do."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, saying: "Al-kasb al-tayyib (good earning) and al-'amal al-salih (righteous deed)."

Al-'Askari, in al-Amthal, related from 'Ali concerning the verse, saying: "Al-qana'a (contentment)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, saying: "Al-qunu' (contentment)." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to supplicate: "O Allah, make me content with what You have provided me, bless it for me, and replace for me every absent thing with good."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah related from Ibn 'Amr that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, he has succeeded who embraces Islam, is provided with sufficient sustenance, and Allah makes him content with what He has given him."

al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, he has succeeded who is guided to Islam, whose livelihood is sufficient, and who is content with it."

'Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf and Ibn al-Mundhir related from 'Ata', saying: "Seeking refuge (al-isti'adhah) is obligatory for every recitation, in prayer and otherwise, on account of His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾. And what has been transmitted regarding the legislation of seeking refuge during recitation is what we have already mentioned."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾, that it means: the authority of Satan is over those who take Satan as an ally and act in disobedience to Allah.

Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾ and His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried﴾, he said: 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh used to write for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but Satan caused him to slip, so he joined the disbelievers. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that he be killed on the day of the Conquest, but 'Uthman sought protection for him from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he granted him protection.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾, that it is like His saying: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106].

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach in Mecca a smith named Balʿam, who was a non-Arab (a'jami). The polytheists would see the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entering to him and leaving from his presence, so they said: 'He is only taught by Balʿam.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And We certainly know that they say﴾," the verse.

al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from him concerning the verse, saying: They said: "Only 'Abd ibn al-Hadrami, who is the owner of books, teaches Muhammad." So Allah revealed this verse.

Adam ibn Abi Iyas, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi related from 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim al-Hadrami, who said: "We had two slaves from the people of 'Ayn al-Tamr, one called Yasar and the other Jabr. They used to make swords in Mecca, and they used to read the Injil. The Prophet (ﷺ) would sometimes pass by them while they were reading, so he would stop and listen. The polytheists said: 'He is only learning from them.' So this verse was revealed."

This is the start of an exhortation to every believer to do every righteous deed, and a generalization of the promise. The meaning of ﴿whoever does righteousness﴾ is whoever does a righteous deed, of whatever kind. The specification "male or female (ﷺ)" is added even though the word "whoever" already includes both, for the sake of emphasis and to strengthen the promise. It has been said that the word "whoever" apparently refers to males, so the explicit mention of male and female clarifies that it covers both sexes. The clause ﴿while he is a believer﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Almighty God made faith a condition for the stated reward, because the deed of a disbeliever is not counted, as He says: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:23). Then He mentioned the reward for one who does such righteous deeds, saying: ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾. There has been disagreement about what the good life consists of. It has been said that it is lawful provision (al-rizq al-ḥalāl). This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It has been said that it is contentment (al-qanaʿa). This was said by al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Zayd ibn Wahb, and Wahb ibn Munabbih.

It is also narrated from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās.

It has been said that it is being granted success in obedience. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It has been said that the good life is the life of Paradise. This is narrated from Mujāhid, Qatāda, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

It is related from al-Ḥasan that he said: "Life is not good for anyone except in Paradise." It has been said that the good life is happiness, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

It has been said that it is knowledge of God (al-maʿrifa bi-Allāh). This is related from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.

Abū Bakr al-Warrāq said: it is the sweetness of obedience.

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī said: it is that the servant's self-management is removed from him and his management is returned to the Truth.

It has been said that it is independence from creation and dependence upon the Truth. Most of the exegetes hold that this good life is in this world and not in the Hereafter, because the life of the Hereafter has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾. We have already mentioned earlier the interpretation of the reward as "the best." He made the pronoun singular in ﴿We will cause him to live﴾ and plural in ﴿We will reward them﴾, in consideration of the wording of "whoever" and of its meaning.

You yourselves have been unable to produce a sūra like it, and you are people of the Arabic tongue, men of eloquence, and leaders of rhetoric. These two sentences are independent (mustaʾnafa), brought to nullify their accusation and to repel their lie.

When Almighty God mentioned their answer, He rebuked and threatened them, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, that is, do not affirm them, ﴿God does not guide them﴾ to the truth, which is the path of salvation, with a guidance that leads to the desired goal, because of what He knows of their wretchedness. ﴿And for them is a great punishment in the Hereafter﴾ because of their disbelief and denial of God's signs.

Then, when they attributed fabrication to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), He answered them by saying: ﴿Only those fabricate lies who do not believe in the signs of God﴾. So how could fabrication come from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who is the foremost of the believers in them and the one calling to belief in them, while these disbelievers are the ones who do not believe in them? They are the ones who fabricate lies.

Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is that only those who, when they see signs that none but God can produce, deny them, fabricate lies. These are the greatest of liars. Then He called them liars, saying: ﴿Those are the liars﴾, that is, those characterized by that are the liars; that is (p-803) lying is an inseparable attribute of theirs and one of their habits, so they are the perfect liars, since there is no greater lie than their denial of God's signs.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Firyābī, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he was asked about the good life mentioned in the verse, and he said: "The good life is lawful provision in this worldly life, and when one reaches his Lord, He will reward him with the best of what he used to do."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, saying: "Al-kasb al-tayyib (good earning) and al-'amal al-salih (righteous deed)."

Al-'Askari, in al-Amthal, related from 'Ali concerning the verse, saying: "Al-qana'a (contentment)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, saying: "Al-qunu' (contentment)." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to supplicate: "O Allah, make me content with what You have provided me, bless it for me, and replace for me every absent thing with good."

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah related from Ibn 'Amr that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, he has succeeded who embraces Islam, is provided with sufficient sustenance, and Allah makes him content with what He has given him."

al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of Fadalah ibn 'Ubayd that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, he has succeeded who is guided to Islam, whose livelihood is sufficient, and who is content with it."

'Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf and Ibn al-Mundhir related from 'Ata', saying: "Seeking refuge (al-isti'adhah) is obligatory for every recitation, in prayer and otherwise, on account of His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾. And what has been transmitted regarding the legislation of seeking refuge during recitation is what we have already mentioned."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾, that it means: the authority of Satan is over those who take Satan as an ally and act in disobedience to Allah.

Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾ and His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried﴾, he said: 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh used to write for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but Satan caused him to slip, so he joined the disbelievers. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that he be killed on the day of the Conquest, but 'Uthman sought protection for him from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he granted him protection.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾, that it is like His saying: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106].

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related, and al-Suyuti said with a weak chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach in Mecca a smith named Balʿam, who was a non-Arab (a'jami). The polytheists would see the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entering to him and leaving from his presence, so they said: 'He is only taught by Balʿam.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And We certainly know that they say﴾," the verse.

al-Hakim (who graded it sound) and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from him concerning the verse, saying: They said: "Only 'Abd ibn al-Hadrami, who is the owner of books, teaches Muhammad." So Allah revealed this verse.

Adam ibn Abi Iyas, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi related from 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim al-Hadrami, who said: "We had two slaves from the people of 'Ayn al-Tamr, one called Yasar and the other Jabr. They used to make swords in Mecca, and they used to read the Injil. The Prophet (ﷺ) would sometimes pass by them while they were reading, so he would stop and listen. The polytheists said: 'He is only learning from them.' So this verse was revealed."

This is the start of an exhortation to every believer to do every righteous deed, and a generalization of the promise. The meaning of ﴿whoever does righteousness﴾ is whoever does a righteous deed, of whatever kind. The specification "male or female (ﷺ)" is added even though the word "whoever" already includes both, for the sake of emphasis and to strengthen the promise. It has been said that the word "whoever" apparently refers to males, so the explicit mention of male and female clarifies that it covers both sexes. The clause ﴿while he is a believer﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Almighty God made faith a condition for the stated reward, because the deed of a disbeliever is not counted, as He says: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:23). Then He mentioned the reward for one who does such righteous deeds, saying: ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾. There has been disagreement about what the good life consists of. It has been said that it is lawful provision (al-rizq al-ḥalāl). This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It has been said that it is contentment (al-qanaʿa). This was said by al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Zayd ibn Wahb, and Wahb ibn Munabbih.

It is also narrated from ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās.

It has been said that it is being granted success in obedience. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

It has been said that the good life is the life of Paradise. This is narrated from Mujāhid, Qatāda, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.

It is related from al-Ḥasan that he said: "Life is not good for anyone except in Paradise." It has been said that the good life is happiness, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

It has been said that it is knowledge of God (al-maʿrifa bi-Allāh). This is related from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.

Abū Bakr al-Warrāq said: it is the sweetness of obedience.

Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tustarī said: it is that the servant's self-management is removed from him and his management is returned to the Truth.

It has been said that it is independence from creation and dependence upon the Truth. Most of the exegetes hold that this good life is in this world and not in the Hereafter, because the life of the Hereafter has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾. We have already mentioned earlier the interpretation of the reward as "the best." He made the pronoun singular in ﴿We will cause him to live﴾ and plural in ﴿We will reward them﴾, in consideration of the wording of "whoever" and of its meaning.

Then, when Almighty God mentioned the righteous deed and its reward, He followed it with the mention of seeking refuge (al-istiʿādha), by which righteous deeds are purified from satanic whisperings. He said: ﴿So when you recite the Qurʾān, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan﴾. The particle "fa" (so) indicates that seeking refuge follows from the righteous deed. It has been said that this verse is connected to His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ (al-Naḥl 16:89), and the implied meaning is: "So when you begin to recite it, seek refuge."

Al-Zajjāj and others among the leading linguists said: its meaning is "when you intend to recite the Qurʾān, seek refuge," and it does not mean "seek refuge after you have recited the Qurʾān." A similar example is: "When you eat, say: In the name of God."

Al-Wāḥidī said: this is the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the jurists that seeking refuge comes before recitation, except what is narrated from Abū Hurayra, Ibn Sīrīn, Dāwūd, Mālik, and Ḥamza among the reciters; they said that seeking refuge is after recitation, following the apparent meaning of the verse. The meaning of "seek refuge in God" is: ask Him, glorified is He, to protect you from the accursed Satan, that is, from his whisperings. The specification of reciting the Qurʾān among the righteous deeds for seeking refuge when one intends to recite it is to alert that it is even more important for the other righteous deeds when one intends them; for if the command to seek refuge comes at the recitation of the Qurʾān, which falsehood cannot approach from before it or from behind it, then it is more fitting at the intention of other than it. So it has been said.

The address is directed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to indicate that others are more deserving than he of performing the seeking of refuge; for if he is commanded to seek refuge to repel Satan's whisperings despite his infallibility, how about the rest of his community? The majority hold that the command in the verse is for recommendation (nadb). It is narrated from ʿAṭāʾ that it is obligatory, following the apparent meaning of the command.

The discussion of seeking refuge has been fully covered earlier in the beginning of this exegesis.

The pronoun in ﴿Indeed, he has no authority﴾ refers either to the matter (al-shaʾn) or to Satan. That is: he has no power to lead astray ﴿those who believe and upon their Lord they rely﴾. Al-Wāḥidī related from all the exegetes that they interpreted "authority" (sulṭān) as "proof" (ḥujja). They said: the meaning is that he has no proof against the believers in leading them astray and calling them to error. The meaning of ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ is that they entrust their affairs to Him in every saying and deed, for faith in God and reliance upon Him prevent Satan from his whisperings to them, and if he whispers to any of them, his whispering does not affect him. This clause (p-802) is an explanation of the command to seek refuge. These who combine faith and reliance are those about whom Iblīs said: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:40), and God said about them: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:42).

Then Almighty God limited Satan's authority, saying: ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾, that is, his power of seduction is only over those who make him a guardian (walī) and obey his whisperings, ﴿and those who associate others with Him﴾. The pronoun in "with Him" refers to God Most High, that is: those who associate others with God. It has been said that it refers to Satan, and the meaning is: those who, because of him and by reason of his whisperings, associate others with God.

﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of a verse﴾. This is the beginning, from Him, glorified is He, of the narration of a disbelieving doubt and its refutation. The meaning of substitution (tabdīl) is removing a thing while placing another in its place. The substitution of a verse is the removal of it by another verse, which is its abrogation (naskh) by another verse. The discussion of abrogation has already been covered in Al-Baqara. They said, that is, the Quraysh disbelievers who were ignorant of the wisdom in abrogation: "You, O Muḥammad, are only a forger (muftarin)," that is, a liar who fabricates against God, inventing against Him what He did not say, since you claim that He commanded you with something and then claim that He commanded you with its opposite. So God, glorified is He, answered them with what shows their ignorance, saying: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ anything of knowledge at all, or they do not know the wisdom in abrogation. For it is based on the interests which God, glorified is He, knows. Thus there may be in the legislation of a thing an interest limited to a certain time, and then after that time the interest lies in the legislation of something else. Had the veil been lifted for these disbelievers, they would have known that this is the path of right, the method of justice, gentleness, and kindness.

Then Almighty God explained to these objectors to the wisdom of abrogation, who claimed that it was not from God and that His Messenger (ﷺ) had invented it, saying: ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down﴾, that is, the Qurʾān indicated by the mention of the verse, ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the Holy Spirit is Gabriel. "Qudus" means purification. The meaning is: it was brought down by the Spirit purified from the defilements of humanity. So it is an idāfa of a qualified noun to its adjective. ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the beginning of its descent is from Him, glorified is He. ﴿with truth﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, while being truly established, for a perfect wisdom, ﴿to make firm those who believe﴾ in faith, so that they say: each of the abrogating and the abrogated is from our Lord. Also, when they know the interests in abrogation, their feet are made firm in faith and their creeds are rooted.

It is also read as "liyathbut" from the causative (al-ithbāt), ﴿and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims﴾. These two are coordinated with the grammatical position of "to make firm," that is: as making them firm, as guidance, and as good tidings. Within this is an allusion to the attainment of the opposites of these qualities by others.

Then Almighty God mentioned another of their doubts, saying: ﴿And We certainly know that they say: "It is only a human being who teaches him"﴾. The "lām" is the preparatory lām (al-lām al-muwaṭṭiʾa), that is: We certainly know that these disbelievers say: "It is only a human of the children of Adam, other than an angel, who teaches Muḥammad the Qurʾān."

The people of knowledge differed about the identity of this human being whom they accused of what they alleged. It has been said he was the slave of al-Fākih ibn al-Mughīra, whose name was Jabr, and he was a Christian who then became Muslim. When the disbelievers of Quraysh heard from the Prophet (ﷺ) reports of earlier generations, despite his being unlettered, they said: "It is only Jabr who teaches him."

It has been said his name was Yaʿīsh, a slave of the Ḥaḍramī family, who used to read foreign books.

It has been said he was a slave of the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy.

It has been said they were two slaves: the name of one was Yasār, and the name of the other was Jabr, and they were sword-polishers who made swords. They used to read a book belonging to them. It has been said they used to read the Torah and the Gospel.

It has been said they meant Salmān al-Fārisī. It has been said they meant a Christian in Mecca named Balʿām, who used to read the Torah.

It has been said they meant a Christian man named Abū Maysara, who spoke Roman (Greek), and in one narration his name was ʿAddās.

Al-Naḥḥās said: these statements are not contradictory, for it is possible that they claimed all of them teach him. But it is not possible to combine them with respect to the statement of the one who said it was Salmān, because this verse is Meccan, and he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) in Medina.

Then Almighty God answered their saying, saying: ﴿The tongue of the one to whom they incline is foreign﴾. Al-Ilḥād (deviation) means inclination. It is said: laḥada and alḥada, that is, he deviated from the straight course. It has already been mentioned in Al-Aʿrāf. Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read "yalḥadūna" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and the ḥāʾ. The rest read it with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a kasra on the ḥāʾ. That is: the tongue of the one toward whom they incline and whom they claim teaches you is foreign. It is said: a man is aʿjam and a woman is ʿajmāʾ, that is, they cannot express clearly. ʿUjma is concealment, and it is the opposite of clarity (bayān). The Arabs call everyone who does not know their language and does not speak it "aʿjamī."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the aʿjam is the one who has a foreign quality in his speech even if he is an Arab, while the aʿjamī is one whose origin is from the non-Arab peoples (al-ʿajam). Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the ʿajamī is one attributed to the non-Arabs (al-ʿajam) who does not speak eloquently, whether he is an Arab or a non-Arab; likewise the aʿjam. The aʿjamī is one attributed to the non-Arabs even if he is eloquent.

﴿And this is a clear Arabic tongue﴾. The reference is to the Qurʾān, and it is called a "tongue" because the Arabs call a qaṣīda or a verse a "tongue." From this is the statement of the poet:

"A tongue of evil you bring us, and you betrayed; I did not think you would betray."

Or the intended meaning of "tongue" is eloquence, so it is as if He said: this Qurʾān has Arabic eloquence and clear expression; how then do you claim that a human from the non-Arabs teaches it? You yourselves have been unable to produce a sūra like it, and you are people of the Arabic tongue, men of eloquence, and leaders of rhetoric. These two sentences are independent (mustaʾnafa), brought to nullify their accusation and to repel their lie.

When Almighty God mentioned their answer, He rebuked and threatened them, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, that is, do not affirm them, ﴿God does not guide them﴾ to the truth, which is the path of salvation, with a guidance that leads to the desired goal, because of what He knows of their wretchedness. ﴿And for them is a great punishment in the Hereafter﴾ because of their disbelief and denial of God's signs.

Then, when they attributed fabrication to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), He answered them by saying: ﴿Only those fabricate lies who do not believe in the signs of God﴾. So how could fabrication come from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who is the foremost of the believers in them and the one calling to belief in them, while these disbelievers are the ones who do not believe in them? They are the ones who fabricate lies.

The polytheists said: 'He is only learning from them.' So this verse was revealed."

The verse says: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief...﴾. The scholars differed over its grammatical analysis (i'rab). Most of them held that it is a substitute (badal) either for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraz). The meaning is: "Only those who disbelieve fabricate lies." He excepted from them the one who was compelled, so he does not fall under the ruling on fabrication.

Then He said: ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, meaning, believes in it, his soul is content with it and at rest in it, ﴿upon them is wrath﴾. Or it may be a substitute for the subject, which is ﴿those﴾ [al-Nahl: 105], or for the predicate, which is ﴿the liars﴾ [al-Nahl: 105]. Al-Zajjaj held the first view. Al-Akhfash said: "man" (whoever) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and it is sufficient to mention the predicate of the second "man," as in your saying: "Whoever of you comes to us, we will honour him." It was also said that it is in the accusative on the basis of dham (vituperation). It was also said that "man" is conditional, and its answer is omitted because the answer of "man" in ﴿but whoever opens his breast﴾ indicates it. This is like the view of al-Akhfash, except that he differed in applying the term of the condition to "man" while the answer is in its predicate. So it is as if it were said: "Whoever disbelieves in God, upon them is wrath, except the one who was compelled; but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath." The exception of the compelled from the disbeliever is valid even though he is not a disbeliever, because after his belief there appeared from him what would not appear except from a disbeliever were it not for compulsion.

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars are agreed that whoever is compelled to disbelief, to the point that he fears death for himself, there is no sin upon him if he disbelieves while his heart is at rest in faith. His wife does not become separated from him, and he is not judged by the ruling of disbelief.

It is related from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that if he openly shows disbelief, he is an apostate outwardly, while between himself and God he remains upon Islam. His wife becomes separated from him, he is not prayed over if he dies, and he does not inherit from his father if he dies a Muslim. This view is rejected and refuted by its proponent, being countered by the Book and the Sunnah. Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and Sahnun held that this concession mentioned in this verse applies only to speech, but for action there is no concession, such as being compelled to prostrate to other than God. The apparent meaning of the verse refutes this, for it is general concerning whoever is compelled, without any distinction between speech and action. There is no evidence for these people who restrict the verse to speech. The specificity of the occasion of revelation (khusus al-sabab) carries no weight against the generality of the wording, as is established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

The clause ﴿and his heart is at rest in faith﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the excepted term, meaning: "except one who disbelieved under compulsion, while his heart is at rest in faith, his belief unchanged." After this grave warning, which is the gathering for the apostates of God's wrath and His terrible punishment...

The reference in His words ﴿that﴾ is either to disbelief after belief, or to the threat of wrath and punishment. The particle ﴿bi-annahum﴾ ("because") is causal, meaning: that is because of their preferring the life of this world ﴿over the Hereafter﴾, and that God does not guide the disbelieving people. It is conjoined to ﴿annahum istahabbu﴾, meaning: that is because they preferred, and because God does not guide the disbelieving people to belief in Him.

Then He described them with His words: ﴿Those are﴾, meaning, those described with the foul qualities mentioned, ﴿those whose hearts, hearing and sight God has sealed.﴾ So they did not understand the admonitions nor did they hear them, nor did they see the signs by which the truth is established. Then he said to the other: "Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." The verse says: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief...﴾. The scholars differed over its grammatical analysis (i'rab). Most of them held that it is a substitute (badal) either for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraz). The meaning is: "Only those who disbelieve fabricate lies." He excepted from them the one who was compelled, so he does not fall under the ruling on fabrication.

It was also said that it is in the accusative on the basis of dham (vituperation). It was also said that "man" is conditional, and its answer is omitted because the answer of "man" in ﴿but whoever opens his breast﴾ indicates it. This is like the view of al-Akhfash, except that he differed in applying the term of the condition to "man" while the answer is in its predicate. There is no evidence for these people who restrict the verse to speech. The specificity of the occasion of revelation (khusus al-sabab) carries no weight against the generality of the wording, as is established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

It is conjoined to ﴿annahum istahabbu﴾, meaning: that is because they preferred, and because God does not guide the disbelieving people to belief in Him.

Then they left him. When he came to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "What is behind you?" He said: "Evil. I was not released until I had reviled you and mentioned their gods favourably." He said: "How do you find your heart?" He said: "At rest in faith." He said: "If they return, then return." So there was revealed ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith﴾. He said: That is ʿAmmar ibn Yasir. ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾ is ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Sarh.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn ʿAsakir related from Abu Malik concerning His words ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith﴾, that he said: It was revealed concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir. There are reports in this regard explicitly stating that it was revealed concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: This verse ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith﴾ was revealed concerning ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa.

Ibn Mardawayh related through the route of Ikrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: In Surat al-Nahl, ﴿upon them is wrath from God, and for them is a great punishment﴾. Then it was abrogated (naskh) and an exception was made from it, saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried...﴾ up to the verse. He said: This is ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, who used to write for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but Satan made him slip, so he joined the disbelievers. The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that he be killed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Then ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan sought protection for him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) granted him protection.

Ibn Jarir related the like of this from Ikrimah and al-Hasan.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: This verse ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried﴾ was revealed concerning those among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who were being tried.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him, who said: There were some people of Makkah who had embraced Islam and used to conceal their Islam. So this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated...﴾ up to the verse. They wrote to them about this: "God has made a way out for you, so come out." Then the polytheists overtook them and fought them. Whoever was saved was saved, and whoever was killed was killed.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from al-Hasan that spies of Musaylima seized two men from the Muslims and brought them to him. He said to one of them: "Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?" He gestured toward his ears and said: "I am deaf." So he ordered him to be killed. Then he said to the other: "Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." So he released him, and he came to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said to him: "As for your companion, he went on his faith; but as for you, you took the concession." This is a mursal report.

The verse says: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief...﴾. The scholars differed over its grammatical analysis (i'rab). Most of them held that it is a substitute (badal) either for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraz). The meaning is: "Only those who disbelieve fabricate lies." He excepted from them the one who was compelled, so he does not fall under the ruling on fabrication.

Then He said: ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, meaning, believes in it, his soul is content with it and at rest in it, ﴿upon them is wrath﴾. Or it may be a substitute for the subject, which is ﴿those﴾ [al-Nahl: 105], or for the predicate, which is ﴿the liars﴾ [al-Nahl: 105]. Al-Zajjaj held the first view. Al-Akhfash said: "man" (whoever) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and it is sufficient to mention the predicate of the second "man," as in your saying: "Whoever of you comes to us, we will honour him." It was also said that it is in the accusative on the basis of dham (vituperation). It was also said that "man" is conditional, and its answer is omitted because the answer of "man" in ﴿but whoever opens his breast﴾ indicates it. This is like the view of al-Akhfash, except that he differed in applying the term of the condition to "man" while the answer is in its predicate. So it is as if it were said: "Whoever disbelieves in God, upon them is wrath, except the one who was compelled; but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath." The exception of the compelled from the disbeliever is valid even though he is not a disbeliever, because after his belief there appeared from him what would not appear except from a disbeliever were it not for compulsion.

Al-Qurtubi said: The scholars are agreed that whoever is compelled to disbelief, to the point that he fears death for himself, there is no sin upon him if he disbelieves while his heart is at rest in faith. His wife does not become separated from him, and he is not judged by the ruling of disbelief.

It is related from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that if he openly shows disbelief, he is an apostate outwardly, while between himself and God he remains upon Islam. His wife becomes separated from him, he is not prayed over if he dies, and he does not inherit from his father if he dies a Muslim. This view is rejected and refuted by its proponent, being countered by the Book and the Sunnah. Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i and Sahnun held that this concession mentioned in this verse applies only to speech, but for action there is no concession, such as being compelled to prostrate to other than God. The apparent meaning of the verse refutes this, for it is general concerning whoever is compelled, without any distinction between speech and action. There is no evidence for these people who restrict the verse to speech. The specificity of the occasion of revelation (khusus al-sabab) carries no weight against the generality of the wording, as is established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

The clause ﴿and his heart is at rest in faith﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the excepted term, meaning: "except one who disbelieved under compulsion, while his heart is at rest in faith, his belief unchanged." After this grave warning, which is the gathering for the apostates of God's wrath and His terrible punishment...

The reference in His words ﴿that﴾ is either to disbelief after belief, or to the threat of wrath and punishment. The particle ﴿bi-annahum﴾ ("because") is causal, meaning: that is because of their preferring the life of this world ﴿over the Hereafter﴾, and that God does not guide the disbelieving people. It is conjoined to ﴿annahum istahabbu﴾, meaning: that is because they preferred, and because God does not guide the disbelieving people to belief in Him.

Then He described them with His words: ﴿Those are﴾, meaning, those described with the foul qualities mentioned, ﴿those whose hearts, hearing and sight God has sealed.﴾ So they did not understand the admonitions nor did they hear them, nor did they see the signs by which the truth is established. The reality of sealing (tab') has already been investigated at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Then He ascribed to them another deficiency, different from the one mentioned earlier, saying: ﴿And those are the heedless﴾, heedless of what is intended for them. The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) indicates that they are extreme in heedlessness, for there is no heedlessness greater than this heedlessness of theirs.

﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers.﴾ That is, the complete losers, who reach a degree of loss beyond which there is no degree. The investigation of the meaning of la jaram has already been made in several places, among them the one in this surah.

﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ from the abode of disbelief to the abode of Islam. The predicate of inna is omitted, the estimated reading being "surely Forgiving, Merciful." It was omitted because of the indication of the later predicate of the second inna, "your Lord." It was also said that the predicate is "for those who emigrated," meaning: your Lord is for them, in support and succour, not against them. But this is remote. It was also said that its predicate is His words ﴿surely Forgiving, Merciful﴾, and the second "inna your Lord" is an emphasis of the first.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: Here "then" (thumma) indicates the distance between the condition of these people, meaning those concerning whom the verse was revealed, and the condition of those, namely ʿAmmar and his companions. This is indicated by what is related, that it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, and its explanation will come. ﴿After they were tried﴾, that is, the disbelievers tried them by torturing them so that they would return to disbelief. It is also read "fatanu" in the active voice, meaning: those who tried the believers and tortured them for Islam, then they strove in the way of God and were patient over what the disbelievers inflicted upon them, and over the hardships of the obligations they bore. ﴿Surely Forgiving, Merciful﴾, that is, abundantly forgiving and merciful toward them. The meaning of the verse according to the reading of those who read "fatanu" in the active voice is clear and evident: that is, your Lord, for those disbelievers who tried whoever embraced Islam and tortured them, then strove and were patient, is surely Forgiving, Merciful. As for the reading in the passive voice, which is the reading of the majority, the meaning is: those tried ones who uttered the word of disbelief under compulsion, while their breasts were not expanded to disbelief, if their deeds were sound and they strove for God and were patient under hardships, He is surely Forgiving to them and Merciful to them. But if the occasion of this verse is ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, who apostatised from Islam and then returned to Islam after that, the meaning is: this one who was tried in his religion by apostasy, when he embraces Islam, strives and is patient, God is Forgiving to him and Merciful to him. The pronoun in "baʿdiha" refers either to the trial, or to the emigration, struggle and patience, or to all of them.

﴿On the day when every soul comes pleading for itself.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "The day when it comes" (yawma ta'ti) is in the accusative, governed either by His words "merciful," or by an implied verb such as "remember," or "remind them," or "warn them." The phrase "soul" (nafs) being annexed to "soul" has been questioned, for there must be a difference between the annexed and the annexed-to. It is answered that by the first "soul" is meant the whole body of the human being, and by the second "soul" is meant the self (dhat). So it is as if it were said: "On the day when every person comes pleading for his very self, concerned with nothing else." The meaning of pleading for it is making excuses for it. He is pleading and contending for his own self, having no leisure for anything else on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) intended to emigrate to Madinah, he said to his companions: "Disperse from me. Whoever has strength, let him delay until the end of the night; and whoever has no strength, let him go at the beginning of the night. When you hear of me that the earth has settled me, then join me." So Bilal the muezzin and Khabbab, ʿAmmar and a slave girl from Quraysh who had embraced Islam, rose in the morning, and the polytheists seized them along with Abu Jahl. They offered Bilal that he should disbelieve, but he refused. So they began placing an iron coat of mail in the sun and then dressing him in it. When they dressed him in it, he said: "One! One!" As for Khabbab, they dragged him through the thorns. As for ʿAmmar, he said to them a word that pleased them, as taqiyya. As for the slave girl, Abu Jahl drove four stakes for her, then stretched her out and thrust a spear into her private part until he killed her. Then they released Bilal, Khabbab and ʿAmmar, and they joined the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him of what had happened to them. He was distressed over ʿAmmar because of what he had said. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "How was your heart when you said what you said? Was it expanded with what you said, or not?" He said: "No." So God revealed: ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith﴾.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn ʿAsakir related, through the route of Abu ʿUbayda ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAmmar, from his father, who said: The polytheists seized ʿAmmar ibn Yasir and did not leave him until he reviled the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned their gods favourably. Then they left him. When he came to the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "What is behind you?" He said: "Evil. I was not released until I had reviled you and mentioned their gods favourably." He said: "How do you find your heart?" He said: "At rest in faith." He said: "If they return, then return." So there was revealed ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith﴾. He said: That is ʿAmmar ibn Yasir. ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾ is ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Sarh.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn ʿAsakir related from Abu Malik concerning His words ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith﴾, that he said: It was revealed concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir. There are reports in this regard explicitly stating that it was revealed concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: This verse ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith﴾ was revealed concerning ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa.

Ibn Mardawayh related through the route of Ikrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: In Surat al-Nahl, ﴿upon them is wrath from God, and for them is a great punishment﴾. Then it was abrogated (naskh) and an exception was made from it, saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried...﴾ up to the verse. He said: This is ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, who used to write for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but Satan made him slip, so he joined the disbelievers. The Prophet (ﷺ) ordered that he be killed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. Then ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan sought protection for him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) granted him protection.

Ibn Jarir related the like of this from Ikrimah and al-Hasan.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: This verse ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried﴾ was revealed concerning those among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who were being tried.

Ibn Mardawayh related from him, who said: There were some people of Makkah who had embraced Islam and used to conceal their Islam. So this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated...﴾ up to the verse. They wrote to them about this: "God has made a way out for you, so come out." Then the polytheists overtook them and fought them. Whoever was saved was saved, and whoever was killed was killed.

Ibn Abi Shaybah related from al-Hasan that spies of Musaylima seized two men from the Muslims and brought them to him. He said to one of them: "Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?" He gestured toward his ears and said: "I am deaf." So he ordered him to be killed. Then he said to the other: "Do you testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." So he released him, and he came to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said to him: "As for your companion, he went on his faith; but as for you, you took the concession." This is a mursal report.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 112–119:

His saying: ﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town﴾. We have already mentioned that "daraba" (presented/struck) is here construed with the meaning of "ja'ala" (made), so that "qaryatan" (a town) is the first object and "mathalan" (a parable) the second. "Qaryatan" was placed later so that no separation would occur between it and its attributes. We also mentioned that it is permissible for "daraba" to be in its original sense, not construed with another meaning, in which case "mathalan" is its first object and "qaryatan" is an apposition (badal) to it.

The exegetes differ as to whether the intended town is a specific town, or whether it is an unspecified town, meaning every people whom Allah blessed and whom blessing made arrogant. The majority adopted the first view and stated explicitly that it is Makkah, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, saying: "O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Yusuf," so they were afflicted with famine until they ate the bones.

The second view is more preponderant, because the indefiniteness of "qaryatin" indicates it. Makkah enters this general (badali) scope primarily; moreover the threat is more forceful and the parable more complete, and other than Makkah is similar to it. And on the assumption that Makkah is intended, the parable still contains a warning to others from a fate like its fate. Then He described the town as ﴿being secure﴾, not fearful, tranquil, not disturbed, meaning its people did not fear and were not disturbed. ﴿Its provision came to it﴾, meaning what its people obtain sustenance by, abundantly, from every place from which what is in them is brought to it. ﴿But it denied the favours of Allah﴾, meaning its people denied them. "An'um" is the plural of "ni'mah," like "ashudd" is the plural of "shiddah"; it was also said to be the plural of "nu'mā," like "bu'sā" and "ab'us." This denial on their part is their disbelief in Allah, glorified is He, and their denial of His messengers. ﴿So Allah made it taste﴾, meaning He made its people taste ﴿the garment of hunger and fear﴾. This was called a "garment" because the signs of emaciation, paleness of complexion and bad condition that appear upon them are like a garment; so its name was borrowed for it, and the "tasting" (idhaqa) was attributed to it. Its origin is tasting with the mouth; then it was borrowed for general experiencing, with the indication of severity of affliction, because it combines two perceptions: the perception of touch and of taste.

It is related that Ibn al-Rawandi the heretic said to Ibn al-A'rabi, the imam of language and literature: "Can a garment be tasted?" Ibn al-A'rabi said to him: "No harm, you ape! Suppose Muhammad was not a prophet, was he not an Arab?" It was as if he were criticising the verse on the basis that the appropriate phrasing would be "then Allah clothed them with the garment of hunger," or "then Allah made them taste the taste of hunger."

Ibn al-A'rabi refuted him.

The scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-bayan) have answered that this is an instance of "tajrid" (the stripped metaphor). That is, he borrowed "garment" for what covers a person of certain calamities, such as hunger and fear, because it envelops him as a garment envelops the wearer; then the attribute was mentioned suitable to the borrowed-for thing, which is hunger and fear, because the use of "tasting" for experiencing hunger and fear was, in their usage, treated as literal; they say "so-and-so tasted misery and harm," and another made him taste it. So the metaphor was stripped (mujarradah), whereas had he said "fa-kasahā" (then He clothed it), it would have been "murashshahah" (the metaphor being nurtured by a supporting term).

It was said: although the nurturing of a metaphor is commendable in terms of intensification, stripping has a preference in that the side of the borrowed-for thing is observed, so the speech becomes clearer. It was also said that the origin of tasting is with the mouth, then it may be borrowed and placed in the position of knowing and testing, and from this is the poet's saying:

Whoever tastes the world, I have tasted it, and both its sweetness and its torment have been driven to us.

Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyath, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu ʿAmr, as narrated from him by ʿAbd al-Warith, read "al-khawfa" with the accusative, coordinating it with "libas" (garment). The rest read it with the nominative (ḍamma), coordinating it with "al-juʿ" (hunger).

Al-Farra' said: All the attributes were applied to the town except His saying "yaṣnaʿūn" (they used to do), as an indication that the intended meaning in reality is its people.

﴿And there had certainly come to them﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿a messenger from among them﴾, from their own kind, whom they know and whose lineage they know. So he commanded them with what benefits them and forbade them from what harms them, but they denied him in what he brought. ﴿Then the punishment seized them﴾, the punishment descending upon them from Allah, glorified is He, while they were, in the state of being seized by the punishment, wrongdoers to themselves by casting themselves into everlasting punishment, and to others by harming them and barring them from the way of Allah. This statement is part of the completion of the parable presented.

It was also said that the punishment here is the hunger that afflicted them, and it was said it is the killing on the day of Badr.

Then, when Allah, glorified is He, admonished them with what He mentioned of the state of the people of the aforementioned town, He commanded them to eat of what Allah had provided them from the spoils and the like. He used "fa" (then) to signal that this is consequent upon abandoning disbelief.

The meaning: since you have believed and abandoned disbelief, then eat the lawful good, which is the spoils, and leave the wicked things, which are carrion and blood. ﴿And be grateful for the favour of Allah﴾, the favour with which He has blessed you, and recognise its due ﴿if it is Him you worship﴾, and you do not worship other than Him; or, if your claim is true that by worshipping the gods you intend the worship of Allah, the Exalted. It was also said that the "fa" in "fa-kulū" attaches to the command to give thanks, and it was attached to the command to eat because eating is a means to gratitude.

﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾. Glorified is He repeated the mention of these prohibitions in al-Baqarah, al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, and in this surah, to cut off excuses and remove doubt. Then He mentioned the concession regarding partaking of any of what was mentioned, saying: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The discussion of all that is mentioned here has been covered in full previously.

Then He refuted the way of the disbelievers in adding to these prohibitions, such as the baḥīrah and sā'ibah, and in reducing from them, such as declaring carrion and blood lawful. So He said: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely﴾. Al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj said: "ma" here is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah), and "al-kadhiba" (the lie) is in the accusative governed by "lā taqūlū" (do not say), meaning: do not say the lie for the sake of the description your tongues utter, and its meaning is: do not prohibit or permit on account of a statement your tongues utter without any proof. It is permissible for "ma" to be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), with "al-kadhiba" in the accusative governed by "taṣifu" (describes), meaning: do not say of that which your tongues describe, the lie concerning it, ﴿"This is lawful, and this is unlawful"﴾; the word "fīhi" (concerning it) is omitted because it is known. Thus "This is lawful and this is unlawful" is an apposition (badal) to "al-kadhiba." It is also permissible that there is an ellipsis in the speech, with an implied "say," meaning: do not say of what your tongues describe, so that it says "This is lawful and this is unlawful," or [it is] saying "This is lawful and this is unlawful." It is also permissible that "al-kadhiba" be in the accusative governed by "taṣifu" and "ma" be verbal-noun, meaning: do not say "This is lawful and this is unlawful" for the description your tongues make of the lie.

It was read "al-kudhubu" (with ḍamma on the kāf, dhāl and bāʾ), as an attribute of "al-alsina" (the tongues). al-Hasan read it with fatḥa on the kāf and kasra on the dhāl and bāʾ, as an attribute of "mā."

It was also said it is in apposition (badal) to "mā," meaning: do not say the lie, which your tongues describe, "This is lawful and this is unlawful." The lām in ﴿so that you may fabricate against Allah the lie﴾ is the lām of consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah), not the lām of purpose, meaning: that will be followed by your fabrication against Allah of the lie through permitting and forbidding, and the ascription of that to Him without it being from Him. ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah the lie﴾, whatever fabrication it is, ﴿will not succeed﴾ in any kind of success, which is attaining the sought-after object.

The nominative of "matāʿun qalīlun" (a little enjoyment) is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject. al-Zajjaj said: That is, their enjoyment is a little enjoyment; or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: for them is a little enjoyment. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, to which they will be returned in the Hereafter.

Then He singled out the prohibitions of the Jews for mention, saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade﴾, meaning We forbade it upon them specifically and not upon others, ﴿what We have related to you﴾ by His saying: ﴿We forbade every animal with claws, and of the cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat﴾ [al-An'am: 146], and so on. "Min qablu" (previously) is connected either to "qaṣaṣnā" (We related) or to "ḥarramnā" (We forbade). ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by that prohibition, rather We recompensed them for their transgression, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, in that they committed the causes of that, so We forbade them those things as a punishment for them.

Then Glorified is He explained that fabricating against Allah and opposing His command does not prevent them from repentance and attaining forgiveness, so He said: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who do evil in ignorance﴾, meaning while they are clothed in ignorance. The explanation of this verse has been given before in Surah al-Nisa'. ﴿Then repent after that﴾, meaning after their doing evil. This contains emphasis, since "thumma" (then) already indicates sequence, so He reinforced it by adding the mention of sequence. ﴿And reform their deeds, which had corruption in them through the evil they did﴾. Then He repeated that for emphasis and affirmation, saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord, after it﴾, meaning after repentance, ﴿is surely Forgiving and Merciful﴾, abundantly forgiving, of vast mercy.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town﴾, that he said: it means Makkah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿAṭiyyah regarding the verse the like of it, and added: Do you not see that He said: ﴿And there had certainly come to them a messenger from among them, but they denied him﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Shihab, who said: The town of which Allah said ﴿was secure and tranquil﴾ is Yathrib.

I say: I do not know what proof led him to this specification, nor what indication stood for him on that. And when did the abode of the Hijrah and the dwelling of the Ansar disbelieve in the favours of Allah, and at what time did Allah make it taste the garment of hunger and fear? It is the one that expels its impurity as the furnace expels the impurity of iron, as this is authentically established from the truthful and the believed one (ﷺ).

It is also authentically established from him that he said: "And Madinah is better for them, if they only knew."

Its origin is tasting with the mouth; then it was borrowed for general experiencing, with the indication of severity of affliction, because it combines two perceptions: the perception of touch and of taste.

It is related that Ibn al-Rawandi the heretic said to Ibn al-A'rabi, the imam of language and literature: "Can a garment be tasted?" Ibn al-A'rabi said to him: "No harm, you ape! It was as if he were criticising the verse on the basis that the appropriate phrasing would be "then Allah clothed them with the garment of hunger," or "then Allah made them taste the taste of hunger."

It was said: although the nurturing of a metaphor is commendable in terms of intensification, stripping has a preference in that the side of the borrowed-for thing is observed, so the speech becomes clearer. It was also said that the origin of tasting is with the mouth, then it may be borrowed and placed in the position of knowing and testing, and from this is the poet's saying:

Whoever tastes the world, I have tasted it, and both its sweetness and its torment have been driven to us.

Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyath, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu ʿAmr, as narrated from him by ʿAbd al-Warith, read "al-khawfa" with the accusative, coordinating it with "libas" (garment). The rest read it with the nominative (ḍamma), coordinating it with "al-juʿ" (hunger).

It was also said that the "fa" in "fa-kulū" attaches to the command to give thanks, and it was attached to the command to eat because eating is a means to gratitude.

﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾. Glorified is He repeated the mention of these prohibitions in al-Baqarah, al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, and in this surah, to cut off excuses and remove doubt. Then He mentioned the concession regarding partaking of any of what was mentioned, saying: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The discussion of all that is mentioned here has been covered in full previously.

Thus "This is lawful and this is unlawful" is an apposition (badal) to "al-kadhiba." It is also permissible that there is an ellipsis in the speech, with an implied "say," meaning: do not say of what your tongues describe, so that it says "This is lawful and this is unlawful," or [it is] saying "This is lawful and this is unlawful." It is also permissible that "al-kadhiba" be in the accusative governed by "taṣifu" and "ma" be verbal-noun, meaning: do not say "This is lawful and this is unlawful" for the description your tongues make of the lie.

"Min qablu" (previously) is connected either to "qaṣaṣnā" (We related) or to "ḥarramnā" (We forbade). ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by that prohibition, rather We recompensed them for their transgression, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, in that they committed the causes of that, so We forbade them those things as a punishment for them.

The explanation of this verse has been given before in Surah al-Nisa'. ﴿Then repent after that﴾, meaning after their doing evil. This contains emphasis, since "thumma" (then) already indicates sequence, so He reinforced it by adding the mention of sequence. ﴿And reform their deeds, which had corruption in them through the evil they did﴾. Then He repeated that for emphasis and affirmation, saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord, after it﴾, meaning after repentance, ﴿is surely Forgiving and Merciful﴾, abundantly forgiving, of vast mercy.

Whoever tastes the world, I have tasted it, and both its sweetness and its torment have been driven to us.

Whoever tastes the world, I have tasted it, and both its sweetness and its torment have been driven to us.
