Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Nadrah, who said: I read this verse in Surah al-Nahl: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely: "This is lawful, and this is unlawful"﴾, to the end of the verse, and I have not ceased to fear issuing fatwas until this day of mine.

I say: He spoke truly, may Allah have mercy on him. For this verse, by the generality of its wording, encompasses the fatwa of one who issues a ruling contrary to what is in the Book of Allah or in the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), as frequently occurs from those who prefer opinion and put it ahead of transmitted reports, or from the ignorant who lack knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah, such as the mere followers (muqallidah). Indeed they are deserving that they be prevented from their fatwas and restrained from their ignorance, for they issued rulings without knowledge from Allah, without guidance and without an illuminating Book, so they went astray and led others astray. They and whoever seeks their fatwa are as the poet said:

Like a blind she-camel whose reins are led by a blind man over the crooked, wayward road.

Al-Tabarani related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: A man may say: "Allah has commanded such-and-such, or forbidden such-and-such," and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to him: "You have lied." Or he says: "Allah has forbidden such-and-such, or made lawful such-and-such," and Allah says to him: "You have lied."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade what We have related to you﴾, that he said: it is in Surah al-An'am.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah something similar, and said: where He says: ﴿And to those who were Jews﴾ up to His saying ﴿and indeed We are truthful﴾ [al-An'am: 146].

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 112–119:

His saying: ﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town﴾. We have already mentioned that "daraba" (presented/struck) is here construed with the meaning of "ja'ala" (made), so that "qaryatan" (a town) is the first object and "mathalan" (a parable) the second. "Qaryatan" was placed later so that no separation would occur between it and its attributes. We also mentioned that it is permissible for "daraba" to be in its original sense, not construed with another meaning, in which case "mathalan" is its first object and "qaryatan" is an apposition (badal) to it.

The exegetes differ as to whether the intended town is a specific town, or whether it is an unspecified town, meaning every people whom Allah blessed and whom blessing made arrogant. The majority adopted the first view and stated explicitly that it is Makkah, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against them, saying: "O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Yusuf," so they were afflicted with famine until they ate the bones.

The second view is more preponderant, because the indefiniteness of "qaryatin" indicates it. Makkah enters this general (badali) scope primarily; moreover the threat is more forceful and the parable more complete, and other than Makkah is similar to it. And on the assumption that Makkah is intended, the parable still contains a warning to others from a fate like its fate. Then He described the town as ﴿being secure﴾, not fearful, tranquil, not disturbed, meaning its people did not fear and were not disturbed. ﴿Its provision came to it﴾, meaning what its people obtain sustenance by, abundantly, from every place from which what is in them is brought to it. ﴿But it denied the favours of Allah﴾, meaning its people denied them. "An'um" is the plural of "ni'mah," like "ashudd" is the plural of "shiddah"; it was also said to be the plural of "nu'mā," like "bu'sā" and "ab'us." This denial on their part is their disbelief in Allah, glorified is He, and their denial of His messengers. ﴿So Allah made it taste﴾, meaning He made its people taste ﴿the garment of hunger and fear﴾. This was called a "garment" because the signs of emaciation, paleness of complexion and bad condition that appear upon them are like a garment; so its name was borrowed for it, and the "tasting" (idhaqa) was attributed to it. Its origin is tasting with the mouth; then it was borrowed for general experiencing, with the indication of severity of affliction, because it combines two perceptions: the perception of touch and of taste.

It is related that Ibn al-Rawandi the heretic said to Ibn al-A'rabi, the imam of language and literature: "Can a garment be tasted?" Ibn al-A'rabi said to him: "No harm, you ape! Suppose Muhammad was not a prophet, was he not an Arab?" It was as if he were criticising the verse on the basis that the appropriate phrasing would be "then Allah clothed them with the garment of hunger," or "then Allah made them taste the taste of hunger."

Ibn al-A'rabi refuted him.

The scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamaʾ al-bayan) have answered that this is an instance of "tajrid" (the stripped metaphor). That is, he borrowed "garment" for what covers a person of certain calamities, such as hunger and fear, because it envelops him as a garment envelops the wearer; then the attribute was mentioned suitable to the borrowed-for thing, which is hunger and fear, because the use of "tasting" for experiencing hunger and fear was, in their usage, treated as literal; they say "so-and-so tasted misery and harm," and another made him taste it. So the metaphor was stripped (mujarradah), whereas had he said "fa-kasahā" (then He clothed it), it would have been "murashshahah" (the metaphor being nurtured by a supporting term).

It was said: although the nurturing of a metaphor is commendable in terms of intensification, stripping has a preference in that the side of the borrowed-for thing is observed, so the speech becomes clearer. It was also said that the origin of tasting is with the mouth, then it may be borrowed and placed in the position of knowing and testing, and from this is the poet's saying:

Whoever tastes the world, I have tasted it, and both its sweetness and its torment have been driven to us.

Ḥafṣ ibn Ghiyath, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu ʿAmr, as narrated from him by ʿAbd al-Warith, read "al-khawfa" with the accusative, coordinating it with "libas" (garment). The rest read it with the nominative (ḍamma), coordinating it with "al-juʿ" (hunger).

Al-Farra' said: All the attributes were applied to the town except His saying "yaṣnaʿūn" (they used to do), as an indication that the intended meaning in reality is its people.

﴿And there had certainly come to them﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿a messenger from among them﴾, from their own kind, whom they know and whose lineage they know. So he commanded them with what benefits them and forbade them from what harms them, but they denied him in what he brought. ﴿Then the punishment seized them﴾, the punishment descending upon them from Allah, glorified is He, while they were, in the state of being seized by the punishment, wrongdoers to themselves by casting themselves into everlasting punishment, and to others by harming them and barring them from the way of Allah. This statement is part of the completion of the parable presented.

It was also said that the punishment here is the hunger that afflicted them, and it was said it is the killing on the day of Badr.

Then, when Allah, glorified is He, admonished them with what He mentioned of the state of the people of the aforementioned town, He commanded them to eat of what Allah had provided them from the spoils and the like. He used "fa" (then) to signal that this is consequent upon abandoning disbelief.

The meaning: since you have believed and abandoned disbelief, then eat the lawful good, which is the spoils, and leave the wicked things, which are carrion and blood. ﴿And be grateful for the favour of Allah﴾, the favour with which He has blessed you, and recognise its due ﴿if it is Him you worship﴾, and you do not worship other than Him; or, if your claim is true that by worshipping the gods you intend the worship of Allah, the Exalted. It was also said that the "fa" in "fa-kulū" attaches to the command to give thanks, and it was attached to the command to eat because eating is a means to gratitude.

﴿He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾. Glorified is He repeated the mention of these prohibitions in al-Baqarah, al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, and in this surah, to cut off excuses and remove doubt. Then He mentioned the concession regarding partaking of any of what was mentioned, saying: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The discussion of all that is mentioned here has been covered in full previously.

Then He refuted the way of the disbelievers in adding to these prohibitions, such as the baḥīrah and sā'ibah, and in reducing from them, such as declaring carrion and blood lawful. So He said: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely﴾. Al-Kisa'i and al-Zajjaj said: "ma" here is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah), and "al-kadhiba" (the lie) is in the accusative governed by "lā taqūlū" (do not say), meaning: do not say the lie for the sake of the description your tongues utter, and its meaning is: do not prohibit or permit on account of a statement your tongues utter without any proof. It is permissible for "ma" to be a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), with "al-kadhiba" in the accusative governed by "taṣifu" (describes), meaning: do not say of that which your tongues describe, the lie concerning it, ﴿"This is lawful, and this is unlawful"﴾; the word "fīhi" (concerning it) is omitted because it is known. Thus "This is lawful and this is unlawful" is an apposition (badal) to "al-kadhiba." It is also permissible that there is an ellipsis in the speech, with an implied "say," meaning: do not say of what your tongues describe, so that it says "This is lawful and this is unlawful," or [it is] saying "This is lawful and this is unlawful." It is also permissible that "al-kadhiba" be in the accusative governed by "taṣifu" and "ma" be verbal-noun, meaning: do not say "This is lawful and this is unlawful" for the description your tongues make of the lie.

It was read "al-kudhubu" (with ḍamma on the kāf, dhāl and bāʾ), as an attribute of "al-alsina" (the tongues). al-Hasan read it with fatḥa on the kāf and kasra on the dhāl and bāʾ, as an attribute of "mā."

It was also said it is in apposition (badal) to "mā," meaning: do not say the lie, which your tongues describe, "This is lawful and this is unlawful." The lām in ﴿so that you may fabricate against Allah the lie﴾ is the lām of consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah), not the lām of purpose, meaning: that will be followed by your fabrication against Allah of the lie through permitting and forbidding, and the ascription of that to Him without it being from Him. ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah the lie﴾, whatever fabrication it is, ﴿will not succeed﴾ in any kind of success, which is attaining the sought-after object.

The nominative of "matāʿun qalīlun" (a little enjoyment) is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject. al-Zajjaj said: That is, their enjoyment is a little enjoyment; or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: for them is a little enjoyment. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, to which they will be returned in the Hereafter.

Then He singled out the prohibitions of the Jews for mention, saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade﴾, meaning We forbade it upon them specifically and not upon others, ﴿what We have related to you﴾ by His saying: ﴿We forbade every animal with claws, and of the cattle and sheep We forbade them their fat﴾ [al-An'am: 146], and so on. "Min qablu" (previously) is connected either to "qaṣaṣnā" (We related) or to "ḥarramnā" (We forbade). ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by that prohibition, rather We recompensed them for their transgression, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, in that they committed the causes of that, so We forbade them those things as a punishment for them.

Then Glorified is He explained that fabricating against Allah and opposing His command does not prevent them from repentance and attaining forgiveness, so He said: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who do evil in ignorance﴾, meaning while they are clothed in ignorance. The explanation of this verse has been given before in Surah al-Nisa'. ﴿Then repent after that﴾, meaning after their doing evil. This contains emphasis, since "thumma" (then) already indicates sequence, so He reinforced it by adding the mention of sequence. ﴿And reform their deeds, which had corruption in them through the evil they did﴾. Then He repeated that for emphasis and affirmation, saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord, after it﴾, meaning after repentance, ﴿is surely Forgiving and Merciful﴾, abundantly forgiving, of vast mercy.

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town﴾, that he said: it means Makkah.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿAṭiyyah regarding the verse the like of it, and added: Do you not see that He said: ﴿And there had certainly come to them a messenger from among them, but they denied him﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir related something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Shihab, who said: The town of which Allah said ﴿was secure and tranquil﴾ is Yathrib.

I say: I do not know what proof led him to this specification, nor what indication stood for him on that. And when did the abode of the Hijrah and the dwelling of the Ansar disbelieve in the favours of Allah, and at what time did Allah make it taste the garment of hunger and fear? It is the one that expels its impurity as the furnace expels the impurity of iron, as this is authentically established from the truthful and the believed one (ﷺ).

It is also authentically established from him that he said: "And Madinah is better for them, if they only knew."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid regarding His saying: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely﴾, the verse, that he said: it refers to the baḥīrah and the sā'ibah.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Nadrah, who said: I read this verse in Surah al-Nahl: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely: "This is lawful, and this is unlawful"﴾, to the end of the verse, and I have not ceased to fear issuing fatwas until this day of mine.

I say: He spoke truly, may Allah have mercy on him. For this verse, by the generality of its wording, encompasses the fatwa of one who issues a ruling contrary to what is in the Book of Allah or in the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), as frequently occurs from those who prefer opinion and put it ahead of transmitted reports, or from the ignorant who lack knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah, such as the mere followers (muqallidah). Indeed they are deserving that they be prevented from their fatwas and restrained from their ignorance, for they issued rulings without knowledge from Allah, without guidance and without an illuminating Book, so they went astray and led others astray. They and whoever seeks their fatwa are as the poet said:

Like a blind she-camel whose reins are led by a blind man over the crooked, wayward road.

Al-Tabarani related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: A man may say: "Allah has commanded such-and-such, or forbidden such-and-such," and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will say to him: "You have lied." Or he says: "Allah has forbidden such-and-such, or made lawful such-and-such," and Allah says to him: "You have lied."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade what We have related to you﴾, that he said: it is in Surah al-An'am.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah something similar, and said: where He says: ﴿And to those who were Jews﴾ up to His saying ﴿and indeed We are truthful﴾ [al-An'am: 146].

When Allah, glorified is He, finished refuting the doubts of the polytheists and invalidating their accusations, and since Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was among the monotheists and was the exemplar of many of the prophets, Allah mentioned him at the end of this surah, saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah﴾. Ibn al-A'rabi said: a learned man is called an ummah, and the ummah is the man who gathers all goodness.

Al-Wahidi said: most of the people of tafsir (exegesis) said it means a teacher of goodness. On this view, the meaning of Ibrahim being an ummah is that he was a teacher of goodness, or one who combined the qualities of goodness, or one who knew the laws (shara'i') that Allah had taught him. It was also said that "ummah" means "one who is followed" (ma'mum), i.e., people take guidance from him to gain goodness, as Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader (imam) for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. "Qanit" means obedient, and the meanings of qunut have already been explained in al-Baqarah.

"Hanif" means one who turns away from false religions toward the religion of truth, and its explanation has already been given in al-An'am. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ with Allah, as the disbelievers of Quraysh claimed, that he was upon their false religion.

﴿Grateful for His favours﴾ which Allah bestowed upon him, even if they were few, as the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah) indicates. He is grateful for what was abundant of them, all the more so. ﴿He chose him﴾, i.e., selected him for prophethood and singled him out for it. ﴿And guided him to a straight path﴾, which is the religion of Islam and the religion of truth.

﴿And We gave him in this world a good (hasanah)﴾, i.e., a good quality or a good condition. It was said that it is a righteous offspring, and it was said that it is a good reputation, and it was said that it is prophethood, and it was said that it is the blessing upon him from us in the tashahhud (testimony recited in prayer), and it was said that it is that all the people of the religions take him as their ally. There is no obstacle to the view that what Allah gave him includes all of that and other qualities of goodness. ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous﴾, in accordance with his supplication to his Lord when he said: ﴿And join me with the righteous. And grant me a tongue of honesty among the later generations. And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 83–85].

﴿Then We revealed to you﴾, O Muhammad, despite the height of your rank, the loftiness of your station, and your being the master of the children of Adam: ﴿to follow the religion of Ibrahim﴾. The root meaning of millah (religion, creed) is a name for what Allah legislated for His servants through the tongue of one of His prophets. It was also said that what is intended here is the Prophet's ﷺ following the religion of Ibrahim in tawhid and calling to it.

Ibn Jarir said: in disavowing idols and adopting the religion of Islam. It was said: in the rites of Hajj. It was said: in the fundamentals, not the branches. It was said: in all of his law except what was abrogated (naskh) of it. This last is the apparent meaning.

The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow the prophets, despite being their master. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So by their guidance, follow [their] guidance﴾ [al-An'am]. The word ﴿hanifan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of Ibrahim. It is permissible for the hal to be from him because the religion is like a part of him. It has been established in the science of grammar (nahw) that a hal from a genitive noun (mudaf ilayh) is permissible if the governing noun (mudaf) requires action in the noun it governs, or if it is a part of it, or like a part of it. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ is a repetition of what preceded, for the purpose explained above.

﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾. I.e., the penalty of the Sabbath, which is transformation (maskh), was only imposed upon those who differed concerning it; or, the obligation of honouring the Sabbath and refraining from hunting on it was only imposed upon those who differed concerning it, not upon other nations.

The scholars differed concerning the manner of the disagreement that occurred among them regarding the Sabbath. One group said: Musa commanded them to observe Friday, specified it for them, and informed them of its virtue over other days, but they opposed him and said that the Sabbath was more excellent. So Allah said to him: "Leave them and what they chose for themselves."

It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, commanded them to honour one day of the week, and their ijtihad (independent reasoning) differed about it. The Jews specified Saturday because Allah finished creation on it, and the Christians specified Sunday because Allah began creation on it. So Allah bound each of them to what their ijtihad led them to, and He specified Friday for this Ummah without leaving them to their own reasoning, out of His grace and blessing.

The connection of this verse with what precedes is that the Jews used to claim that the Sabbath was among the laws of Ibrahim. So Allah, glorified is He, informed that He only prescribed the Sabbath for those who differed concerning it and did not prescribe it for Ibrahim or for anyone else. ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them﴾, i.e., between those who differed concerning it, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾. He will then recompense each one for it according to what he deserves, reward or punishment, just as He did with the transformation of one group of them and the deliverance of another.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to call his Ummah to Islam, saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾. The object is omitted for generality, since he was sent to all of mankind. The way of Allah is Islam, pursued ﴿with wisdom﴾, i.e., with a sound, firmly established statement. It was said that this refers to conclusive proofs that produce certainty. ﴿And good instruction (al-mawizah al-hasanah)﴾ is a statement containing good admonition that the listener finds pleasing, and which is itself good in view of the benefit the listener derives from it. It was said that this refers to persuasive, probable proofs that necessitate assent through accepted premises. It was said: there are no methods for calling except these two. However, the caller may, when facing a fierce opponent, need to use opposition, contradiction, and similar forms of disputation. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And argue with them in a way that is best﴾, i.e., by the method that is the best of the methods of argument. Allah, glorified is He, only commanded good argument because the caller is in the right, his aim is sound, while his opponent is in falsehood and his aim is corrupt. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾. When Allah, glorified is He, urged calling by the methods mentioned, He explained that guidance and rightness are not in the hand of the Prophet ﷺ, but rest with Allah, the Exalted. So He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing﴾, i.e., He is the One who knows who goes astray and who is guided. ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾, i.e., of those who see the truth and aim at it without obstinacy. He legislated the calling for you and commanded you to do it only to cut off excuses, complete the proof, and remove doubt, and nothing else is incumbent upon you.

Then, since calling entails obligating those who are called to return to the truth, and if they refuse they are fought, He commanded the caller to be just in punishment, saying: ﴿And if you punish﴾, i.e., if you wish to retaliate, ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, i.e., with the same as what was done to you, and do not exceed that.

Ibn Jarir said: this verse was revealed concerning one who has been wronged, that when he has the power, he should not take from his oppressor except the equivalent of his wrong, and not go beyond it to something else. This is correct, because although it has been said that the verse has a specific occasion of revelation, as will come, the consideration is the generality of its wording, and its generality conveys this meaning which he mentioned. Allah, glorified is He, called the first act, which is the act of the one who initiated evil, a "punishment," even though punishment is only the second act, the act of the one who repays, for the sake of mushakala (rhetorical correspondence). This is a known device found in many places in the Mighty Book.

Then Allah, glorified is He, urged forgiveness, saying: ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is better for the patient﴾, i.e., if you are patient and refrain from retaliating with the like, then patience is better for you than taking your right. The phrase "the patient" is placed in the position of the pronoun, as praise from Allah for them, that they are patient in the face of hardships.

The majority of scholars held that this verse is muhkam (not abrogated), because it concerns patience in refraining from retaliation and praise of the patient in general. It was said that it is mansukh (abrogated) by the verses of fighting, but there is no basis for that.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to be patient, saying: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except through Allah﴾, i.e., by His enabling and His making you firm. The exception here is "mufarragh" (an exception whose antecedent is not stated, and which takes the most general sense), meaning: your patience, accompanied by anything whatsoever, is not except through His enabling you. In this is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.

Then He forbade him from grief, saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, i.e., over the disbelievers in their turning away from you; or, do not grieve over the martyrs of Uhud, for they have arrived at the mercy of Allah. ﴿And do not be in distress over what they plot﴾. Ibn Kathir (?) — no. Rather: "Qara'a al-Jumhur" (the majority of readers) read it with a fatha on the dad, and Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: the two are the same, meaning the fathah and the kasrah.

Al-Farra' said: "al-dayq" with a fatha is what your chest cannot contain, while "al-diq" with a kasra is what is in something that is spacious, such as a house or a garment. Al-Akhfash said the same. This is an inverted expression (min al-kalam al-maqlub), because "dayq" is a description of a person, in which he is, not a thing in which the person is. It seems he intended describing the distress as being so great that it becomes like a thing encompassing the person from all sides. The meaning of ﴿from what they plot﴾ is: from their scheming against you concerning what will come in time.

Then He concluded this surah with a verse comprehensive of all the commands and prohibitions, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him﴾, i.e., who avoid sins in their various kinds, ﴿and those who are doers of good﴾ by performing acts of obedience and carrying out what they were commanded. It was said the meaning is: Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him by not exceeding in punishment, and those who are doers of good in the essence of retaliation. Thus the first refers to His saying ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, and the second refers to His saying ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is better for the patient﴾. It was also said that ﴿those who fear Him﴾ refers to magnifying the command of Allah, and ﴿those who are doers of good﴾ refers to compassion toward the servants of Allah, the Exalted.

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about the ummah, what is it? He said: "The one who teaches people goodness." They said: "Then what is the qanit?" He said: "The one who obeys Allah and His Messenger."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah, qanitan to Allah﴾, he said: he was upon Islam, and there was no one in his time among his people upon Islam except him, so for that reason Allah said: ﴿was an ummah, qanitan to Allah﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning His saying "kana ummatan": "an imam in goodness," and "qanitan": "obedient."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas ibn Malik who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No servant for whom an ummah bears witness will fail to have Allah accept their testimony." And "ummah" means a man or more, and Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah﴾, and "ummah" means a man or more.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Amr: "Jibril led Ibrahim in the Dhuhr and 'Asr prayers at 'Arafat, then he stood until the sun set, then he pushed on with him. Then he prayed Maghrib and 'Isha' at Jam', then he prayed Fajr with him as quickly as any one of you Muslims prays. Then he stood with him until, when it was as slow as any Muslim's prayer is slow, he pushed on with him. Then he threw the jamrah, then he slaughtered, then he shaved, then he took him to the House and circumambulated with him." Then Allah said to His Prophet: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Ibrahim, hanifan﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾, he said: "They intended Friday, but they took Saturday in its place."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of al-Suddi from Abu Malik and Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the verse, he said: "By their making it lawful for themselves. Musa saw a man carrying wood on the Sabbath, so he struck his neck."

In the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We are the last, but the first on the Day of Resurrection. Except that they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. Then this is their day which was obligatory upon them, meaning Friday. They differed about it, so Allah guided us to it. So people are followers of us in it: the Jews tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow."

Muslim and others narrated a similar hadith from Hudhayfah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 120–128 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best﴾, that he said: "Turn away from their harm to you."

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it ḥasan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Khuzaymah in al-Fawa'id, Ibn Ḥibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "When the Day of Uhud came, sixty-four men from the Ansar were struck down, and six from the Muhajirun, among them Hamzah, and they mutilated them. The Ansar said: 'If we ever gain the upper hand over them on a day like this, we will surely exceed them in punishment.' Then, when the Day of the Conquest of Makkah came, Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished. But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'We will be patient and will not punish. Refrain from the people, except for four.'"

Ibn Sa'd, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifah, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) "stood over Hamzah where he had been martyred, and he looked at a sight that he had never seen anything more painful to his heart than it. He looked at him, mutilated, and said: 'May Allah have mercy upon you, for, as far as I know, you were one who upheld the ties of kinship and was constant in doing good. Were it not for the grief of those after you over you, it would have pleased me to leave you until Allah raises you up from various beasts and birds. By Allah, I will mutilate seventy of them in your place.' Then Jibril descended while the Prophet (ﷺ) was standing, with the final verses of Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And if you punish, then punish...﴾ to the end of the verse. So the Prophet (ﷺ) made expiation for his oath, refrained from what he had intended, and was patient."

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿And if you punish...﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "This was when Allah commanded His Prophet to fight those who fought him. Then Surat Bara'ah was revealed, and [the verse about] the expiry of the sacred months. So this verse is abrogated (mansukh)."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾, that he said: "They feared Him regarding what was forbidden to them, and they did good regarding what was obligatory upon them."

When Allah, glorified is He, finished refuting the doubts of the polytheists and invalidating their accusations, and since Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was among the monotheists and was the exemplar of many of the prophets, Allah mentioned him at the end of this surah, saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah﴾. Ibn al-A'rabi said: a learned man is called an ummah, and the ummah is the man who gathers all goodness.

Al-Wahidi said: most of the people of tafsir (exegesis) said it means a teacher of goodness. On this view, the meaning of Ibrahim being an ummah is that he was a teacher of goodness, or one who combined the qualities of goodness, or one who knew the laws (shara'i') that Allah had taught him. It was also said that "ummah" means "one who is followed" (ma'mum), i.e., people take guidance from him to gain goodness, as Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader (imam) for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. "Qanit" means obedient, and the meanings of qunut have already been explained in al-Baqarah.

"Hanif" means one who turns away from false religions toward the religion of truth, and its explanation has already been given in al-An'am. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ with Allah, as the disbelievers of Quraysh claimed, that he was upon their false religion.

﴿Grateful for His favours﴾ which Allah bestowed upon him, even if they were few, as the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah) indicates. He is grateful for what was abundant of them, all the more so. ﴿He chose him﴾, i.e., selected him for prophethood and singled him out for it. ﴿And guided him to a straight path﴾, which is the religion of Islam and the religion of truth.

﴿And We gave him in this world a good (hasanah)﴾, i.e., a good quality or a good condition. It was said that it is a righteous offspring, and it was said that it is a good reputation, and it was said that it is prophethood, and it was said that it is the blessing upon him from us in the tashahhud (testimony recited in prayer), and it was said that it is that all the people of the religions take him as their ally. There is no obstacle to the view that what Allah gave him includes all of that and other qualities of goodness. ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous﴾, in accordance with his supplication to his Lord when he said: ﴿And join me with the righteous. And grant me a tongue of honesty among the later generations. And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 83–85].

﴿Then We revealed to you﴾, O Muhammad, despite the height of your rank, the loftiness of your station, and your being the master of the children of Adam: ﴿to follow the religion of Ibrahim﴾. The root meaning of millah (religion, creed) is a name for what Allah legislated for His servants through the tongue of one of His prophets. It was also said that what is intended here is the Prophet's ﷺ following the religion of Ibrahim in tawhid and calling to it.

Ibn Jarir said: in disavowing idols and adopting the religion of Islam. It was said: in the rites of Hajj. It was said: in the fundamentals, not the branches. It was said: in all of his law except what was abrogated (naskh) of it. This last is the apparent meaning.

The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow the prophets, despite being their master. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So by their guidance, follow [their] guidance﴾ [al-An'am]. The word ﴿hanifan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of Ibrahim. It is permissible for the hal to be from him because the religion is like a part of him. It has been established in the science of grammar (nahw) that a hal from a genitive noun (mudaf ilayh) is permissible if the governing noun (mudaf) requires action in the noun it governs, or if it is a part of it, or like a part of it. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ is a repetition of what preceded, for the purpose explained above.

﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾. I.e., the penalty of the Sabbath, which is transformation (maskh), was only imposed upon those who differed concerning it; or, the obligation of honouring the Sabbath and refraining from hunting on it was only imposed upon those who differed concerning it, not upon other nations.

The scholars differed concerning the manner of the disagreement that occurred among them regarding the Sabbath. One group said: Musa commanded them to observe Friday, specified it for them, and informed them of its virtue over other days, but they opposed him and said that the Sabbath was more excellent. So Allah said to him: "Leave them and what they chose for themselves."

It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, commanded them to honour one day of the week, and their ijtihad (independent reasoning) differed about it. The Jews specified Saturday because Allah finished creation on it, and the Christians specified Sunday because Allah began creation on it. So Allah bound each of them to what their ijtihad led them to, and He specified Friday for this Ummah without leaving them to their own reasoning, out of His grace and blessing.

The connection of this verse with what precedes is that the Jews used to claim that the Sabbath was among the laws of Ibrahim. So Allah, glorified is He, informed that He only prescribed the Sabbath for those who differed concerning it and did not prescribe it for Ibrahim or for anyone else. ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them﴾, i.e., between those who differed concerning it, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾. He will then recompense each one for it according to what he deserves, reward or punishment, just as He did with the transformation of one group of them and the deliverance of another.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to call his Ummah to Islam, saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾. The object is omitted for generality, since he was sent to all of mankind. The way of Allah is Islam, pursued ﴿with wisdom﴾, i.e., with a sound, firmly established statement. It was said that this refers to conclusive proofs that produce certainty. ﴿And good instruction (al-mawizah al-hasanah)﴾ is a statement containing good admonition that the listener finds pleasing, and which is itself good in view of the benefit the listener derives from it. It was said that this refers to persuasive, probable proofs that necessitate assent through accepted premises. It was said: there are no methods for calling except these two. However, the caller may, when facing a fierce opponent, need to use opposition, contradiction, and similar forms of disputation. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And argue with them in a way that is best﴾, i.e., by the method that is the best of the methods of argument. Allah, glorified is He, only commanded good argument because the caller is in the right, his aim is sound, while his opponent is in falsehood and his aim is corrupt. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾. When Allah, glorified is He, urged calling by the methods mentioned, He explained that guidance and rightness are not in the hand of the Prophet ﷺ, but rest with Allah, the Exalted. So He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing﴾, i.e., He is the One who knows who goes astray and who is guided. ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾, i.e., of those who see the truth and aim at it without obstinacy. He legislated the calling for you and commanded you to do it only to cut off excuses, complete the proof, and remove doubt, and nothing else is incumbent upon you.

Then, since calling entails obligating those who are called to return to the truth, and if they refuse they are fought, He commanded the caller to be just in punishment, saying: ﴿And if you punish﴾, i.e., if you wish to retaliate, ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, i.e., with the same as what was done to you, and do not exceed that.

Ibn Jarir said: this verse was revealed concerning one who has been wronged, that when he has the power, he should not take from his oppressor except the equivalent of his wrong, and not go beyond it to something else. This is correct, because although it has been said that the verse has a specific occasion of revelation, as will come, the consideration is the generality of its wording, and its generality conveys this meaning which he mentioned. Allah, glorified is He, called the first act, which is the act of the one who initiated evil, a "punishment," even though punishment is only the second act, the act of the one who repays, for the sake of mushakala (rhetorical correspondence). This is a known device found in many places in the Mighty Book.

Then Allah, glorified is He, urged forgiveness, saying: ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is better for the patient﴾, i.e., if you are patient and refrain from retaliating with the like, then patience is better for you than taking your right. The phrase "the patient" is placed in the position of the pronoun, as praise from Allah for them, that they are patient in the face of hardships.

The majority of scholars held that this verse is muhkam (not abrogated), because it concerns patience in refraining from retaliation and praise of the patient in general. It was said that it is mansukh (abrogated) by the verses of fighting, but there is no basis for that.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to be patient, saying: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except through Allah﴾, i.e., by His enabling and His making you firm. The exception here is "mufarragh" (an exception whose antecedent is not stated, and which takes the most general sense), meaning: your patience, accompanied by anything whatsoever, is not except through His enabling you. In this is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.

Then He forbade him from grief, saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, i.e., over the disbelievers in their turning away from you; or, do not grieve over the martyrs of Uhud, for they have arrived at the mercy of Allah. ﴿And do not be in distress over what they plot﴾. Ibn Kathir (?) — no. Rather: "Qara'a al-Jumhur" (the majority of readers) read it with a fatha on the dad, and Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: the two are the same, meaning the fathah and the kasrah.

Al-Farra' said: "al-dayq" with a fatha is what your chest cannot contain, while "al-diq" with a kasra is what is in something that is spacious, such as a house or a garment. Al-Akhfash said the same. This is an inverted expression (min al-kalam al-maqlub), because "dayq" is a description of a person, in which he is, not a thing in which the person is. It seems he intended describing the distress as being so great that it becomes like a thing encompassing the person from all sides. The meaning of ﴿from what they plot﴾ is: from their scheming against you concerning what will come in time.

Then He concluded this surah with a verse comprehensive of all the commands and prohibitions, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him﴾, i.e., who avoid sins in their various kinds, ﴿and those who are doers of good﴾ by performing acts of obedience and carrying out what they were commanded. It was said the meaning is: Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him by not exceeding in punishment, and those who are doers of good in the essence of retaliation. Thus the first refers to His saying ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, and the second refers to His saying ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is better for the patient﴾. It was also said that ﴿those who fear Him﴾ refers to magnifying the command of Allah, and ﴿those who are doers of good﴾ refers to compassion toward the servants of Allah, the Exalted.

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about the ummah, what is it? He said: "The one who teaches people goodness." They said: "Then what is the qanit?" He said: "The one who obeys Allah and His Messenger."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah, qanitan to Allah﴾, he said: he was upon Islam, and there was no one in his time among his people upon Islam except him, so for that reason Allah said: ﴿was an ummah, qanitan to Allah﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning His saying "kana ummatan": "an imam in goodness," and "qanitan": "obedient."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas ibn Malik who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No servant for whom an ummah bears witness will fail to have Allah accept their testimony." And "ummah" means a man or more, and Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah﴾, and "ummah" means a man or more.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Amr: "Jibril led Ibrahim in the Dhuhr and 'Asr prayers at 'Arafat, then he stood until the sun set, then he pushed on with him. Then he prayed Maghrib and 'Isha' at Jam', then he prayed Fajr with him as quickly as any one of you Muslims prays. Then he stood with him until, when it was as slow as any Muslim's prayer is slow, he pushed on with him. Then he threw the jamrah, then he slaughtered, then he shaved, then he took him to the House and circumambulated with him." Then Allah said to His Prophet: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Ibrahim, hanifan﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾, he said: "They intended Friday, but they took Saturday in its place."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of al-Suddi from Abu Malik and Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the verse, he said: "By their making it lawful for themselves. Musa saw a man carrying wood on the Sabbath, so he struck his neck."

In the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We are the last, but the first on the Day of Resurrection. Except that they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. Then this is their day which was obligatory upon them, meaning Friday. They differed about it, so Allah guided us to it. So people are followers of us in it: the Jews tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow."

Muslim and others narrated a similar hadith from Hudhayfah.

He will then recompense each one for it according to what he deserves, reward or punishment, just as He did with the transformation of one group of them and the deliverance of another.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to call his Ummah to Islam, saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾. The object is omitted for generality, since he was sent to all of mankind. The way of Allah is Islam, pursued ﴿with wisdom﴾, i.e., with a sound, firmly established statement. It was said that this refers to conclusive proofs that produce certainty. ﴿And good instruction (al-mawizah al-hasanah)﴾ is a statement containing good admonition that the listener finds pleasing, and which is itself good in view of the benefit the listener derives from it. It was said that this refers to persuasive, probable proofs that necessitate assent through accepted premises. It was said: there are no methods for calling except these two. However, the caller may, when facing a fierce opponent, need to use opposition, contradiction, and similar forms of disputation. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And argue with them in a way that is best﴾, i.e., by the method that is the best of the methods of argument. Allah, glorified is He, only commanded good argument because the caller is in the right, his aim is sound, while his opponent is in falsehood and his aim is corrupt. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾. When Allah, glorified is He, urged calling by the methods mentioned, He explained that guidance and rightness are not in the hand of the Prophet ﷺ, but rest with Allah, the Exalted. So He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing﴾, i.e., He is the One who knows who goes astray and who is guided. ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾, i.e., of those who see the truth and aim at it without obstinacy. He legislated the calling for you and commanded you to do it only to cut off excuses, complete the proof, and remove doubt, and nothing else is incumbent upon you.

Then, since calling entails obligating those who are called to return to the truth, and if they refuse they are fought, He commanded the caller to be just in punishment, saying: ﴿And if you punish﴾, i.e., if you wish to retaliate, ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, i.e., with the same as what was done to you, and do not exceed that.

Ibn Jarir said: this verse was revealed concerning one who has been wronged, that when he has the power, he should not take from his oppressor except the equivalent of his wrong, and not go beyond it to something else. This is correct, because although it has been said that the verse has a specific occasion of revelation, as will come, the consideration is the generality of its wording, and its generality conveys this meaning which he mentioned. Allah, glorified is He, called the first act, which is the act of the one who initiated evil, a "punishment," even though punishment is only the second act, the act of the one who repays, for the sake of mushakala (rhetorical correspondence). This is a known device found in many places in the Mighty Book.

Then Allah, glorified is He, urged forgiveness, saying: ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is better for the patient﴾, i.e., if you are patient and refrain from retaliating with the like, then patience is better for you than taking your right. The phrase "the patient" is placed in the position of the pronoun, as praise from Allah for them, that they are patient in the face of hardships.

The majority of scholars held that this verse is muhkam (not abrogated), because it concerns patience in refraining from retaliation and praise of the patient in general. It was said that it is mansukh (abrogated) by the verses of fighting, but there is no basis for that.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to be patient, saying: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except through Allah﴾, i.e., by His enabling and His making you firm. The exception here is "mufarragh" (an exception whose antecedent is not stated, and which takes the most general sense), meaning: your patience, accompanied by anything whatsoever, is not except through His enabling you. In this is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.

Then He forbade him from grief, saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, i.e., over the disbelievers in their turning away from you; or, do not grieve over the martyrs of Uhud, for they have arrived at the mercy of Allah. ﴿And do not be in distress over what they plot﴾. Ibn Kathir (?) — no. Rather: "Qara'a al-Jumhur" (the majority of readers) read it with a fatha on the dad, and Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: the two are the same, meaning the fathah and the kasrah.

Al-Farra' said: "al-dayq" with a fatha is what your chest cannot contain, while "al-diq" with a kasra is what is in something that is spacious, such as a house or a garment. Al-Akhfash said the same. This is an inverted expression (min al-kalam al-maqlub), because "dayq" is a description of a person, in which he is, not a thing in which the person is. It seems he intended describing the distress as being so great that it becomes like a thing encompassing the person from all sides. The meaning of ﴿from what they plot﴾ is: from their scheming against you concerning what will come in time.

Then He concluded this surah with a verse comprehensive of all the commands and prohibitions, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him﴾, i.e., who avoid sins in their various kinds, ﴿and those who are doers of good﴾ by performing acts of obedience and carrying out what they were commanded. It was said the meaning is: Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him by not exceeding in punishment, and those who are doers of good in the essence of retaliation. Thus the first refers to His saying ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, and the second refers to His saying ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is better for the patient﴾. It was also said that ﴿those who fear Him﴾ refers to magnifying the command of Allah, and ﴿those who are doers of good﴾ refers to compassion toward the servants of Allah, the Exalted.

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about the ummah, what is it? He said: "The one who teaches people goodness." They said: "Then what is the qanit?" He said: "The one who obeys Allah and His Messenger."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah, qanitan to Allah﴾, he said: he was upon Islam, and there was no one in his time among his people upon Islam except him, so for that reason Allah said: ﴿was an ummah, qanitan to Allah﴾.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning His saying "kana ummatan": "an imam in goodness," and "qanitan": "obedient."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas ibn Malik who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No servant for whom an ummah bears witness will fail to have Allah accept their testimony." And "ummah" means a man or more, and Allah says: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah﴾, and "ummah" means a man or more.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Amr: "Jibril led Ibrahim in the Dhuhr and 'Asr prayers at 'Arafat, then he stood until the sun set, then he pushed on with him. Then he prayed Maghrib and 'Isha' at Jam', then he prayed Fajr with him as quickly as any one of you Muslims prays. Then he stood with him until, when it was as slow as any Muslim's prayer is slow, he pushed on with him. Then he threw the jamrah, then he slaughtered, then he shaved, then he took him to the House and circumambulated with him." Then Allah said to His Prophet: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Ibrahim, hanifan﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾, he said: "They intended Friday, but they took Saturday in its place."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the chain of al-Suddi from Abu Malik and Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the verse, he said: "By their making it lawful for themselves. Musa saw a man carrying wood on the Sabbath, so he struck his neck."

In the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We are the last, but the first on the Day of Resurrection. Except that they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. Then this is their day which was obligatory upon them, meaning Friday. They differed about it, so Allah guided us to it. So people are followers of us in it: the Jews tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow."

Muslim and others narrated a similar hadith from Hudhayfah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 16, verses 120–128 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And argue with them in the way that is best﴾, that he said: "Turn away from their harm to you."

al-Tirmidhi, who graded it ḥasan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Khuzaymah in al-Fawa'id, Ibn Ḥibban, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "When the Day of Uhud came, sixty-four men from the Ansar were struck down, and six from the Muhajirun, among them Hamzah, and they mutilated them. The Ansar said: 'If we ever gain the upper hand over them on a day like this, we will surely exceed them in punishment.' Then, when the Day of the Conquest of Makkah came, Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished. But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'We will be patient and will not punish. Refrain from the people, except for four.'"

Ibn Sa'd, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, Abu Nu'aym in al-Ma'rifah, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) "stood over Hamzah where he had been martyred, and he looked at a sight that he had never seen anything more painful to his heart than it. He looked at him, mutilated, and said: 'May Allah have mercy upon you, for, as far as I know, you were one who upheld the ties of kinship and was constant in doing good. Were it not for the grief of those after you over you, it would have pleased me to leave you until Allah raises you up from various beasts and birds. By Allah, I will mutilate seventy of them in your place.' Then Jibril descended while the Prophet (ﷺ) was standing, with the final verses of Surat al-Nahl: ﴿And if you punish, then punish...﴾ to the end of the verse. So the Prophet (ﷺ) made expiation for his oath, refrained from what he had intended, and was patient."

Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words ﴿And if you punish...﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "This was when Allah commanded His Prophet to fight those who fought him. Then Surat Bara'ah was revealed, and [the verse about] the expiry of the sacred months. So this verse is abrogated (mansukh)."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾, that he said: "They feared Him regarding what was forbidden to them, and they did good regarding what was obligatory upon them."

When Allah, glorified is He, finished refuting the doubts of the polytheists and invalidating their accusations, and since Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was among the monotheists and was the exemplar of many of the prophets, Allah mentioned him at the end of this surah, saying: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah﴾. Ibn al-A'rabi said: a learned man is called an ummah, and the ummah is the man who gathers all goodness.

Al-Wahidi said: most of the people of tafsir (exegesis) said it means a teacher of goodness. On this view, the meaning of Ibrahim being an ummah is that he was a teacher of goodness, or one who combined the qualities of goodness, or one who knew the laws (shara'i') that Allah had taught him. It was also said that "ummah" means "one who is followed" (ma'mum), i.e., people take guidance from him to gain goodness, as Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, I am making you a leader (imam) for the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124]. "Qanit" means obedient, and the meanings of qunut have already been explained in al-Baqarah.

"Hanif" means one who turns away from false religions toward the religion of truth, and its explanation has already been given in al-An'am. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ with Allah, as the disbelievers of Quraysh claimed, that he was upon their false religion.

﴿Grateful for His favours﴾ which Allah bestowed upon him, even if they were few, as the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah) indicates. He is grateful for what was abundant of them, all the more so. ﴿He chose him﴾, i.e., selected him for prophethood and singled him out for it. ﴿And guided him to a straight path﴾, which is the religion of Islam and the religion of truth.

﴿And We gave him in this world a good (hasanah)﴾, i.e., a good quality or a good condition. It was said that it is a righteous offspring, and it was said that it is a good reputation, and it was said that it is prophethood, and it was said that it is the blessing upon him from us in the tashahhud (testimony recited in prayer), and it was said that it is that all the people of the religions take him as their ally. There is no obstacle to the view that what Allah gave him includes all of that and other qualities of goodness. ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous﴾, in accordance with his supplication to his Lord when he said: ﴿And join me with the righteous. And grant me a tongue of honesty among the later generations. And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 83–85].

﴿Then We revealed to you﴾, O Muhammad, despite the height of your rank, the loftiness of your station, and your being the master of the children of Adam: ﴿to follow the religion of Ibrahim﴾. The root meaning of millah (religion, creed) is a name for what Allah legislated for His servants through the tongue of one of His prophets. It was also said that what is intended here is the Prophet's ﷺ following the religion of Ibrahim in tawhid and calling to it.

Ibn Jarir said: in disavowing idols and adopting the religion of Islam. It was said: in the rites of Hajj. It was said: in the fundamentals, not the branches. It was said: in all of his law except what was abrogated (naskh) of it. This last is the apparent meaning.

The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow the prophets, despite being their master. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So by their guidance, follow [their] guidance﴾ [al-An'am]. The word ﴿hanifan﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of Ibrahim. It is permissible for the hal to be from him because the religion is like a part of him. It has been established in the science of grammar (nahw) that a hal from a genitive noun (mudaf ilayh) is permissible if the governing noun (mudaf) requires action in the noun it governs, or if it is a part of it, or like a part of it. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ is a repetition of what preceded, for the purpose explained above.

﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾. I.e., the penalty of the Sabbath, which is transformation (maskh), was only imposed upon those who differed concerning it; or, the obligation of honouring the Sabbath and refraining from hunting on it was only imposed upon those who differed concerning it, not upon other nations.

The scholars differed concerning the manner of the disagreement that occurred among them regarding the Sabbath. One group said: Musa commanded them to observe Friday, specified it for them, and informed them of its virtue over other days, but they opposed him and said that the Sabbath was more excellent. So Allah said to him: "Leave them and what they chose for themselves."

It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, commanded them to honour one day of the week, and their ijtihad (independent reasoning) differed about it. The Jews specified Saturday because Allah finished creation on it, and the Christians specified Sunday because Allah began creation on it. So Allah bound each of them to what their ijtihad led them to, and He specified Friday for this Ummah without leaving them to their own reasoning, out of His grace and blessing.

The connection of this verse with what precedes is that the Jews used to claim that the Sabbath was among the laws of Ibrahim. So Allah, glorified is He, informed that He only prescribed the Sabbath for those who differed concerning it and did not prescribe it for Ibrahim or for anyone else. ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them﴾, i.e., between those who differed concerning it, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾. He will then recompense each one for it according to what he deserves, reward or punishment, just as He did with the transformation of one group of them and the deliverance of another.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to call his Ummah to Islam, saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾. The object is omitted for generality, since he was sent to all of mankind. The way of Allah is Islam, pursued ﴿with wisdom﴾, i.e., with a sound, firmly established statement. It was said that this refers to conclusive proofs that produce certainty. ﴿And good instruction (al-mawizah al-hasanah)﴾ is a statement containing good admonition that the listener finds pleasing, and which is itself good in view of the benefit the listener derives from it. It was said that this refers to persuasive, probable proofs that necessitate assent through accepted premises. It was said: there are no methods for calling except these two. However, the caller may, when facing a fierce opponent, need to use opposition, contradiction, and similar forms of disputation. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿And argue with them in a way that is best﴾, i.e., by the method that is the best of the methods of argument. Allah, glorified is He, only commanded good argument because the caller is in the right, his aim is sound, while his opponent is in falsehood and his aim is corrupt. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾. When Allah, glorified is He, urged calling by the methods mentioned, He explained that guidance and rightness are not in the hand of the Prophet ﷺ, but rest with Allah, the Exalted. So He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing﴾, i.e., He is the One who knows who goes astray and who is guided. ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾, i.e., of those who see the truth and aim at it without obstinacy. He legislated the calling for you and commanded you to do it only to cut off excuses, complete the proof, and remove doubt, and nothing else is incumbent upon you.

Then, since calling entails obligating those who are called to return to the truth, and if they refuse they are fought, He commanded the caller to be just in punishment, saying: ﴿And if you punish﴾, i.e., if you wish to retaliate, ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, i.e., with the same as what was done to you, and do not exceed that.

Ibn Jarir said: this verse was revealed concerning one who has been wronged, that when he has the power, he should not take from his oppressor except the equivalent of his wrong, and not go beyond it to something else. This is correct, because although it has been said that the verse has a specific occasion of revelation, as will come, the consideration is the generality of its wording, and its generality conveys this meaning which he mentioned. Allah, glorified is He, called the first act, which is the act of the one who initiated evil, a "punishment," even though punishment is only the second act, the act of the one who repays, for the sake of mushakala (rhetorical correspondence). This is a known device found in many places in the Mighty Book.

Then Allah, glorified is He, urged forgiveness, saying: ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is better for the patient﴾, i.e., if you are patient and refrain from retaliating with the like, then patience is better for you than taking your right. The phrase "the patient" is placed in the position of the pronoun, as praise from Allah for them, that they are patient in the face of hardships.

The majority of scholars held that this verse is muhkam (not abrogated), because it concerns patience in refraining from retaliation and praise of the patient in general. It was said that it is mansukh (abrogated) by the verses of fighting, but there is no basis for that.

Then Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to be patient, saying: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except through Allah﴾, i.e., by His enabling and His making you firm. The exception here is "mufarragh" (an exception whose antecedent is not stated, and which takes the most general sense), meaning: your patience, accompanied by anything whatsoever, is not except through His enabling you. In this is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.

Then He forbade him from grief, saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, i.e., over the disbelievers in their turning away from you; or, do not grieve over the martyrs of Uhud, for they have arrived at the mercy of Allah. ﴿And do not be in distress over what they plot﴾. Ibn Kathir (?) — no. Rather: "Qara'a al-Jumhur" (the majority of readers) read it with a fatha on the dad, and Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: the two are the same, meaning the fathah and the kasrah.

Al-Farra' said: "al-dayq" with a fatha is what your chest cannot contain, while "al-diq" with a kasra is what is in something that is spacious, such as a house or a garment. Al-Akhfash said the same. This is an inverted expression (min al-kalam al-maqlub), because "dayq" is a description of a person, in which he is, not a thing in which the person is. It seems he intended describing the distress as being so great that it becomes like a thing encompassing the person from all sides. The meaning of ﴿from what they plot﴾ is: from their scheming against you concerning what will come in time.

Then He concluded this surah with a verse comprehensive of all the commands and prohibitions, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him﴾, i.e., who avoid sins in their various kinds, ﴿and those who are doers of good﴾ by performing acts of obedience and carrying out what they were commanded. It was said the meaning is: Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him by not exceeding in punishment, and those who are doers of good in the essence of retaliation. Thus the first refers to His saying ﴿then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾, and the second refers to His saying ﴿But if you endure patiently, it is better for the patient﴾. It was also said that ﴿those who fear Him﴾ refers to magnifying the command of Allah, and ﴿those who are doers of good﴾ refers to compassion toward the servants of Allah, the Exalted.

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about the ummah, what is it? He said: "The one who teaches people goodness." They said: "Then what is the qanit?" He said: "The one who obeys Allah and His Messenger."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him concerning His saying "kana ummatan": "an imam in goodness," and "qanitan": "obedient."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Amr: "Jibril led Ibrahim in the Dhuhr and 'Asr prayers at 'Arafat, then he stood until the sun set, then he pushed on with him. Then he prayed Maghrib and 'Isha' at Jam', then he prayed Fajr with him as quickly as any one of you Muslims prays. Then he stood with him until, when it was as slow as any Muslim's prayer is slow, he pushed on with him. Then he threw the jamrah, then he slaughtered, then he shaved, then he took him to the House and circumambulated with him." Then Allah said to His Prophet: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Ibrahim, hanifan﴾.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it﴾, he said: "They intended Friday, but they took Saturday in its place."

In the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We are the last, but the first on the Day of Resurrection. Except that they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. Then this is their day which was obligatory upon them, meaning Friday. They differed about it, so Allah guided us to it. So people are followers of us in it: the Jews tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow."
